judgmentFull: The Lord discomfited Sisera and all his host. Barak pursued the chariots and army to Harosheth, and none of that host remained (Judges 4:15-16). Judges 5:20-21 describes the stars fighting and the river Kishon sweeping the enemy away. The fighting was real, but the power that made the pursuit victorious belonged to the Lord.

When Barak reached Jael's tent, she showed him Sisera dead (Judges 4:22). Both words had been fulfilled: the host was delivered, and the captain's death brought honour to a woman. Barak could not claim the part assigned to another, but neither was the deliverance withheld from Israel because of his earlier hesitation.

Hebrews 11:32-34 names Barak among the faithful and speaks of weakness made strong and armies put to flight. His history holds correction and faith together. He was corrected in the honour of the journey, yet obeyed the command to go; the Lord gave the victory, and Barak joined Deborah in praising him (Judges 5:1-2).

verses.text: 6And she sent and called Barak the son of Abinoam out of Kedesh–naphtali, and said unto him, Hath not the Lord God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor, and take with thee ten thousand men of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun? 7And I will draw unto thee to the river Kishon Sisera, the captain of Jabin’s army, with his chariots and his multitude; and I will deliver him into thine hand. 8And Barak said unto her, If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go. 9And she said, I will surely go with thee: notwithstanding the journey that thou takest shall not be for thine honour; for the Lord shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. And Deborah arose, and went with Barak to Kedesh.

entries.commentary: When Ehud was dead, the children of Israel again did evil, and the Most High sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor, whose captain was Sisera, which dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles. Sisera had nine hundred chariots of iron, and twenty years he mightily oppressed the children of Israel, and they cried unto the Most High.

Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, judged Israel at that time, dwelling under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in mount Ephraim, and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment. She calls Barak the son of Abinoam and gives him the commandment of the Most High: draw toward mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun, and I will draw unto thee Sisera with his chariots and his multitude to the river Kishon, and deliver him into thine hand. Barak answers, if thou wilt go with me, then I will go, but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go. Deborah agrees to go, but tells him the journey shall not be for his honour, for the Most High shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.

Barak calls Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh and goes up with ten thousand men at his feet, and Deborah goes up with him. Heber the Kenite, of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses, had severed himself from the Kenites and pitched his tent by Kedesh. Sisera gathers all nine hundred chariots of iron unto the river of Kishon, and Deborah says unto Barak, up, for this is the day in which the Lord hath delivered Sisera into thine hand; is not the Lord gone out before thee? The Most High discomfits Sisera and all his chariots and all his host with the edge of the sword before Barak; Sisera lights down off his chariot and flees away on his feet, and all his host falls upon the edge of the sword; there was not a man left.

Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber. Jael invites him in, covers him with a mantle, and gives him milk to drink when he asks for water. He tells her to stand in the door and say no man is there; then Jael takes a nail of the tent and a hammer in her hand, goes softly unto him as he sleeps fast and weary, and smites the nail into his temples and fastens it into the ground, and he dies. The word through Deborah stands: Sisera was sold into the hand of a woman. When Barak comes pursuing, Jael shows him Sisera lying dead with the nail in his temples. So God subdued that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel, and their hand prospered and prevailed until they had destroyed him. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant)

name: Jael
charge: Blessed above women in the tent: the nail, the hammer, and Sisera
summary: Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Heber the Kenite, whose house was at peace with Jabin. Jael covered him with a mantle, gave him milk, and when he slept drove a tent nail through his temples into the ground. Deborah's song puts the blessing on her twice over.
offense: Sisera fled from the defeated host to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. He chose that refuge because there was peace between Jabin and Heber's house (Judges 4:17). The agreement gave him confidence in the household, but it did not overturn the word already spoken: the Lord would sell Sisera into a woman's hand (Judges 4:9). Jael invited him in and covered him. When he asked for water, she gave him milk; he then asked her to stand at the door and deny that a man was within (Judges 4:18-20). The captain who had commanded nine hundred iron chariots now depended upon a woman to conceal him. His military strength had left him, and his expectation of safety rested on her cooperation. She took a tent nail and a hammer and killed him while he slept (Judges 4:21). The decisive act came inside a tent, not at the head of an army. Jael did not need Sisera's rank or equipment to fulfil the part that brought his oppression to an end. When Barak arrived in pursuit, she brought him in to see the fallen captain (Judges 4:22).
judgment: Deborah and Barak's song pronounces Jael blessed above women in the tent and recounts the milk, the nail, the hammer, and Sisera's fall (Judges 5:24-27). The blessing is attached to her deed in Israel's deliverance. The honour Deborah had foretold was not left unnamed; the song placed it upon Jael. Immediately before that blessing stands the curse upon Meroz for not coming to the help of the Lord against the mighty (Judges 5:23). One withheld help; the other acted. The placement weighs participation and refusal side by side. Being near the conflict was not the same as serving in the deliverance, and a convenient peace was not what decided the commendation. The song then turns to Sisera's mother, who waits for his return and supposes the delay is caused by the dividing of spoil (Judges 5:28-30). While his house imagines triumph, Jael has already ended his flight. The closing prayer asks that the Lord's enemies perish and that those who love him be as the sun going forth in strength (Judges 5:31). Jael's act belongs to that reversal: the terror of Israel is laid low, and the deliverance is celebrated.

And when he had turned in unto her into the tent, she covered him with a mantle. 19And he said unto her, Give me, I pray thee, a little water to drink; for I am thirsty. And she opened a bottle of milk, and gave him drink, and covered him. 20Again he said unto her, Stand in the door of the tent, and it shall be, when any man doth come and enquire of thee, and say, Is there any man here? that thou shalt say, No. 21Then Jael Heber’s wife took a nail of the tent, and took an hammer in her hand, and went softly unto him, and smote the nail into his temples, and fastened it into the ground: for he was fast asleep and weary. So he died. 22And, behold, as Barak pursued Sisera, Jael came out to meet him, and said unto him, Come, and I will shew thee the man whom thou seekest. And when he came into her tent, behold, Sisera lay dead, and the nail was in his temples.

Deborah and Barak sing praise to the Lord for the avenging of Israel, when the people willingly offered themselves. That is what the Most High wants from us: a willing heart in all that we do, in the keeping of the commandments, in the keeping of the feast days, and in the praise of him.
The Lord marching out of the field of Edom, the earth trembling, the heavens dropping, and the mountains melting from before the Lord God of Israel is future prophecy; this has not happened yet.

This passage is for all the closet feminists who think Deborah justifies women leading men. She did not lead men into any kind of war; she did not put on body armor and a breastplate, rise up on a horse, and lead the charge. She was the motivating factor to men that were shaky and fearful during that time, a mother in Israel, a guiding light. Verse 9 proves it: my heart is toward the governors of Israel, the leaders who offered themselves willingly among the people. Her heart was with the men who led; she was not ruling over them.

They that are delivered from the noise of archers in the places of drawing water shall rehearse the righteous acts of the Lord. That is where we are right now: in the places of drawing water, rehearsing the righteous acts of the Most High while the arrows are still being shot.

The song rehearses which tribes came out. Out of Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, and Zebulun came governors and they that handle the pen of the writer, and the princes of Issachar were with Deborah and Barak in the valley. For the divisions of Reuben there were great thoughts and great searchings of heart: they were second-guessing themselves. Gilead abode beyond Jordan, Dan remained in ships, and Asher continued on the seashore; the song is getting on the tribes that stayed home. Zebulun and Naphtali were a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field; those tribes are warriors.

The kings of Canaan fought by the waters of Megiddo and took no gain of money; they fought from heaven, and the stars in their courses fought against Sisera. Sisera is the general of the Canaanite host, not Syria; the river Kishon swept them away. The angel of the Lord said curse ye Meroz, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof, because they came not to the help of the Lord against the mighty. Sitting out the battle of the Lord brings a curse.

Blessed above women in the tent shall Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite be. Sisera asked water and she gave him milk; then she put her hand to the nail and her right hand to the workman's hammer, and where he bowed, there he fell down dead.

The mother of Sisera looked out at a window and cried, why is his chariot so long in coming? Her wise ladies answer her with imaginations of victory, that they are dividing the prey and the needlework spoil. She is looking for a son who is never coming home; he lay dead in Jael's tent. So let all thine enemies perish, O Lord: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might. And the land had rest forty years.

The prayer opens asking the Most High to keep not silence, hold not His peace, and be not still, for His enemies make a tumult and they that hate Him have lifted up the head. This shows that God has enemies, and the chapter is about to name God's enemies right now. They have taken crafty counsel against His people, against us the Israelites, and consulted against His hidden ones, saying come let us cut them off from being a nation, that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance. This is why today, nowadays, we are separated from our history, according to [Jeremiah 17:5](/bible/jeremiah/17#v5). -

Here the enemies of God begin to be named. They have consulted together with one consent and are confederate against the Most High: the tabernacles of Edom and the Ishmaelites, of Moab and the Hagarenes. Gebal, and Ammon, and Amalek, the Philistines with the inhabitants of Tyre; Assur also is joined with them, and they have holpen the children of Lot.

David asks the Most High to do unto these enemies as unto the Midianites, as to Sisera and as to Jabin at the brook of Kison, who perished at Endor and became as dung for the earth. He asks that their nobles be made like Oreb and like Zeeb, all their princes as Zebah and as Zalmunna, who said let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession.

He asks the Most High to make them like a wheel, as the stubble before the wind; as the fire burneth a wood and as the flame setteth the mountains on fire, so to persecute them with His tempest and make them afraid with His storm. The aim of the prayer is that their faces be filled with shame, that they may seek His name; that men may know that He whose name alone is JEHOVAH is the Most High over all the earth.

name: Gideon
charge: Throwing down the altar of Baal in his father's house; going against Midian with three hundred, as the Lord said
summary: Threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites, the least in his father's house was called a mighty man of valour. He cut down Baal's altar by night, sent home thirty-one thousand seven hundred men because the Lord said the army was too big, and broke the Midianites with pitchers, lamps and trumpets.
offense: Before the Lord sent a deliverer, he sent a prophet. Midian had destroyed Israel's increase until the people hid in dens and caves, but the prophet named the cause: the Lord had brought them out of Egypt, and they had not obeyed his voice (Judges 6:1-10). Gideon's question—where were the miracles their fathers had told them of?—stood within that answer (Judges 6:13). The Lord had not lost his power. Israel had departed from him. The angel called Gideon a mighty man of valour while he threshed wheat in a winepress to hide it. Gideon answered with his family's poverty and his own low place, but the Lord answered with his presence (Judges 6:11-16). First Corinthians 1:26-29 shows the same order: God chooses what the world counts weak so that flesh will not glory before him. The commission was not founded upon Gideon's standing among men. His first commanded work was at home. He threw down his father's altar of Baal, cut down the grove, and built an altar to the Lord. Fear made him work by night, but he still did what was commanded (Judges 6:25-27). When the men of the city demanded his death, Joash answered that Baal should plead for himself if he were a god (Judges 6:28-32). An idol whose worshippers must defend it cannot be the deliverer of those worshippers. Before Gideon confronted Midian, he confronted the false worship in his own household. The Lord then reduced the army from thirty-two thousand to ten thousand, and from ten thousand to three hundred (Judges 7:2-7). Gideon had to release men he might naturally have wanted to keep. The reason was given: Israel must not boast that its own hand had saved it. Deuteronomy 8:14-18 had warned against that very pride. Obedience required trusting the Lord's choice even when it made the army look weaker.
judgment: The Lord strengthened Gideon before the attack by sending him with Phurah to hear the enemy's dream and its interpretation. Gideon heard that Midian had been delivered into his hand, worshipped, and returned ready to act (Judges 7:9-15). The one who had asked for assurance was prepared for the work, not excused from it. Three companies sounded trumpets, broke their pitchers, held their lamps, and stood every man in his place. The Lord set the enemy's swords against one another (Judges 7:16-22). Numbers 10:9 connects the alarm of trumpets in war with being remembered before the Lord and saved from the oppressor. The trumpets were joined to that covenant remembrance; victory did not come from noise apart from the God who heard it. Other Israelites joined the pursuit, and Ephraim took Oreb and Zeeb. When Ephraim complained, Gideon answered by acknowledging what God had delivered into their hands, and their anger abated (Judges 7:23-25; 8:1-3). He had to lead brethren as well as defeat an enemy. Midian was subdued and the country rested forty years (Judges 8:28). The victory was the Lord's from the calling of the least man to the scattering of the great host.

verses.text: 11And there came an angel of the

entries.commentary: Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years. That is our manner: the Most High delivers us, we get a little bit of freedom, and we go right back to wickedness. The same thing goes on today; we get relaxed, and the Lord has to remind us, putting us right back into hard bondage, that this is not our rest. Because of the Midianites, the children of Israel made them the dens in the mountains, and caves, and strongholds; Israel hid in the mountains of their own land.

When Israel had sown, the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east came up as grasshoppers for multitude, destroyed the increase of the earth, and left no sustenance for Israel, neither sheep, nor ox, nor ass, and Israel was greatly impoverished. That goes right into the curses.

When Israel cried unto the Lord, the Lord sent a prophet to remind them: I brought you up from Egypt out of the house of bondage, and I said, fear not the gods of the Amorites in whose land ye dwell, but ye have not obeyed my voice. The judgment came with a reason attached.

An angel of the Lord came and sat under an oak in Ophrah, while Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress to hide it from the Midianites; that is how hard the oppression sat on the land, that a man hid his own harvest to keep it. The angel greets him: the Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour. The Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat.

Gideon answers, oh my Lord, if the Lord be with us, why then is all this befallen us, and where be all his miracles which our fathers told us of? A lot of us ask that same question today when we watch our people judged in the streets over and over: if we be the chosen people, why does all of this happen to us?

The Lord commissions him: go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites; have not I sent thee? Gideon answers with his pedigree: my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. That is a defeated mentality, and we all have to overcome it, because every one of us was called for a reason, to put a brick in for the kingdom.

The Lord promises, surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man. Gideon asks for a sign that it is really the Lord talking with him; the least in his father's house wanted to be sure he was not talking to himself.

Gideon brings a kid and unleavened cakes, and the angel touches the flesh and the cakes with the end of his staff; fire rises up out of the rock and consumes them, and the angel departs out of his sight, gone just like that. No lighter fluid existed on the earth; the angel made fire come out of the rock, because the angels are made out of that fire.

When Gideon perceived he had seen an angel of the Lord face to face, he feared death, but the Lord said, peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die. Gideon built an altar there and called it Jehovah-shalom, which is, the Lord is peace.

The same night the Lord tells him to throw down his own father's altar of Baal, cut down the grove by it, and build an altar unto the Lord in its place. Notice this: even before the split of the kingdom, the tribes that would become the northern kingdom were already dabbling with Baal, worshipping the Lord in some fashion while holding onto the idol.

In the morning the men of the city found the altar of Baal cast down, and when they inquired, they said, Gideon the son of Joash hath done this thing. He crept at night, but somebody was peeping out a window; he was doing the right thing and still got told on. The grove they worshipped was a carved tree stump, cut and shaped to look like a particular god; that is the idol Gideon cut down. The men demand his death, but Joash stands up for his son: will ye plead for Baal? If he be a god, let him plead for himself, because one hath cast down his altar. Obviously he is no god; he is an idol. So that day Gideon was named Jerubbaal, saying, let Baal plead against him.

The Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east gathered and pitched in the valley of Jezreel, but the Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon; he blew a trumpet, and Abiezer, Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali came up to meet him. Those tribes are warriors; do not get it twisted. You see how Zebulun and Naphtali, who are in the south Americas right now, get down: that warrior spirit is still in them, only right now it has turned on each other, and the Most High is going to correct it and turn it right again.

Gideon asks the fleece signs: dew on the fleece only with dry earth beside, and then the reverse, dew on all the ground with the fleece dry. The Lord commands the dew, the condensation that falls through the night, to land exactly where he pleases; God can do whatever he wants, infinite power.

The Lord tells Gideon the people with him are too many for him to give Midian into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against him, saying, mine own hand hath saved me. That is Israel: look at what I did. The Lord knows how we think.

The people are yet too many; the Lord tries them at the water. Some lapped the water with their hand to their mouth as a dog lappeth, and all the rest bowed down upon their knees to drink; the lappers were three hundred men. What can we learn from this? You have to be willing to let go of some people. The Lord said, of whom I say, this shall not go with thee, the same shall not go: some people are not going to be beneficial to the war ahead of you, and the Lord will move them out of the way, but you have to be ready to let them go.

By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you, and deliver the Midianites into thine hand. The Lord sent the rest of Israel every man unto his tent and retained the three hundred, with victuals and trumpets in their hands. Now you know where the famous story of the three hundred came from: they got it from our ancestors, from Gideon. The nations take our history and make it entertainment, and even the artwork drew those three hundred with locks and braids and gave the other host the same, because the artist knew whose history he was drawing; those three hundred were Israelites.

The same night the Lord sends Gideon down to the outside of the enemy host with Phurah his servant: thou shalt hear what they say, and afterward shall thine hands be strengthened. There he hears a man telling his fellow a dream of a cake of barley bread tumbling into the host and overturning a tent, and his fellow interprets it: this is nothing else save the sword of Gideon, for into his hand hath God delivered Midian. The Lord put that dream into the mind of the enemy and sent Gideon down to hear it, so he could go into the battle valiant and strong, without any doubt. When Gideon heard the dream and the interpretation, he worshipped, and returned to say, arise; for the Lord hath delivered into your hand the host of Midian.

Gideon divides the three hundred into three companies, a hundred to the left flank, a hundred down the middle, a hundred to the right, and puts a trumpet in every man's hand, with empty pitchers and lamps within the pitchers. Look on me, and do likewise: pay attention, and when I blow the trumpet, blow ye also on every side of the camp, and say, the sword of the Lord, and of Gideon.

Gideon and his hundred come to the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch, when they had but newly set the watch; in war you always have watchmen taking first, second, and third watch, and Gideon struck right in between the changing of the watchmen. The three companies blew the trumpets, brake the pitchers, held the lamps in their left hands and the trumpets in their right, and cried, the sword of the Lord, and of Gideon; and every man stood in his place round about the camp. Three hundred against thousands, you have to do something to mess with their mind: those horns blowing in unison put fear in the nations, and all the host ran, and cried, and fled. And the Lord set every man's sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host. The enemy destroyed itself; that is the Lord fighting the battle.

The men of Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh gathered themselves and pursued after the Midianites, and Gideon sent messengers throughout all mount Ephraim to come down and take the waters before them; and Ephraim took two princes of Midian, slaying Oreb upon the rock Oreb and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb. Ephraim, stand up; get this spirit back and come join your brothers in the war, because Judah is calling you right now. For those that may not know, that is you so-called Hispanics, you Puerto Ricans: you are Ephraim.

The men of Ephraim chode with Gideon sharply: why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? Ephraim has an attitude because they got called late to the battle and wanted in from the beginning. Gideon answers with wisdom: is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? God delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb; what was I able to do in comparison of you? He gave them the best possible situation, the enemy fed right into their hands with nowhere to go, and then their anger was abated toward him.

Gideon and the three hundred pass over Jordan, faint, yet pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna the kings of Midian. He asks the men of Succoth for loaves of bread for his men, and the princes of Succoth answer, are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? They try to play neutral ground for fear the kings might come against them if they helped. Gideon promises Succoth that when the Lord has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into his hand, he will tear their flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers; and when the men of Penuel answer him the same way, he promises to break down their tower when he comes again in peace.

Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of the host of the children of the east, for there fell an hundred and twenty thousand men that drew sword. Three hundred against those numbers: you know God was with them. Gideon went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents and smote the host while it was secure, and when the two kings fled, he pursued and took them, and discomfited all the host.

Returning from battle, Gideon caught a young man of Succoth who described unto him the princes and elders of the city, and he came back to Succoth with Zebah and Zalmunna in hand: behold the kings with whom ye did upbraid me. Gideon and his men had finished off Midian on an empty stomach because of them. He took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth; he taught them a lesson, that when the army of the Lord comes through faint and weary and asks for bread, you do not turn them away. And he beat down the tower of Penuel and slew the men of the city.

Zebah and Zalmunna describe the men they slew at Tabor: each one resembled the children of a king. Those were powerful men, and they were Gideon's brethren, the sons of his mother; as the Lord liveth, if ye had saved them alive, I would not slay you. Gideon tells Jether his firstborn, up, and slay them, but the youth drew not his sword, for he feared, because he was yet a youth. We have all had that moment of getting the nudge from pops and being nervous; the son was young, and that is understandable, but you see Gideon being a father, taking his son to the war and teaching him the ways he must walk.

The men of Israel ask Gideon to rule over them, both he, his son, and his son's son, for delivering them from the hand of Midian. Israel has always needed a leader, because we are lost sheep; we need somebody to guide us in the way we must go, or we wander off the path of righteousness. It has always been that way, and you see it playing out right here. Gideon refuses: I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you; the Lord shall rule over you.

Gideon requests of every man the earrings of his prey, for the enemy had golden earrings because they were Ishmaelites; and they willingly gave them, a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold, beside the ornaments, collars, purple raiment, and camel chains of the kings. Gideon made an ephod thereof and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it, which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.

Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more, and the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon. Gideon had threescore and ten sons, for he had many wives, and his concubine in Shechem bare him a son whose name he called Abimelech; and Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age. The sum of the history of Gideon, who is also named Jerubbaal, is this: the victory does not come in the strength of numbers, in how many guns or how many bullets you have. The victory of battle comes from the Lord, and that is why we have to trust in the Lord with all our heart and endure to the end, keeping these commandments until the return of our King of kings.

It came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal-berith their god, and remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side; neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal. The same cycle turns again the moment the judge is gone. That is the whole lesson of the book: our deliverance is never our own hand, and our downfall is always our own forgetting. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

When thou goest out to battle and seest horses and chariots and a people more than thou, be not afraid, for the Lord thy God is with thee, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt. That goes for us now, because we are still in a battle. We are not physically out battling the nations as our forefathers were when they took the land; we are in a spiritual battle, for the nations are confederate against Israel being a nation any more and against our remembrance of Israel and our laws. This whole world is set up for our people to go into sin and iniquity. Fear makes people trim their ways: afraid of family at the pagan holiday table, tucking their fringes in certain places, scared to be seen in the truth. Stand boldly; the Lord has not given us the spirit of fear, for that spirit came from Satan himself.

When Israel came nigh unto the battle, the priest approached and spoke: let not your hearts faint, fear not, do not tremble, neither be ye terrified, for the Lord your God is he that goeth with you to fight for you against your enemies to save you. A lot of times you do not see that the Lord is fighting for you in the spirit; that is where faith comes in, for the Bible is a faith-based book. You have to have faith that the Most High is fighting for you, with angels encamped round about the righteous, as David told us.

The officers sent home the man that had built a new house and not dedicated it, the man that had planted a vineyard and not eaten of it, and the man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her, lest he die in the battle and another man take his portion. You could very well die fighting for your people, so go enjoy these things first: dedicate your new house unto the Lord, eat the fruits of your labour from your vineyard, take your wife, then come to war for your people.

The fearful and fainthearted man was also sent home, lest his brethren's heart faint as well as his heart. The spirit of fear spreads: one man's fear makes the next man wonder what he knows, and soon the whole company questions the battle.

When the officers finished speaking, they made captains of the armies to lead the people, because you cannot have order without a ranking structure. Everybody cannot be calling the shots; there is one shot caller and the people follow, and that same order set in Moses' time is why a body under rank is proficient in everything it does.

When thou comest nigh unto a city to fight against it, first proclaim peace unto it. If it answered peace and opened, all the people found in it became tributaries unto Israel and served them. In this time Israel had the power to make nations tributaries. Right now we are not even a nation, just a people with Bibles and nothing established; but wait until Christ comes, for Israel will be established as a nation again and rule the earth, and the nations will be tributaries.

Israel came to a land with terms: agree, pay the tribute, and there is peace. If the city would make no peace but made war, Israel besieged it, and when the Lord delivered it into their hands, every male was smitten with the edge of the sword. The women, the little ones, the cattle, and all the spoil of the city Israel took unto themselves and ate the spoil of their enemies which the Lord their God had given them.

That was the rule for the cities very far off. But of the cities of the nations given Israel for an inheritance, thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth; everything had to die, from humans to animals. The Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites were to be utterly destroyed for a stated purpose: that they teach you not to do after all their abominations which they have done unto their gods, their whoredoms, their idolatry, and their wicked ways of living, so that Israel sin not against the Lord.

In a long siege the trees for meat were not to be destroyed by forcing an axe against them, for thou mayest eat of them; the tree of the field is man's life. Only the trees known not to be trees for meat could be cut down to build bulwarks against the city that maketh war with thee, until it be subdued.

name: The men of Succoth and Penuel
charge: Refusing bread to the Lord's army in pursuit, and taunting them with it
summary: Gideon and his three hundred came to Jordan faint, yet pursuing, and asked loaves of bread. Succoth and Penuel both answered with a sneer: are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? He told them what he would do when he came back, and he came back.
offense: Gideon's three hundred crossed Jordan faint, yet pursuing. They had not abandoned the work, but their bodies needed bread. Gideon asked Succoth for loaves because he was pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian (Judges 8:4-5). This was an opportunity to sustain brethren in the deliverance of Israel, not a demand that the city invent a victory of its own. The princes answered by asking whether the kings were already in his hand. Penuel answered in the same manner (Judges 8:6-8). They made help depend on an outcome already secured: capture the kings first, and then speak of bread. Their answer sought safety from involvement while other men carried the danger. Exhaustion became an occasion for taunting rather than mercy. This refusal belongs beside Meroz, cursed for not coming to help against the mighty (Judges 5:23). A man can withhold the service within his reach without ever joining the enemy's army. The three hundred needed support in an unfinished pursuit; to wait until there was no risk was to withhold what was needed when it mattered. The law of loving one's neighbour required more than acknowledging him after his success (Leviticus 19:18).
judgment: Gideon declared what would follow when the Lord delivered the kings into his hand: thorns and briers for Succoth and the breaking down of Penuel's tower (Judges 8:7-9). He continued the pursuit, struck the remaining host while it was secure, and captured Zebah and Zalmunna (Judges 8:10-12). The condition the cities had used to refuse him was answered by the prisoners he brought back.

He that is wounded in the stones or hath his privy member cut off shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord. This law repeats what was already given: the priests' law in Leviticus lists the same blemishes that barred a man from approaching to offer the bread of his God, including him that hath his stones broken.

A bastard shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord, even to his tenth generation: the children begotten of forbidden unions with the nations were shut out of the congregation. The prophets tie the bastard to Ashdod: a bastard shall dwell in Ashdod. Ashdod was one of the cities given to the tribe of Judah in the inheritance, but Israel did not drive out all the inhabitants and lost it. In the days of Nehemiah, Jews had married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab, and their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod and could not speak in the Jews' language. Why is that? Because the mothers do the raising of the children.

An Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord, even to their tenth generation, for ever. In the time of Nehemiah this very law was read out of the book of Moses in the audience of the people, and when they heard it our people separated from Israel all the mixed multitude whom they had intermarried with and had children with.

The reason for the ban: Ammon and Moab met not Israel with bread and with water in the way when they came forth out of Egypt, and hired Balaam the son of Beor of Pethor to curse them. The history is in Numbers: Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, was sore afraid because the people were many, and sent the elders of Moab and Midian with the rewards of divination to call Balaam to curse Israel. Nevertheless the Lord thy God would not hearken unto Balaam, but turned the curse into a blessing, because the Lord thy God loveth thee; therefore Israel was never to seek their peace nor their prosperity.

Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite, for he is thy brother: this was a temporary law. Edom broke the brotherly covenant; he did pursue his brother with the sword, did cast off all pity, his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever. Edom's hatred is a perpetual hatred: he shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity, and as we see our people being slaughtered by Esau, that anger continues even to this very day. Thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian, because thou wast a stranger in his land: many brothers and sisters do not want to deal with that part and only want to deal with Edom, but Egypt likewise came under judgment for the violence against the children of Judah, because they shed innocent blood in their land.

When the host goeth forth against thine enemies, then keep thee from every wicked thing: when Israel went to war, they were to keep themselves from every wicked thing. The example is Achan: Israel was warned in any wise to keep from the accursed thing, lest they make the camp of Israel a curse and trouble it, and Achan the son of Carmi of the tribe of Judah took of the accursed thing, the Babylonish garment, and the anger of the Lord was kindled against the children of Israel. Because of that trespass Israel could not stand before their enemies but turned their backs, for they were accursed; the Lord would not be with them any more except they destroyed the accursed from among them, and Achan and his family and all that belonged to him were destroyed and burned, and a heap set upon them, because he broke the covenant.

Any man that was not clean by reason of uncleanness that chanceth him by night went abroad out of the camp; when evening came he washed himself with water, and when the sun was down he came into the camp again.

There was a place without the camp to go forth abroad, and a paddle upon the weapon to dig and cover that which cometh from thee: to make it plain, if you had to ease yourself, you went outside the camp to do it. Verse 14 explains why: the Lord thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee and to give up thine enemies before thee; therefore shall thy camp be holy, that he see no unclean thing in thee and turn away from thee. That is what we just read happened with Achan the son of Carmi: he brought an unclean thing into the camp, and the Most High turned from Israel in battle. God says he is in the midst of Israel and none else; the Lord would go before us and fight our battles, and that is why he wanted no unclean thing in the camp, for we are holy and the camp was to be holy.

There shall be no whore of the daughters of Israel, nor a sodomite of the sons of Israel. A sodomite is the biblical word for a homosexual, and the whore of the daughters of Israel here is the same sin in the daughters, what we today would call lesbians. There is a heavy push in the world today for our men to be homosexuals and our sisters to be lesbians; popular entertainers are used to influence the younger generation to sin, just as young rappers were dressed in skirts and dresses until it became cool to be gay. This is what we have to bring our people back from: by being an example, the men being an example, the sisters being an example in the way they dress and carry themselves, and by having families, reinstituting a father and a mother in the divine order the Most High God established. Thou shalt not bring the hire of a whore or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord thy God, for even both these are abomination unto the Lord. Without are dogs: that is not the four-legged barking kind, but the other nations. Christ told a woman of another nation it is not meet to take the children's bread and cast it to dogs, and she said, Truth, Lord; and four-legged dogs did not pierce Christ's hands and feet, for the dogs that compassed him were the other nations, in that case the Romans.

Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother, usury of money, of victuals, of any thing: when you read the definition of usury, that is interest. We are not to charge interest to each other when we loan each other anything. Unto a stranger thou mayest lend upon usury: the blessing is that Israel shall lend unto many nations and shall not borrow, the head and not the tail. That is our rightful place on the earth when we keep these commandments: we should lend unto them and may take usury upon what we lend to them, but we should not do that to our own people. The same law was already read in Exodus: if thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer.

The Most High tells the prophet to cry aloud and spare not, to lift up his voice like a trumpet and show the people their transgression and the house of Jacob their sins. The people seek him daily and delight to know his ways as a nation that did righteousness, and they ask why they have fasted and afflicted their soul and he has taken no knowledge of it.

Their fasting is for strife and debate and to smite with the fist of wickedness, and such a fast will not make their voice to be heard on high. The Most High is not looking for a man to bow his head like a bulrush and spread sackcloth and ashes. The fast he has chosen is to loose the bands of wickedness, undo the heavy burdens, let the oppressed go free, break every yoke, deal thy bread to the hungry, bring the poor that are cast out to thy house, and cover the naked. The reward is that thy light breaks forth as the morning, thy health springs forth speedily, thy righteousness goes before thee, and the glory of the Lord is thy reward; then thou shalt call and the Lord shall answer. "The putting forth of the finger" is when you blame other people. Somebody comes and says a brother did this or that, and instead of taking it, the brother says, "no, but what about her, look what she did." You have to take accountability for your own actions; this is about taking accountability.

If thou draw out thy soul to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul, thy light shall rise in obscurity and thy darkness be as the noonday, and the Lord shall guide thee continually and make fat thy bones. Thou shalt be like a watered garden and a spring of water whose waters fail not, and they that come of thee shall build the old waste places and be called the repairer of the breach, the restorer of paths to dwell in.

If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy own pleasure on his holy day, and call the sabbath a delight and honor him, then thou shalt delight thyself in the Lord. He will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken it.

My son, forget not my law, and let thine heart keep my commandments, for length of days, long life, and peace shall they add to thee. Let not mercy and truth forsake thee; bind them about thy neck and write them upon the table of thine heart, so shalt thou find favor and good understanding in the sight of the Most High and man.

Trust in the Most High with all thine heart and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge Him and He shall direct thy paths. Be not wise in thine own eyes; fear the Most High and depart from evil. It shall be health to thy navel and marrow to thy bones.

Honor the Most High with thy substance and with the firstfruits of all thine increase, so shall thy barns be filled with plenty and thy presses shall burst out with new wine. My son, despise not the chastening of the Most High, neither be weary of His correction, for whom the Most High loveth He correcteth, even as a father the son in whom he delighteth.

Happy is the man that findeth wisdom and the man that getteth understanding, for the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver and the gain thereof than fine gold. Wisdom far, far exceeds riches, because we read in verse 1 of chapter 1 about those that are greedy of gain; the only gain you should be greedy of is keeping the commandments and growing in your spirit. She is more precious than rubies, and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her. Nothing can be compared to the wisdom of the Most High. Length of days is in her right hand, and in her left hand riches and honor. Her ways are ways of pleasantness and all her paths are peace. She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her, and happy is everyone that retaineth her.

The Most High by wisdom hath founded the earth; by understanding He hath established the heavens; by His knowledge the depths are broken up and the clouds drop down the dew. My son, let not them depart from thine eyes; keep sound wisdom and discretion, so shall they be life unto thy soul and grace to thy neck. Then shalt thou walk in thy way safely and thy foot shall not stumble; when thou liest down thou shalt not be afraid, and thy sleep shall be sweet.

Be not afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked when it cometh, for the Most High shall be thy confidence and shall keep thy foot from being taken. Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it. Say not unto thy neighbor go and come again and tomorrow I will give, when thou hast it by thee. Devise not evil against thy neighbor, seeing he dwelleth securely by thee, and strive not with a man without cause if he have done thee no harm.

Envy thou not the oppressor and choose none of his ways, for the forward is abomination to the Most High, but His secret is with the righteous. The curse of the Most High is in the house of the wicked, but He blesseth the habitation of the just. Surely He scorneth the scorners, but He giveth grace unto the lowly. The wise shall inherit glory, but shame shall be the promotion of fools.

name: Gideon's ephod
charge: Making an ephod from the spoil; Israel whoring after it
summary: Gideon refused the crown and said the Lord should rule, then asked for the golden earrings of the spoil and made an ephod of them and put it in Ophrah. All Israel went a whoring after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his house.
offense: After Midian's defeat, Israel offered Gideon rule for himself, his son, and his son's son. He refused and said the Lord should rule over them (Judges 8:22-23). Those were right words, but the test did not end when he refused the crown. He next asked for the golden earrings from the spoil, and the people willingly spread a garment and cast them into it (Judges 8:24-25). The earrings weighed seventeen hundred shekels of gold, besides other royal ornaments and apparel. Gideon made an ephod and placed it in Ophrah, and all Israel went there a whoring after it (Judges 8:26-27). Spoil taken in the Lord's deliverance was turned into a snare against the Lord's worship. The willingness of the donors did not make the use of their gifts righteous. Gideon had begun by throwing down his father's altar of Baal. Now an object he made drew Israel away (Judges 6:25-27; 8:27). A former act of obedience did not make every later act safe. First Timothy 6:10 warns that the love of money causes men to err from the faith and pierce themselves through with sorrows. The danger of the spoil was what the heart and hands did with it after the battle was won.
judgment: The ephod became a snare to Gideon and his house (Judges 8:27). The man who had refused to replace the Lord as ruler had nevertheless furnished the people with an occasion of unfaithfulness. The judgment is already present in that word, snare: what appeared valuable and honourable caught the household that possessed it. Midian remained subdued and the land rested forty years in Gideon's days (Judges 8:28). Peace did not prove that the ephod was acceptable. Israel could enjoy the fruit of the earlier deliverance while another departure grew among them. A successful past is no measure by which to excuse a present offense. After Gideon's death, Israel returned to Baalim, made Baal-berith their god, forgot the Lord who had delivered them, and showed no kindness to Gideon's house (Judges 8:33-35). Forgetting the Lord and forgetting the service of his deliverer stood together. The history proceeds from a household snare into a national return to false worship. Right words about the Lord's rule must be followed by conduct that keeps the people under that rule.

entries.commentary: The men of Ephraim chode with Gideon sharply: why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? Ephraim has an attitude because they got called late to the battle and wanted in from the beginning. Gideon answers with wisdom: is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer? God delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb; what was I able to do in comparison of you? He gave them the best possible situation, the enemy fed right into their hands with nowhere to go, and then their anger was abated toward him.

Gideon and the three hundred pass over Jordan, faint, yet pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna the kings of Midian. He asks the men of Succoth for loaves of bread for his men, and the princes of Succoth answer, are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? They try to play neutral ground for fear the kings might come against them if they helped. Gideon promises Succoth that when the Lord has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into his hand, he will tear their flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers; and when the men of Penuel answer him the same way, he promises to break down their tower when he comes again in peace.

Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of the host of the children of the east, for there fell an hundred and twenty thousand men that drew sword. Three hundred against those numbers: you know God was with them. Gideon went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents and smote the host while it was secure, and when the two kings fled, he pursued and took them, and discomfited all the host.

Returning from battle, Gideon caught a young man of Succoth who described unto him the princes and elders of the city, and he came back to Succoth with Zebah and Zalmunna in hand: behold the kings with whom ye did upbraid me. Gideon and his men had finished off Midian on an empty stomach because of them. He took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth; he taught them a lesson, that when the army of the Lord comes through faint and weary and asks for bread, you do not turn them away. And he beat down the tower of Penuel and slew the men of the city.

Zebah and Zalmunna describe the men they slew at Tabor: each one resembled the children of a king. Those were powerful men, and they were Gideon's brethren, the sons of his mother; as the Lord liveth, if ye had saved them alive, I would not slay you. Gideon tells Jether his firstborn, up, and slay them, but the youth drew not his sword, for he feared, because he was yet a youth. We have all had that moment of getting the nudge from pops and being nervous; the son was young, and that is understandable, but you see Gideon being a father, taking his son to the war and teaching him the ways he must walk.

The men of Israel ask Gideon to rule over them, both he, his son, and his son's son, for delivering them from the hand of Midian. Israel has always needed a leader, because we are lost sheep; we need somebody to guide us in the way we must go, or we wander off the path of righteousness. It has always been that way, and you see it playing out right here. Gideon refuses: I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you; the Lord shall rule over you.

Gideon requests of every man the earrings of his prey, for the enemy had golden earrings because they were Ishmaelites; and they willingly gave them, a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold, beside the ornaments, collars, purple raiment, and camel chains of the kings. Gideon made an ephod thereof and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it, which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.

Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more, and the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon. Gideon had threescore and ten sons, for he had many wives, and his concubine in Shechem bare him a son whose name he called Abimelech; and Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age. The sum of the history of Gideon, who is also named Jerubbaal, is this: the victory does not come in the strength of numbers, in how many guns or how many bullets you have. The victory of battle comes from the Lord, and that is why we have to trust in the Lord with all our heart and endure to the end, keeping these commandments until the return of our King of kings.

It came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal-berith their god, and remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side; neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal. The same cycle turns again the moment the judge is gone. That is the whole lesson of the book: our deliverance is never our own hand, and our downfall is always our own forgetting. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Midian seven years. That is our manner: the Most High delivers us, we get a little bit of freedom, and we go right back to wickedness. The same thing goes on today; we get relaxed, and the Lord has to remind us, putting us right back into hard bondage, that this is not our rest. Because of the Midianites, the children of Israel made them the dens in the mountains, and caves, and strongholds; Israel hid in the mountains of their own land.

When Israel had sown, the Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east came up as grasshoppers for multitude, destroyed the increase of the earth, and left no sustenance for Israel, neither sheep, nor ox, nor ass, and Israel was greatly impoverished. That goes right into the curses.

When Israel cried unto the Lord, the Lord sent a prophet to remind them: I brought you up from Egypt out of the house of bondage, and I said, fear not the gods of the Amorites in whose land ye dwell, but ye have not obeyed my voice. The judgment came with a reason attached.

An angel of the Lord came and sat under an oak in Ophrah, while Gideon threshed wheat by the winepress to hide it from the Midianites; that is how hard the oppression sat on the land, that a man hid his own harvest to keep it. The angel greets him: the Lord is with thee, thou mighty man of valour. The Most High already saw the warrior in the man hiding wheat.

Gideon answers, oh my Lord, if the Lord be with us, why then is all this befallen us, and where be all his miracles which our fathers told us of? A lot of us ask that same question today when we watch our people judged in the streets over and over: if we be the chosen people, why does all of this happen to us?

The Lord commissions him: go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites; have not I sent thee? Gideon answers with his pedigree: my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. That is a defeated mentality, and we all have to overcome it, because every one of us was called for a reason, to put a brick in for the kingdom.

The Lord promises, surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man. Gideon asks for a sign that it is really the Lord talking with him; the least in his father's house wanted to be sure he was not talking to himself.

Gideon brings a kid and unleavened cakes, and the angel touches the flesh and the cakes with the end of his staff; fire rises up out of the rock and consumes them, and the angel departs out of his sight, gone just like that. No lighter fluid existed on the earth; the angel made fire come out of the rock, because the angels are made out of that fire.

When Gideon perceived he had seen an angel of the Lord face to face, he feared death, but the Lord said, peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die. Gideon built an altar there and called it Jehovah-shalom, which is, the Lord is peace.

The same night the Lord tells him to throw down his own father's altar of Baal, cut down the grove by it, and build an altar unto the Lord in its place. Notice this: even before the split of the kingdom, the tribes that would become the northern kingdom were already dabbling with Baal, worshipping the Lord in some fashion while holding onto the idol.

In the morning the men of the city found the altar of Baal cast down, and when they inquired, they said, Gideon the son of Joash hath done this thing. He crept at night, but somebody was peeping out a window; he was doing the right thing and still got told on. The grove they worshipped was a carved tree stump, cut and shaped to look like a particular god; that is the idol Gideon cut down. The men demand his death, but Joash stands up for his son: will ye plead for Baal? If he be a god, let him plead for himself, because one hath cast down his altar. Obviously he is no god; he is an idol. So that day Gideon was named Jerubbaal, saying, let Baal plead against him.

The Midianites, the Amalekites, and the children of the east gathered and pitched in the valley of Jezreel, but the Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon; he blew a trumpet, and Abiezer, Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali came up to meet him. Those tribes are warriors; do not get it twisted. You see how Zebulun and Naphtali, who are in the south Americas right now, get down: that warrior spirit is still in them, only right now it has turned on each other, and the Most High is going to correct it and turn it right again.

Gideon asks the fleece signs: dew on the fleece only with dry earth beside, and then the reverse, dew on all the ground with the fleece dry. The Lord commands the dew, the condensation that falls through the night, to land exactly where he pleases; God can do whatever he wants, infinite power.

Abimelech was the son of Jerubbaal by his concubine in Shechem. He went to Shechem unto his mother's brethren, his uncles on his mother's side, and had them ask the men of Shechem whether it was better for all seventy sons of Jerubbaal to reign over them, or for one man to reign. Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh: he reminded them that he was family. When people do that, they want you to remember that blood is thicker than water, so you will back them whether or not it is right.

His mother's brethren spake of him in the ears of all the men of Shechem, whispering for their nephew, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, He is our brother. They chose him by kinship, not by righteousness. They gave him threescore and ten pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith, money out of their idol's house to back his rise. Politics has always worked this way: people will put a man in office not because he is best for the job, but because he is family or because they know him. Baal was the chief god of the Canaanites, worshipped as the god of the elements who brought rain and made the ground fruitful, and sometimes as the god of war. Baal-berith, also called El-berith, was the Canaanite god of Shechem in the twelfth century BC, a sub god under Baal. With that money Abimelech hired vain and light persons, wicked and empty men, which followed him.

He went unto his father's house at Ophrah and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, threescore and ten persons, upon one stone. He killed his own family to clear his way to a throne. Notwithstanding, Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.

All the men of Shechem and all the house of Millo gathered together and made Abimelech king by the plain of the pillar that was in Shechem. They endorsed the man who had just used their money and his hired men to murder his seventy brothers.

When they told it to Jotham, he went and stood in the top of mount Gerizim, lifted up his voice, and cried, Hearken unto me, ye men of Shechem, that God may hearken unto you. This young brother was fearless; he stood up alone and rebuked the men who had made his brothers' killer king. In his parable the trees went forth on a time to anoint a king over them. The olive tree would not leave its fatness, wherewith by it they honour God and man; the fig tree would not forsake its sweetness and good fruit; the vine would not leave its wine, which cheereth God and man. The profitable trees refused to be promoted over the trees. Only the bramble accepted: if in truth ye anoint me king over you, then come and put your trust in my shadow; and if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon. The worthless bush took the crown, and its answer carried the threat of fire.

Jotham applied the parable: if ye have done truly and sincerely in that ye have made Abimelech king, and if ye have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house, then rejoice ye in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you. He reminded them of what they owed his father: my father fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hand of Midian; and ye are risen up against my father's house this day, and have slain his sons, threescore and ten persons upon one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his maidservant, king over the men of Shechem, because he is your brother. They did it only because he was kin to them. But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the men of Shechem and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech. That is what the parable of the bramble was about: he prophesied that they would destroy one another, and it came to pass.
Jotham ran away and fled to Beer and dwelt there, for fear of Abimelech his brother. His brother already had a reputation for killing; he knew he could be next.

When Abimelech had reigned three years over Israel, God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech. Read that carefully: the Lord sent the evil spirit. When somebody's spirit suddenly changes toward you, we tend to think it is just that person; the scripture shows the Most High is the one who stirs these things. War and strife between nations are not coincidence, karma, or mother nature; those are the world's false ideas and idols. The Most High is in the midst of these things, mustering the host, the armies above and below, and he even puts it on the spirit of one wicked man to go against another. The reason is given: that the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother, which slew them, and upon the men of Shechem, which aided him in the killing of his brethren. The hired men and the backers carried the blood guilt too. Abimelech ran for three years and everything looked good, but you are not getting away with evil.
The men of Shechem set liers in wait for him in the top of the mountains, and they robbed all that came along that way by them; and it was told Abimelech. The treachery the Most High sent had begun.

Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brethren and went over to Shechem, and the men of Shechem put their confidence in him. They went out into the fields, gathered their vineyards, trode the grapes, made merry, went into the house of their god, did eat and drink, and cursed Abimelech. Gaal talked big: who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? is not he the son of Jerubbaal? and Zebul his officer? serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem: for why should we serve him? He asked why they should be serving this Israelite at all. Would to God this people were under my hand! then would I remove Abimelech. He was talking cash money with wine in him: increase thine army, and come out.

When Zebul the ruler of the city, Abimelech's officer, heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled. He sent messengers unto Abimelech privily, saying, Behold, Gaal and his brethren fortify the city against thee. Zebul counselled Abimelech to rise up by night with his people and lie in wait in the field, and in the morning, as soon as the sun was up, to set upon the city. This is the same hand we read of in verse 23; the Lord is in the midst of this whole treachery, turning it back on all of them.

Abimelech and all the people with him rose up by night and laid wait against Shechem in four companies. When Gaal saw the people coming down from the top of the mountains, Zebul told him, Thou seest the shadow of the mountains as if they were men, playing him until it was too late. Then Zebul threw his own words back at him: where is now thy mouth, wherewith thou saidst, Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him? is not this the people that thou hast despised? go out, I pray now, and fight with them. All of that big talk disappeared when the fight showed up. Gaal went out before the men of Shechem and fought with Abimelech, and Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him, and many were overthrown and wounded, even unto the entering of the gate. Abimelech dwelt at Arumah, and Zebul thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem.

On the morrow the people went out into the field, and it was told Abimelech. He divided his men into three companies, laid wait in the field, rose up against the people, and smote them. Abimelech fought against the city all that day; he took the city, slew the people that was therein, beat down the city, and sowed it with salt.

When all the men of the tower of Shechem heard that, they entered into an hold of the house of the god Berith. Abimelech gat him up to mount Zalmon, cut down a bough from the trees with an axe, laid it on his shoulder, and said unto the people that were with him, What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done. They cut every man his bough, put them to the hold, and set the hold on fire upon them, so that all the men of the tower of Shechem died also, about a thousand men and women. Remember, these are the people whose money and endorsement made him king: I am your brother, make me king. Now he turned on Shechem itself and burned them; the fire out of the bramble that Jotham prophesied was devouring the men of Shechem.

Then went Abimelech to Thebez, and there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women of the city fled to the top of it. Abimelech came unto the tower and went hard unto the door to burn it with fire, and a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull. A millstone is a heavy stone; it crushed his skull. He called hastily unto the young man his armourbearer: draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him. It was counted a shame for a man of war to die by the hand of a woman, as when Jael put Sisera to death earlier in this book. His young man thrust him through, and he died. He reigned only three years. Killing his seventy brothers bought him a three year reign and a crushed skull; it was to no profit. If you are doing wickedness behind closed doors and think the Most High does not see it, he sees it, and he brings swift judgment.

Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren; and all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads. Both sides were judged; for three years they reigned and everything looked good, then the Most High brought the judgment. Upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal. Our forefather Jotham, a young man at the time, prophesied their destruction, and it came to pass. We read these accounts for the history, but look deeper and apply them to our lives: if there is evil being done behind closed doors, the Most High will judge it in front of everybody, like he judged Abimelech.

An image in itself is not the sin, except for that white image of the beast; making images to bow down to them and serve them is the transgression, for the Lord thy God is a jealous God. Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation: Israel is yet this day in captivity, scattered for a reproach and a curse, according to all the iniquities of the fathers which departed from the Lord. Right now Israel is paying for the sins of the fathers; that is why the people are scattered to the four corners of the earth.

And shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me, and keep my commandments. Judith recounted how the Most High tried the fathers for the examination of their hearts: he tried Abraham and Isaac, and Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria keeping the sheep of Laban, serving twenty years with his wages changed and given Leah when he looked for Rachel. In Judith's day there was no tribe, family, people, nor city that worshipped gods made with hands, as had been aforetime; for that cause she trusted the Lord would not despise the nation. Mercy rests on them that know none other God, not Allah, not Buddha, not a white Jesus.

Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. The word says remember because Israel would forget it: in this captivity the people were forced to serve other gods and their religions, and the Sabbath was lost through forced conversion. Look up the blue laws, also known as Sunday laws; they help give understanding of why the Bible says remember the Sabbath day.

An altar of stone was not to be built of hewn stone, for lifting up a tool upon it pollutes it; neither go up by steps unto the altar, that thy nakedness be not discovered thereon. The priests were given linen breeches to cover their nakedness from the loins even unto the thighs when they came near the altar, and Israel was called in this same reading to be a kingdom of priests, so do not be simple and say that law was only for Aaron and his sons. Those breeches were made for men and not for women, as the law of the garments also shows.

name: Abimelech son of Gideon
charge: Murder of seventy brothers on one stone; usurping a crown
summary: Gideon's son by a Shechemite concubine hired vain and light persons with silver from the house of Baal-berith, killed his seventy brothers on one stone, and had himself made king at Shechem. Only Jotham escaped, and his parable from Mount Gerizim pronounced the sentence.
offense: Abimelech appealed to his mother's brethren in Shechem and asked whether they preferred seventy sons of Jerubbaal to rule them or one man who was their own bone and flesh (Judges 9:1-2). They promoted him because he was their brother. Kinship took the place of judgment, and money from the house of Baal-berith financed the choice: seventy pieces of silver paid the vain and light men who followed him (Judges 9:3-4). He went to his father's house at Ophrah and slew his brethren upon one stone; Jotham escaped by hiding. Shechem then made the killer king (Judges 9:5-6). Their part was not confined to approving him afterward. They supplied the means by which he established his rule. The blood would be laid upon the man who killed and upon the men who strengthened his hands (Judges 9:24). Jotham spoke from Mount Gerizim. In his parable, the olive, fig, and vine would not forsake their fruitfulness to reign over the trees, but the bramble offered its shadow and threatened fire (Judges 9:7-15). He applied it to the ingratitude shown his father's house: Gideon had risked his life to deliver them, and they had answered by destroying his sons. If their choice was not true and sincere, Abimelech and Shechem would consume one another (Judges 9:16-20).
judgment: Three years passed before the alliance broke. God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem so that the blood of Gideon's sons would be requited upon both parties (Judges 9:22-24). The interval had not erased the murder. Numbers 32:23 warns that sin will find the offender out; a season of apparent success is not acquittal. Shechem dealt treacherously, trusted Gaal, and cursed Abimelech; Abimelech returned with ambush and slaughter. He destroyed the city and burned the stronghold where about a thousand men and women had taken refuge (Judges 9:26-49). The man they had called their brother brought the fire Jotham had pronounced. The god whose treasury financed his rise could not shelter those who fled into its house. At Thebez, Abimelech approached another tower to burn it, but a woman cast a piece of millstone upon his head and crushed his skull. He ordered his armour-bearer to kill him so that men would not say a woman slew him (Judges 9:50-54). Even at death he sought control of his reputation. The history still records the woman and the stone. God rendered Abimelech's wickedness upon him and Shechem's evil upon its own head; Jotham's curse came upon them (Judges 9:56-57). The killer and his backers did not cancel one another's guilt by becoming enemies. Their conflict became the means by which both were repaid.
