name: Mephibosheth
charge: Answering the king, What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am; and let him take all
summary: Lame on both feet from the day his nurse dropped him fleeing the news of Gilboa, the last of Saul's line was fetched from Lodebar and given all the land of his grandfather and a place at the king's table continually. When David fled from Absalom his servant slandered him and took the property. When David returned, Mephibosheth met him unwashed and unshaven since the day the king departed, and when the land was divided said, let him take all, forasmuch as my lord the king is come again in peace.
offense: Mephibosheth was five when the news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths caused his nurse to flee with him. He fell in her haste and became lame (2 Samuel 4:4). Years later he was summoned from Lodebar to the king who now ruled in his grandfather's place. He came with reverence and fear, but David's purpose was kindness for Jonathan's sake (2 Samuel 9:1-7). His standing rested upon the covenant between his father and David, not his ability to serve in battle or strengthen the king politically. He received the kindness humbly (2 Samuel 9:8). The promise had reached a member of the former royal house who could offer little power in return. David's care made remembrance of Jonathan a continuing work rather than a passing expression of grief. During Absalom's rebellion Ziba accused Mephibosheth of remaining in Jerusalem to recover Saul's kingdom. When David returned, Mephibosheth came with his neglected feet, beard, and clothes bearing the marks of mourning. He explained that Ziba had deceived and slandered him (2 Samuel 16:1-4; 19:24-28). His answer to the king's order to divide the land was that Ziba could have it all, since David had returned safely (2 Samuel 19:29-30). His joy in the king's preservation stood above the disputed estate.
judgment: David restored Saul's land and appointed Ziba's household to cultivate it, while Mephibosheth ate continually at the king's table as one of his sons (2 Samuel 9:9-13). Provision included both the inheritance's produce and an honoured place in the household. His disability did not exclude him from the kindness pledged to his father. When the Gibeonites required seven of Saul's house, David spared Jonathan's son because of the Lord's oath between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7). The broken covenant that brought judgment upon Saul's house was met by a kept covenant preserving Mephibosheth. The king did not allow the pressure of one obligation to make him forget another.

name: Baanah and Rechab
charge: Murder of Ish-bosheth in his bed
summary: Two captains of Saul's son entered his house at noon under pretense of fetching wheat, killed him as he lay on his bed, cut off his head, and carried it all night to David at Hebron expecting a reward.
offense: After Abner's death, Ishbosheth's hands were feeble and Israel was troubled. Rechab and Baanah, captains from his own company, entered his house in the heat of the day as though fetching wheat and killed him upon his bed (2 Samuel 4:1-7). Their access became the means of betrayal. They did not meet him in an open contest but took advantage of his rest within his own house. They carried his head through the night to David and called the killing the Lord's vengeance upon Saul and his seed (2 Samuel 4:8). The claim attempted to make murder into religious service. David's rise did not mean that any deed removing a rival had been commanded by God. The promise of the kingdom was not permission to put innocent blood beneath it. David answered by naming the Lord who had redeemed his soul from adversity (2 Samuel 4:9). His deliverance did not depend upon these men. He had already put to death the messenger who expected favour for reporting Saul's death; he would not now reward men who brought proof of a killing in a bedroom (2 Samuel 4:10-11).
judgment: David called Ishbosheth a righteous person slain by wicked men and required his blood from their hands (2 Samuel 4:11). The judgment distinguished a political opponent from a person whom it was lawful to murder. The king would not receive the brothers' account of divine vengeance as an answer to what they had done. He ordered their execution. Their hands and feet were cut off, and their bodies were hung over the pool in Hebron; Ishbosheth's head was buried in Abner's sepulchre (2 Samuel 4:12). The murderers were publicly judged, while the remains they had carried as a reward-bearing token were given burial. The same distinction later governed David's charge against Joab: blood shed through treachery in peace did not become lawful because the killer served the king (1 Kings 2:5-6). Rechab and Baanah misjudged both David and the Lord whose name they used. Advantage offered to a ruler did not remove the ruler's obligation to judge the act.

He had already put to death the messenger who expected favour for reporting Saul's death; he would not now reward men who brought proof of a killing in a bedroom (2 Samuel 4:10-11).
judgmentFull: David called Ishbosheth a righteous person slain by wicked men and required his blood from their hands (2 Samuel 4:11). The judgment distinguished a political opponent from a person whom it was lawful to murder. The king would not receive the brothers' account of divine vengeance as an answer to what they had done.

He ordered their execution. Their hands and feet were cut off, and their bodies were hung over the pool in Hebron; Ishbosheth's head was buried in Abner's sepulchre (2 Samuel 4:12). The murderers were publicly judged, while the remains they had carried as a reward-bearing token were given burial.

The same distinction later governed David's charge against Joab: blood shed through treachery in peace did not become lawful because the killer served the king (1 Kings 2:5-6). Rechab and Baanah misjudged both David and the Lord whose name they used. Advantage offered to a ruler did not remove the ruler's obligation to judge the act.

entries.commentary: When Saul's son Ishbosheth heard that Abner was dead in Hebron, his hands were feeble and all the Israelites were troubled. Ishbosheth had two captains of bands, Baanah and Rechab, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite of the children of Benjamin, for Beeroth also was reckoned to Benjamin; and the Beerothites had fled to Gittaim.

Jonathan's son Mephibosheth was lame of his feet. When the tidings came of Saul and Jonathan out of Jezreel, he was five years old, and his nurse took him up and fled, and in her haste he fell and became lame. She fled because a new king taking over would customarily kill all the descendants of the former king to make sure none could overthrow him. That is why the nurse ran with the child.

The sons of Rimmon came about the heat of the day to the house of Ishbosheth, who lay on a bed at noon in the hottest part of the day, and came into the midst of the house as though they would fetch wheat, and smote him under the fifth rib. Rechab and Baanah escaped, having smitten and slain him on his bed; and they beheaded him and took his head and got away through the plain all night, and brought the head to David at Hebron, saying, Behold the head of Ishbosheth thine enemy, and claiming the Lord had avenged the king this day of Saul and his seed. They did too much; they went overboard. Israel being out of order took the matter upon themselves. David had no quarrel with Saul's sons; it was Saul who sought his life.

David answered Rechab and Baanah that as the Lord liveth, who had redeemed his soul out of all adversity, the man who told him Saul was dead, thinking to bring good tidings, he had taken hold of and slain in Ziklag; that was the reward he gave for such tidings. How much more, he said, when wicked men had slain a righteous person in his own house upon his bed, should he not require his blood of their hand and take them away from the earth. The man was at rest, asleep, not even a man-to-man contest for the kingdom; it was not how the Most High brings His purpose to pass. David commanded his young men, and they slew Rechab and Baanah, cut off their hands and feet, and hanged them up over the pool in Hebron, but took the head of Ishbosheth and buried it in the sepulchre of Abner. The Most High has His own way of doing things; His people are not to put the cart before the horse. This is why David is called a man after the Most High's own heart. He did not accept wickedness done in his name or let the murderers slide; he called them out and they received judgment for taking a man's life not ordained of the Lord nor commanded by the king. Let all things be done decently and in order.

If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve, and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing. If he came in by himself he goes out by himself; if he were married when he came in, his wife goes out with him. Deuteronomy repeats the same judgment for a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman sold unto thee. [Nehemiah 5](/bible/nehemiah/5) shows how brethren came into servitude: in the dearth some mortgaged lands, vineyards, and houses to buy corn, some borrowed money for the king's tribute, and some brought their sons and daughters into bondage. The brother that waxes poor is not to be compelled to serve as a bondservant, but as an hired servant, and not ruled over harshly. If the master gave him a wife and she bare him sons or daughters, the wife and her children are the master's, and he goes out by himself; he did not bring them in. His two choices are to go out alone, or to plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children, have his ear bored through with an aul at the door post, and serve his master for ever. Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

If a man sell his daughter to be a maidservant, she shall not go out as the menservants do. The reason is that her master betrothed her to himself, or unto his son; she is a wife, not a six-year servant, so the release of the menservants does not apply to her. If she please not her master who hath betrothed her to himself, he must let her be redeemed; he has no power to sell her unto a strange nation, seeing he hath dealt deceitfully with her. The deceit is that he betrothed her to himself and then would not deal with her, keeping her to himself when she could have been another man's wife. If he take him another wife, her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage shall he not diminish; the duty of marriage is the marriage bed. If he lay with her, she belongs to him and he cannot send her away; and if he do not these three unto her, then shall she go out free without money. He must take care of her.

If a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand, a place was appointed whither he shall flee. That is the case of the slayer that kills his neighbour ignorantly, as when a man hews wood with his neighbour and the axe head slips from the helve and lights upon him that he die: he flees to the appointed city and lives, lest the avenger of blood overtake him while his heart is hot, for he was not worthy of death, having hated him not in time past. But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour to slay him with guile, thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die. Men would run and grab the horns of the altar, but wilful murder found no refuge there.

If men strive and one smite another so that he keep his bed, he that smote him shall pay for the loss of his time and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed. That is restitution: paying for the time the man was down and could not work and provide for his family. That is what the court system calls a civil suit today.

If a man smite his servant with a rod and he die under his hand, he shall surely be punished; but if he continue a day or two, he shall not be punished, for he is his money. The wisdom writings teach not to be ashamed of much correction of children, nor of making the side of an evil servant to bleed. An evil servant that will not get right could be corrected physically, so long as he was not killed.

If men strive and hurt a woman with child so that her fruit depart from her, this judgment covers the miscarriage: if no mischief follow, he is punished as the woman's husband lays upon him and the judges determine; and if any mischief follow, then life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, wound for wound.

If an ox gore a man or a woman that they die, the ox is stoned and his flesh not eaten, and the owner is quit. But if the ox were wont to push with his horns in time past, and it hath been testified to his owner, and he hath not kept him in, and it kill a man or a woman, the ox is stoned and his owner also put to death. Most do not have oxen today, but the same judgment reaches the yard dogs, the pit bulls, German shepherds, and rottweilers. If the dog has bitten before and it was reported to you, and it gets out again through a snapped chain or a breach in the fence and mauls or kills somebody, the scripture holds the owner responsible unto death; that is why animal control writes the ticket and warns you to keep your dogs in. The law is slack right now, as Habakkuk says, so many punishments worthy of death in the scriptures, like rape or this judgment, come out today as a fine or a slap on the hand.

On the day Israel passed over Jordan into the land, they were to set up great stones, plaster them with plaster, and write upon them all the words of this law. Here is the difference between the truth and Islam and every other religion. The stone is not to be worshipped or thought to be a god; you set it up and put the laws on it so you can remember the laws.

The stones were to be set up in mount Ebal, and an altar of whole stones built there unto the Most High; no iron tool was to be lifted upon them. Burnt offerings and peace offerings were offered there, and the people were to eat and rejoice before the Most High. Thou shalt write upon the stones all the words of this law very plainly. That is what the Most High wants remembered most: not the stone itself, but the law written on it.

Moses and the priests the Levites told all Israel: this day thou art become the people of the Lord thy God; therefore obey his voice and do his commandments and statutes. Even the other nations' own books witness to it. The Martyrdom of Man says that "God made all men equal" is a fine sounding phrase but not a scientific fact, and that those who outlive hardships and sufferings which fall on all alike owe their existence to some superiority not only of body but of mind. There is no way we could have lasted this long through what we have been through if we were not the people of the Most High: thousands of years run out of the homeland, living among our enemies, put on ships and transported all over the world, and still surviving from 1492 on up here in Babylon the great.

Moses charged the people that day: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph (which is Ephraim and Manasseh), and Benjamin were to stand upon mount Gerizim to bless the people. Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali were to stand upon mount Ebal to curse. Half the tribes stood on one side and half on the other, one saying one thing and the other answering.

The Levites were to speak with a loud voice unto all the men of Israel: cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image, an abomination unto the Most High, the work of the hands of the craftsman, and putteth it in a secret place. And all the people shall answer and say, Amen. Every curse that follows carried that same answer from the whole congregation.
Cursed be he that setteth light by his father or his mother. Setting light by them means disrespecting your parents and not obeying them.

Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour's landmark. Every man in Israel was allotted a certain plot of land for his inheritance individually. If you moved that landmark trying to make your own land bigger, the Most High says cursed be upon you. The allotments are recorded in Joshua and in [Numbers 27](/bible/numbers/27), where the inheritance laws are given.
Cursed be he that maketh the blind to wander out of the way. Do not mistreat those we call the disabled.

Cursed be he that perverteth the judgment of the stranger, fatherless, and widow. This goes back to Deuteronomy chapter 1, where the judges were charged to judge righteously between every man and his brother and the stranger with him, and to respect no persons in judgment.
Cursed be he that lieth with his father's wife, because he uncovereth his father's skirt. That is nasty stuff, and the curse of the whole congregation stood against it.
Cursed be he that lieth with any manner of beast. Bestiality is the practice of Esau, and Israel was cursed for touching it.
Cursed be he that lieth with his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother. This goes back to Leviticus chapter 18, where the nakedness laws were first given.
Cursed be he that lieth with his mother in law, and all the people shall say, Amen. Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, and all the people shall say, Amen.
Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. That is your hitman right there in verse 25: taking payment to kill the innocent puts you under the curse.

Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them. At that time this encompassed everything, including the law of sacrifice. It also applies to us today, because sacrifice is alive and well; it just transformed. We still sacrifice, only it is no longer animals but our bodies. Our bodies must be holy and without blemish before the Most High, because the law says you cannot bring anything with blemishes into the house of the Lord. If your sacrifice is not holy and acceptable, the Son is not taking you to present you before the Father. Christ magnified the law, as Isaiah says.

name: Uzzah and the ark
charge: Touching the ark, transported unlawfully
summary: The ark had been taken by the Philistines in the days of the judges and had rested in the house of Abinadab. David gathered thirty thousand chosen men to bring it up, and they set it upon a new cart driven by Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab. At Nachon's threshingfloor the oxen shook the cart, Uzzah put forth his hand and took hold of the ark, and God smote him there for his error, and he died by the ark.
offense: David and the congregation agreed to bring the ark up from the house of Abinadab. They placed it upon a new cart, and music and rejoicing accompanied the journey (2 Samuel 6:1-5). The purpose was welcome to the people, but the manner of carrying the ark had already been commanded. Approval by an assembly did not replace the Lord's due order. Numbers 4:15 required the holy things to be covered before the appointed bearers approached and forbade them to touch them lest they die. The ark's staves were to remain in their rings (Exodus 25:14-15). The Philistines had returned it upon a cart, but Israel was responsible for the instruction given to Israel. A new vehicle was not an improvement upon obedience. At the threshingfloor the oxen shook it, and Uzzah put out his hand to hold the ark (2 Samuel 6:6). His reach answered an immediate danger, but it crossed a boundary the law had not left to personal judgment. Even Aaron was forbidden to enter the holy place at all times, a warning given after the deaths of his sons (Leviticus 16:1-2). Nearness to holy service required greater care, not freedom from its limits.
judgment: The Lord's anger was kindled against Uzzah, and he died there beside the ark. David was displeased at the breach and afraid, asking how the ark could come to him (2 Samuel 6:7-9). The celebration was stopped by a judgment that made the neglected command impossible to dismiss. Psalms 119:120 joins trembling in the flesh to fear of the Lord's judgments. The ark remained three months in Obed-edom's house. When David returned to bring it up, he did not merely try the same journey with more confidence. He declared that none but the Levites ought to carry it, called them to sanctify themselves, and acknowledged that the first breach came because they had not sought the Lord after the due order (1 Chronicles 15:2, 12-13). The failure was confessed as theirs, not assigned to Uzzah alone. The Levites then bore the ark upon their shoulders with the staves as Moses had commanded (1 Chronicles 15:14-15). Rejoicing continued, but now the service followed the word. The distinction between the journeys was not whether David wanted to honour the Lord. It was whether that honour was offered in the manner the Lord had appointed.

The purpose was welcome to the people, but the manner of carrying the ark had already been commanded. Approval by an assembly did not replace the Lord's due order.

Numbers 4:15 required the holy things to be covered before the appointed bearers approached and forbade them to touch them lest they die. The ark's staves were to remain in their rings (Exodus 25:14-15). The Philistines had returned it upon a cart, but Israel was responsible for the instruction given to Israel. A new vehicle was not an improvement upon obedience.

At the threshingfloor the oxen shook it, and Uzzah put out his hand to hold the ark (2 Samuel 6:6). His reach answered an immediate danger, but it crossed a boundary the law had not left to personal judgment. Even Aaron was forbidden to enter the holy place at all times, a warning given after the deaths of his sons (Leviticus 16:1-2). Nearness to holy service required greater care, not freedom from its limits.
judgmentFull: The Lord's anger was kindled against Uzzah, and he died there beside the ark. David was displeased at the breach and afraid, asking how the ark could come to him (2 Samuel 6:7-9). The celebration was stopped by a judgment that made the neglected command impossible to dismiss. Psalms 119:120 joins trembling in the flesh to fear of the Lord's judgments.

The ark remained three months in Obed-edom's house. When David returned to bring it up, he did not merely try the same journey with more confidence. He declared that none but the Levites ought to carry it, called them to sanctify themselves, and acknowledged that the first breach came because they had not sought the Lord after the due order (1 Chronicles 15:2, 12-13). The failure was confessed as theirs, not assigned to Uzzah alone.

The Levites then bore the ark upon their shoulders with the staves as Moses had commanded (1 Chronicles 15:14-15). Rejoicing continued, but now the service followed the word. The distinction between the journeys was not whether David wanted to honour the Lord. It was whether that honour was offered in the manner the Lord had appointed.

verses.text: 3And they set the ark of God upon a new cart, and brought it out of the house of Abinadab that was in Gibeah: and Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drave the new cart. 4And they brought it out of the house of Abinadab which was at Gibeah, accompanying the ark of God: and Ahio went before the ark. 5And David and all the house of Israel played before the Lord on all manner of instruments made of fir wood, even on harps, and on psalteries, and on timbrels, and on cornets, and on cymbals.

6And when they came to Nachon’s threshingfloor, Uzzah put forth his hand to the ark of God, and took hold of it; for the oxen shook it. 7And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah; and God smote him there for his error; and there he died by the ark of God. 8And David was displeased, because the Lord had made a breach upon Uzzah: and he called the name of the place Perez–uzzah to this day. 9And David was afraid of the Lord that day, and said, How shall the ark of the Lord come to me?

entries.commentary: David gathered together thirty thousand chosen men of Israel. Not everyone is a warrior, and not everyone goes to the front lines, but everyone in the body is important in some way; the members that seem more feeble are needful, and on them more honor is bestowed. David and all the people went from Baale of Judah to bring up the ark of God, whose name is called by the name of the Lord of hosts that dwelleth between the cherubims. The ark had been taken from Israel by the Philistines in the days of the judges because of sin, and it had been left in the house of Abinadab. Through the wilderness there had been no house for the Lord, so the ark was moved from place to place. They set the ark upon a new cart, and Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, drove it, with Ahio going before the ark, while David and all the house of Israel played before the Lord on harps, psalteries, timbrels, cornets, and cymbals.

When they came to Nachon's threshingfloor, the oxen shook the cart, and Uzzah put forth his hand and took hold of the ark. The anger of the Lord was kindled, and God smote him for his error, and he died there by the ark. Only chosen men could come near the ark. The Lord had warned Aaron not to come at all times into the holy place before the mercy seat that he die not, and had set many stipulations upon it, even after the two sons of Aaron died for offering strange fire. The Most High is holy and not to be handled carelessly. Grabbing the ark was a natural reaction, but the Most High had already declared it holy and untouchable. Everything in that day had to be done to a T; we owe thanks that there is mercy through Christ, for the Lord was not playing about His commandments. David was displeased that the Lord had made a breach upon Uzzah, and he was afraid of the Lord that day, saying, How shall the ark of the Lord come to me? David had seen the power of the Lord, and his flesh trembled for fear of Him and His judgments. David would not remove the ark to the city of David but carried it aside to the house of Obededom the Gittite, where it remained three months; and the Lord blessed Obededom and all his household because of the ark.

When David heard the Lord had blessed the house of Obededom because of the ark, he went and brought up the ark to the city of David with gladness. When those that bore it had gone six paces, he sacrificed oxen and fatlings. David danced before the Lord with all his might, girded with a linen ephod. He was happy and in the spirit, for the Lord had chosen him to bring the ark back among the people. Israel brought up the ark with shouting and the sound of the trumpet. Michal, Saul's daughter, looked through a window and saw David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart. This is a spirit to be careful of: coming out of the spirit on the Lord's day and murmuring against a brother who is rejoicing in the Most High. David set the ark in the tabernacle he had pitched for it, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and blessed the people in the name of the Lord of hosts. He dealt to every one, both men and women, a cake of bread, a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine, and the people departed to their houses.

David returned to bless his own household, still in a good mood. Michal came out to meet him and said sarcastically, How glorious was the king of Israel today, who uncovered himself in the eyes of the handmaids as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovereth himself. She had watched from a distance and could think only of the king dancing with his clothes falling, when the Most High had just brought the ark of God back among Israel. She forgot the greatness of the day and let a murmuring spirit take her. David answered that he danced before the Lord who chose him before her father to be ruler over Israel, therefore he would play before the Lord, and would yet be more vile and base in his own sight, and of the maidservants he would be had in honor. Michal, the daughter of Saul, had no child unto the day of her death; the Lord shut her womb. Do not play with the Most High.

The sons of Kohath were numbered from thirty years old and upward even unto fifty years old, all that enter into the host to do the work in the tabernacle of the congregation. You took on that responsibility at thirty years old. Fifty was basically the age of retirement from the service; the law elsewhere shows the elder then sat down to be a judge amongst his brethren.

This is the service of the sons of Kohath about the most holy things. When the camp set forward, Aaron and his sons took down the covering vail and covered the ark of the testimony with it, with the covering of badgers' skins and a cloth wholly of blue. The design of the ark and the tabernacle, the pure gold dishes, spoons, and vessels, was laid out back in [Exodus 35](/bible/exodus/35) and 36; review it there.

The table of shewbread, the candlestick, the golden altar, and all the instruments of ministry were each wrapped in cloths of blue, scarlet, or purple and covered with badgers' skins before they were put on the staves and bars. Badger skin is something we would consider unclean today, yet the Lord had his holy things covered in it. Under the law of sacrifice, defilement came by touching unclean things to eat them; touching them to make something for the tabernacle still left you unclean until sundown, unable to sacrifice, but the skins themselves served the sanctuary.

After Aaron and his sons made an end of covering the sanctuary, the sons of Kohath came to bear it, but they shall not touch any holy thing, lest they die. The Most High is very particular about the most holy things. The Lord referred to all the tribes together as the camp. If you are not in a camp you are out of order; people avoid camps because a camp carries a certain level of order and subjection, and they want to do their own thing, which is to sit in the midst of sin. All twelve tribes are not gathered together right now, but we are still commanded to rehearse the righteous acts of the Lord, and that takes gathering; the body must move in one unison, in one direction, as a camp.

To the office of Eleazar pertained the oil for the light, the sweet incense, the daily meat offering, the anointing oil, and the oversight of all the tabernacle. The burning of the sweet incense stayed in that priestly line: Zacharias, of the course of Abia, descended from the line of the Kohathites, and his lot was to burn incense in the temple of the Lord. [Luke 1:6](/bible/luke/1#v6) is the New Testament precept for what it means to be righteous: walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless. Highlight that and commit it to memory. The son of Zacharias was John the Baptist, a Levite; and John the Baptist was Elijah back on the earth again, come to do what was prophesied of him. There is no reincarnation, coming back as a bird or such; there is regeneration, and we come back over and over again.

The Most High commanded that the families of the Kohathites not be cut off: Aaron and his sons appointed every one to his service and to his burden, but they shall not go in to see when the holy things are covered, lest they die. It was a heavy responsibility; your life was on the line and you could not be out of order. One slip, one curious peek at the shiny gold before it was covered, and God put you to death on the spot. You had to be serious about your job and follow all instructions. That is the God we are dealing with; that is why Christ came, to give us mercy and grace from that thing.

The sons of Gershon were numbered from thirty to fifty years old for their service: bearing the curtains of the tabernacle, the coverings of badgers' skins, the hangings of the court and the doors, the cords, and all the instruments of their service. Their charge was under the hand of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest. Ithamar had to make sure the priests had covered all the most holy things before the Gershonites came in to bear them; he was responsible for the lives of all the Gershonites that served, and he had to be in order.

The sons of Merari were numbered from thirty to fifty years old, charged with the boards, bars, pillars, sockets, pins, and cords of the tabernacle and the court, reckoned by name, under the hand of Ithamar the son of Aaron. Only Eleazar and Ithamar were left to oversee, because Nadab and Abihu were killed by the Lord for offering strange fire; there were only two sons of Aaron remaining.

The numbered for service were 2,750 Kohathites, 2,630 Gershonites, and 3,200 Merarites; the total of those from thirty to fifty years old that entered the service of the tabernacle was 8,580, eight thousand and five hundred and fourscore. The Lord constantly repeats himself through these chapters to make sure you stay in order and do not go out of order, because going out of order cost your life. That is why you read the same thing in the Bible over and over again.

David prepared a place and pitched a tent for the ark in the city of David. He declared that none ought to carry the ark but the Levites, for the Most High had chosen them to carry it and to minister unto him forever. -

David assembled all Israel and the chief Levites by their families, naming the sons of Kohath, Merari, Gershom, Elizaphan, Hebron, and Uzziel with their chiefs and numbers. He called for the priests Zadok and Abiathar and for the Levites, showing the Most High had set a clear structure among the priesthood.

David charged the chief fathers of the Levites to sanctify themselves before bringing up the ark, because the first attempt failed when they did not seek him after the due order. The Levites bore the ark upon their shoulders with the staves, as Moses commanded according to the word of the Most High. -

David appointed Levites as singers with psalteries, harps, and cymbals, to lift up the voice with joy. Heman, Asaph, and Ethan were appointed to sound cymbals of brass; others played harps and psalteries; the priests blew the trumpets before the ark, and doorkeepers were set. Every rank had its assigned place.

David and the elders and captains went to bring up the ark from the house of Obededom with joy. When the Most High helped the Levites bearing the ark, they offered seven bullocks and seven rams. David was clothed in a robe of fine linen along with the Levites and singers, and wore an ephod of linen. The people were dressed well, and the same custom carried down through Solomon.

All Israel brought up the ark with shouting, cornet, trumpets, cymbals, psalteries, and harps. Michal the daughter of Saul looked out the window and despised David in her heart as he danced and played. In the midst of pure righteousness she was out of the spirit, hating him instead of rejoicing.

name: Obed-edom the Gittite
charge: Keeping the ark of God in his house three months, after it had killed Uzzah
summary: Uzzah had just died for touching the ark, and David was afraid to bring it into the city. It went instead into the house of Obed-edom of Gath, and stayed three months. The Lord blessed him and all his household so visibly that David heard of it and came back for the ark with sacrifices and dancing.
offense: After the breach upon Uzzah, David would not bring the ark into the city of David. He carried it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it remained three months (2 Samuel 6:10-11). The same ark before which judgment had interrupted the procession now stood within a household. The Lord's holiness had not changed; neither had his power to bless. Obed-edom's house received what David had become afraid to bring nearer. Yet the blessing was not a licence to handle the ark however a man pleased. When the journey resumed, the Levites sanctified themselves and carried it upon their shoulders according to the commandment (1 Chronicles 15:12-15). Receiving holy things and observing the order of their service belonged together.
judgment: And the ark of the Lord continued in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months: and the Lord blessed Obed-edom, and all his household. It was told king David, saying, The Lord hath blessed the house of Obed-edom, and all that pertaineth unto him, because of the ark of God. The Chronicles count him afterward among the porters and the singers before the ark, with eight sons and sixty-two able men of his house: for God blessed him.
offenseFull: After the breach upon Uzzah, David would not bring the ark into the city of David. He carried it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it remained three months (2 Samuel 6:10-11). The same ark before which judgment had interrupted the procession now stood within a household. The Lord's holiness had not changed; neither had his power to bless.

Obed-edom's house received what David had become afraid to bring nearer. Yet the blessing was not a licence to handle the ark however a man pleased. David consulted with the captains of thousands and hundreds and every leader, and proposed to all the congregation that they send abroad to their brethren everywhere, with the priests and Levites, to gather to them. the sons of the Gershonite Laadan, chief fathers, even of Laadan the Gershonite, were Jehieli. 22 The sons of Jehieli; Zetham, and Joel his brother, which were over the treasures of the house of the LORD. 23 Of the Amramites, and the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites: 24 And Shebuel the son of Gershom, the son of Moses, was ruler of the treasures. 25 And his brethren by Eliezer; Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine. Jump back to [Psalms 127:3](/bible/psalms/127#v3), for the wife is that fruitful vine, the fruit of the womb that is his reward. Behold, thus shall the man be blessed that feareth the Lord. A man will be blessed with blessed children if he fears the Lord.

name: Michal
charge: Despising the king in her heart for dancing before the ark
summary: As the ark came into the city of David with shouting and trumpets, Michal, Saul's daughter, watched from a window and despised David in her heart for leaping and dancing. She met him with contempt: how glorious was the king of Israel to day.
offense: Michal had once warned David of Saul's attempt upon his life and helped him escape through a window (1 Samuel 19:11-17). But when she saw him leaping and dancing before the Lord as the ark entered the city, she despised him in her heart (2 Samuel 6:16). An earlier act of loyalty did not prevent contempt from taking root later. David had laid aside the display of royal greatness for the service of that day. Chronicles describes him clothed in a robe of fine linen and wearing an ephod of linen (1 Chronicles 15:27). Michal's rebuke treated his public rejoicing as a disgrace before the handmaids. Her concern was how the king appeared in the eyes of servants, while David answered concerning the Lord before whom he rejoiced. David did not attribute the throne to his own dignity. He said that the Lord had chosen him before her father and his house, appointing him ruler over Israel (2 Samuel 6:21). The office was a gift, not a reason to consider himself too great to rejoice before its giver. The king's answer exposed the difference between honouring the Lord and guarding an image of personal importance.
judgment: David declared that he would yet be more vile and base in his own sight, and that the maidservants Michal had mentioned would honour him (2 Samuel 6:22). Her scorn did not govern his worship. He would not make royal appearance the measure of what was fitting before God. The account closes with Michal having no child unto the day of her death (2 Samuel 6:23). Her place as Saul's daughter and David's wife did not turn the contempt into a small matter. The final word upon the encounter was not the preservation of her dignity, but the absence of children. The ark's arrival had brought sacrifices, gifts of food to the people, and David's return to bless his household. Michal met that return with reproach. The contrast is within the house itself: David came to bless, while she condemned the humility with which he had honoured the Lord.

name: David and Bathsheba
charge: Adultery and the arranged death of Uriah
summary: The king took another man's wife, and when she conceived, engineered her husband's death to cover it. The prophet Nathan exposed it with a parable, and David confessed, but the consequences ran through his house for years.
offense: At the season when kings went forth to battle, David remained in Jerusalem. He saw Bathsheba, inquired after her, and was told that she was Uriah's wife before he sent messengers and took her (2 Samuel 11:1-4). Knowledge of the marriage stood before the act. The king's power to summon did not give him a right to another man's wife. When Bathsheba sent word that she was with child, David recalled Uriah from the war. Questions about Joab, the people, and the battle covered the purpose of bringing him home. Uriah would not go to his house while the ark, Israel, Judah, and his lord's servants remained in tents and the open fields (2 Samuel 11:6-11). His faithfulness frustrated the concealment. David then made him drunk, but Uriah still did not go home. The king turned from arranging an appearance to arranging a death. Uriah carried the letter ordering Joab to place him in the hottest battle and retire from him. Other servants fell with him, and David answered the report by saying that the sword devoured one as well as another (2 Samuel 11:13-25). The language of ordinary losses concealed a deliberately ordered killing. After mourning, Bathsheba became David's wife and bore a son. The matter appeared settled within the king's house, but it displeased the Lord (2 Samuel 11:26-27). Adultery had been followed by deceit and bloodshed. Deuteronomy 27:24 pronounces a curse upon the man who secretly smites his neighbour; a command carried through another man's hands did not remove David's responsibility.

Uriah's death was charged to David even though the sword was the sword of the children of Ammon (2 Samuel 12:7-9). entries.commentary: After the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle, David sent Joab and all Israel to destroy the children of Ammon and besiege Rabbah, but David tarried still at Jerusalem. In the evening he walked upon the roof, saw a woman washing herself who was very beautiful, inquired and learned she was Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, sent and took her, and lay with her; and she conceived and told David, I am with child. Masons and people in these fraternities always run here to justify wrongdoing, saying David slept with Bathsheba and the Most High still forgave him. But you are not King David; David was a man like the rest of us, and he messed up, and this is the mess up. About ninety percent of them go right back to David and Bathsheba every time they want to justify some wrongdoing.

David sent to Joab to send him Uriah. When Uriah came, David asked how Joab and the people did and how the war prospered, then told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, sending a mess of meat after him. But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. When David heard it, he asked Uriah why he came not from his journey and went not down. David's plan, which nobody was privy to, was that if Uriah went down and slept with his wife, they could say the child was his. A lot of us do that today: many people raise children that are not theirs, and just because David did it does not make it right.

Uriah told David that the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents, and Joab and the servants of his lord were encamped in the open fields; so how could he go into his house to eat, drink, and lie with his wife? As David lived, he would not do this thing. David kept him another day and made him drunk, but that evening Uriah still went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. Uriah had a sense of loyalty that was probably killing David all the more, because David could not deceive this man into laying with his wife. Even drunk, when a man might just go home to sleep it off, Uriah still slept at David's house and would not go down.

In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah, ordering that Uriah be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and then abandoned, that he might be smitten and die. Joab assigned Uriah to a place where he knew valiant men were, and when the men of the city fought, some of David's servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite died also. David set this man up to get murdered, and Israel does this too, contrary to popular belief. This goes back to Deuteronomy 27: cursed is he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, because nobody knew what David was doing, and cursed is he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. The reward was that woman; he slew an innocent man who had done nothing.

Joab sent and told David all concerning the war, charging the messenger that if the king's wrath arose over drawing so nigh the city, he should then say that Uriah the Hittite was dead also. When the messenger delivered it, David told him to say to Joab, Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another; make the battle stronger and overthrow the city. Other men of Israel died too, not just Uriah, so with David's sin other men died as well. Joab knew what the king really wanted, so he made sure to name Uriah as dead. David's reply was that it is what it is, the mission was accomplished, you win some and lose some; being content with murder is a wicked thing to do.

When the wife of Uriah heard her husband was dead, she mourned for him, and when the mourning was past, David sent and fetched her to his house and she became his wife and bare him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the Most High. It displeased the Most High because it was murder; he set the man up to be murdered on a battlefield, which was not a righteous thing. Bathsheba was not innocent either; she was complicit. When David called for her she went, she did not refuse because she was married, and it was consensual, not rape. She knew she was pregnant, so this was deceitful on both sides.

The Most High sent Nathan unto David, who told him of two men in one city, one rich and one poor. The rich man had many flocks and herds, but the poor man had nothing save one little ewe lamb he had bought and nourished up, which was unto him as a daughter. When a traveler came, the rich man spared his own flock and took the poor man's lamb. David's anger was greatly kindled, and he said the man that had done this shall surely die and restore the lamb fourfold, because he had no pity. Nathan came to David with a parable. When David judged that the man deserved to die for taking the poor man's one lamb, he was unknowingly pronouncing sentence on himself.

Nathan said unto David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the Most High: I anointed thee king over Israel, delivered thee out of the hand of Saul, gave thee thy master's house and wives, and the house of Israel and of Judah, and would have given thee more. Wherefore hast thou despised the commandment to do evil, killing Uriah the Hittite with the sword and taking his wife, slaying him with the sword of the children of Ammon? The Most High said if David would have just asked, He would have given him anything, for He had already given him the kingdom, Saul's house, and protection from Saul. The commandment David despised was what was read in [Deuteronomy 27](/bible/deuteronomy/27). There is a term called suicide by cop; David committed murder by the hand of another nation, because he set the whole thing up.

Thus saith the Most High: Now therefore the sword shall never depart from thine house, because thou hast despised me and taken the wife of Uriah to be thy wife. Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house, and I will take thy wives before thine eyes and give them unto thy neighbour, who shall lie with them in the sight of the sun. Thou didst it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun. As the four chapters go on, and beyond, you are going to see the fruition of what just happened worked out in David's own house.

David said unto Nathan, I have sinned against the Most High. Nathan said the Most High hath also put away thy sin; thou shalt not die. Howbeit, because by this deed thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the Most High to blaspheme, the child also that is born unto thee shall surely die. The judgment of David was that child being put to death. This goes back to Exodus 34: the Most High keeps mercy and forgives iniquity, but will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquities of the fathers upon the children. David got pardoned, but he did not get cleared; the punishment was still coming, one part the men of Israel dying in battle, the other his son having to die and his house having nothing but trouble.

Nathan departed, and the Most High struck the child, so that it was very sick. David besought God for the child, fasted, and lay all night upon the earth, refusing to rise or eat with the elders of his house. On the seventh day the child died, and the servants feared to tell him. When David perceived by their whispering that the child was dead, he arose, washed, anointed himself, changed his apparel, worshiped in the house of the Most High, and then ate bread. When asked why, he said that while the child lived he fasted and wept, for who could tell whether God would be gracious; but now the child was dead, he could not bring him back, he would go to him but the child would not return to him. David did all the fasting and prayer before the child died because he knew it was of the Most High that this would happen; no amount of prayer would bring the child back. David was content, saying he did not want it to happen but had no choice in the matter, for the Most High had said it would be so.

David comforted Bathsheba his wife, went in unto her, and she bare a son, and he called his name Solomon; and the Most High loved him, and sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, who called his name Jedidiah, because of the Most High. Through David's judgment, Solomon was still able to be born; it was all part of the plan of the Most High. The backup master plan behind everything was Christ, who still had to be born through David's lineage; David was still loved and still forgiven, which shows repentance, and that even the mighty among us can fall and yet rise back up.

Joab fought against Rabbah of the children of Ammon and took the royal city, then sent for David to gather the rest of the people and take the city, lest it be called after Joab's name. David gathered all the people, went to Rabbah, took it, and took the king's crown of a talent of gold with the precious stones, and set it on his head. He brought forth great spoil, put the people to labor under saws and axes of iron and to the brickkiln, and did so unto all the cities of Ammon, then returned to Jerusalem. David won against the children of Ammon once again. What we gather from these four chapters is that David was called, he was king, a very mighty man, but he slipped and fell; he had godly sorrow, and in that godly sorrow he was not put to death. If he had been, there would be no Solomon, and through that no Christ. The only one perfect in this world was Christ, in whom there was no iniquity; but the men before us, when they failed, had godly sorrow, repented, and kept the commandments of the Most High even after they fell, rising back up again. --- Topics: [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

To the chief musician, a Psalm of David, written after Nathan the prophet came to him following his sin with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah one of the soldiers in David's army. Nathan got on David about it and corrected him. Now David sends up this prayer, asking the Most High for forgiveness. David appeals to the loving kindness and tender mercies of the Most High, asking that his transgressions be blotted out.
David asks to be washed thoroughly from his iniquity and cleansed from his sin. The question is: how are we going to be washed? -

David says, "I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me." That is something we must do: acknowledge our transgressions. A lot of people do not think we deserve to come over here on slave ships or deserve to be shot down in the streets or deserve the curses put on us. But we sinned against the Most High. The pants your grandma loved wearing, the auntie who thinks she can teach in the church, standing before the scriptures with a covered head, men and women with the head wrong; we set light by the Commandments as if these are small things. We sinned against the Most High. -

Against the Most High only has David sinned and done this evil in his sight, that the Most High might be justified when he speaks and clear when he judges. We are not going to stand before the Most High and be justified talking about "me and Jesus." If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God. Wearing pants, not wearing fringes, crossdressing; none of that will be excused. -
David was shapen in iniquity, and in sin did his mother conceive him, meaning he was born from a natural childbirth.
The Most High desires truth in the inward parts, and in the hidden part he makes us to know wisdom.

Purge me with hyssop and I shall be clean; wash me and I shall be whiter than snow. David says this for a reason, because the ordinances set up in the earth are patterned after what goes on in the heavens, and Christ is our high priest. -
Make me to hear joy and gladness, that the bones which thou hast broken may rejoice. This does not mean the Most High literally broke his bones; it means correction. -
Hide thy face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities. Blessed is the man whose transgressions are covered.
Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. We must understand what we read; this is a renewing of the mind, like Nicodemus asking how a man can be born again. -
Cast me not away from thy presence, and take not thy holy spirit from me. The best thing going for us is to be in the presence of the Most High. -

Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation and uphold me with thy free spirit. David understood the importance of losing the kingdom; from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom suffers violence, and they kill us and get away with it. That is the wages of sin. -
Then will I teach transgressors thy ways, and sinners shall be converted unto thee.
Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, because David had killed the man. The true baptism is not the dipping in water but the answer of a good conscience toward the Most High. -
O Lord, open thou my lips, and my mouth shall show forth thy praise.
For thou desirest not sacrifice, else would I give it; thou delightest not in burnt offerings. Christ left us his example and taught nothing different than David. -
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, a broken and a contrite heart, which the Most High will not despise. Contrite means meek and teachable. -
Do good in thy good pleasure unto Zion; build thou the walls of Jerusalem. In captivity we are like those who built the wall with one hand and fought with the other; it is time to rebuild a nation.
Then shalt thou be pleased with the sacrifices of righteousness, with burnt offering and whole burnt offering; then shall they offer bullocks upon thine altar.

Abijam reigns three years in Jerusalem and walks in all the sins of his father, his heart not perfect with the Most High as David's was. The children did what they saw their fathers do, not merely what was said, which is why the Most High teaches His people to be different. Yet for David's sake the Most High gives him a lamp in Jerusalem, because David did right all his days save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite, a wrong from which David repented. -

After Abijam dies, Asa his son reigns forty-one years and does right in the eyes of the Most High as David his father did. Asa takes the sodomites out of the land, removes the idols his fathers made, and even removes his own mother Maachah from being queen because she made an idol in a grove, which he destroys and burns at the brook Kidron. Though the high places are not removed, Asa's heart is perfect with the Most High all his days, and he brings dedicated silver, gold, and vessels into the house of the Most High.

There is war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel, who builds Ramah to cut off passage to and from Asa. Asa takes silver and gold from the house of the Most High and the king's house and sends it to Benhadad of Syria to break his league with Baasha, and Benhadad smites cities of Israel so Baasha stops building Ramah. Asa uses the stones and timber of Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah. In his old age he is diseased in his feet, then sleeps with his fathers, and Jehoshaphat his son reigns in his place.

Nadab son of Jeroboam reigns over Israel two years and does evil, walking in the way and sin of his father. Baasha conspires against him, kills him, and reigns in his place, then smites all the house of Jeroboam, leaving none that breathed, according to the word spoken by Ahijah the Shilonite. This fulfills, years later, the judgment that Jeroboam's descendants would be destroyed for the sins by which he made Israel to sin.

Baasha reigns twenty-four years in Tirzah and does evil, walking in the way of Jeroboam and in the sin by which he made Israel to sin. The pattern continues: each king who follows takes up the sin of the one before, and the same judgments keep coming.

name: Uriah the Hittite
charge: Refusing the comfort of his own house while the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents
summary: Recalled from the siege of Rabbah so that the king's crime could be covered, he would not go down to his house. He slept at the door of the king's house with the servants. Asked why, he said the ark and Israel and Judah abide in tents, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house? He was made drunk and still would not go, and was sent back carrying the letter that ordered his death.
offense: Uriah the Hittite is numbered among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39). When recalled from the war, he would not receive the comforts of his own house while the ark, Israel, Judah, Joab, and the servants remained in tents and the open fields. He answered David with an oath that he would not do such a thing (2 Samuel 11:11). David's invitation would have been convenient to accept. Uriah had the king's permission to go home, and the king sent a mess of meat after him. Yet he slept at the door of the king's house with the servants (2 Samuel 11:8-9). His concern reached beyond what he was personally allowed to enjoy. He remembered the men still bearing the burden from which he had briefly been recalled. Even when David made him drunk, Uriah did not return to his wife (2 Samuel 11:13). The purpose concealed behind the hospitality failed. The servant maintained his course while the king employed his authority to hide a transgression. David then entrusted him with the letter that ordered his death. Uriah carried it to Joab and returned to the fighting (2 Samuel 11:14-17). The loyalty by which he served his king was used against him. His death did not expose a failure of courage or duty; it exposed the treachery of the command placed over him. Nathan's charge did not let Uriah disappear into the unnamed losses of battle. The Lord declared that David had killed Uriah with the sword and taken his wife (2 Samuel 12:9). The man whom the king had sought to conceal remained named in the judgment against the king. The later summary of David's reign again singled out the matter of Uriah the Hittite (1 Kings 15:5). Matthew also identifies Solomon's mother as her who had been the wife of Urias (Matthew 1:6). The record of the royal line did not erase the marriage that David had violated. Uriah was not delivered from the fatal order. His fidelity must not be measured by whether he escaped suffering. The account honours the servant's conduct while condemning the ruler who exploited it. The throne could command his movements, but it could not make the blood innocent of accusation.

name: Amnon
charge: Rape of his sister Tamar
summary: David's firstborn feigned sickness to get his half-sister alone, and when she pleaded that such a thing should not be done in Israel, forced her, then hated her more than he had loved her and had her thrown out. David was very wroth and did nothing.
offense: Amnon desired Tamar, his sister, and received Jonadab's counsel to feign sickness and ask that she prepare food before him. David sent her without knowing the purpose of the request. Once she had brought the food, Amnon dismissed the others and drew her into the chamber (2 Samuel 13:1-10). A household duty became the means by which he isolated her. Tamar refused him plainly. She named the act folly in Israel and spoke of the shame it would bring upon her and the wickedness it would attach to him. He would not hearken, but overpowered and forced her (2 Samuel 13:11-14). Her words were not a hesitation to be overcome; they were a refusal that he chose to disregard. The law forbade uncovering a sister's nakedness (Leviticus 18:9). Tamar's appeal to speak to the king did not repeal that command. Nor could Amnon's desire make the violence a mutual offense. Deuteronomy 22:25-26 distinguishes the man who forces a woman from the woman against whom he acts, comparing the assault to a man rising against his neighbour and slaying him. Afterward Amnon hated her more than he had loved her and ordered her out. When she protested that this added evil to the first, he would not listen. His servant put her out and bolted the door (2 Samuel 13:15-18). The appetite that had called itself love would neither protect her nor hear her distress once it had obtained its object.
judgment: Tamar rent her garment, put ashes upon her head, and went away crying. She remained desolate in Absalom's house. David heard and was very wroth, but the account records no judicial sentence imposed by him upon Amnon (2 Samuel 13:19-22). Anger within the palace did not repair what had been done to Tamar. Absalom concealed his hatred for two full years. At his sheep-shearing feast he instructed his servants to strike Amnon when his heart was merry with wine, and they killed him (2 Samuel 13:23-29). The death answered a brother's revenge, not an orderly hearing under the law. Amnon's guilt did not make every act against him righteous. The king's sons fled, David mourned, and Absalom escaped to Geshur. The sword Nathan had announced was working within David's own house (2 Samuel 12:10; 13:30-39). The calamity was larger than the death of the offender: Tamar remained desolate, the brothers were scattered, and the father was left to mourn a household he had not kept from violence.
