verses.text: 18And all his servants passed on beside him; and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king. 19Then said the king to Ittai the Gittite, Wherefore goest thou also with us? return to thy place, and abide with the king: for thou art a stranger, and also an exile.

20Whereas thou camest but yesterday, should I this day make thee go up and down with us? seeing I go whither I may, return thou, and take back thy brethren: mercy and truth be with thee. 21And Ittai answered the king, and said, As the Lord liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be. 22And David said to Ittai, Go and pass over. And Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones that were with him.

2And David sent forth a third part of the people under the hand of Joab, and a third part under the hand of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third part under the hand of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said unto the people, I will surely go forth with you myself also.

entries.commentary: Absalom prepared chariots and horses and fifty men to run before him, rose up early, and stood beside the way of the gate. When any man came to the king for judgment, Absalom called him, said his matters were good and right but there was no man deputed of the king to hear him, and wished that he himself were made judge in the land that he might do every man justice. This is the sneakiness Absalom did: he began to underhand the king, winning the love of the people behind the king's back, so that he could later betray him, as the prophecy said the sword would not depart from David's house.

When any man came near to do him obeisance, Absalom put forth his hand, took him, and kissed him, and on this manner he did to all Israel that came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. Instead of going to the king and resolving things, Absalom got into the king's good graces, then went around patting people on the back and stroking them. This is what the bishop calls friendish, showing people friendship without being a true friend.

After forty years Absalom asked leave to go pay his vow in Hebron, and the king said, Go in peace. But Absalom sent spies through all the tribes to say, at the sound of the trumpet, Absalom reigneth in Hebron. Two hundred men went with him from Jerusalem in their simplicity, knowing nothing. Absalom also sent for Ahithophel, David's counsellor, and the conspiracy was strong, for the people increased continually with Absalom. This shows the simplicity of a lot of brothers in Israel: a man who says all the nice things and gains favor in your eyes goes completely against leadership and out of order, and you follow along carnally, not spiritually, because he kissed your hand and told you everything would be all right.

A messenger told David the hearts of the men of Israel were with Absalom, and David told his servants to arise and flee, lest Absalom overtake them suddenly and smite the city with the sword. The king went forth with all his household, leaving ten women who were concubines to keep the house, and all his servants and the Cherethites, Pelethites, and six hundred Gittites passed on before him. David, being the man of war that he is, saw everyone starting to follow Absalom, and instead of sitting there like a dummy, chose to leave and strategize while he was out.

The king told Ittai the Gittite to return, since he was a stranger and an exile who had only just come, and wished him mercy and truth. But Ittai swore that in whatever place the king was, in death or life, there also would his servant be, so David said, Go and pass over, and Ittai passed over with all his men and little ones. All the country wept as the people passed over the brook Kidron toward the wilderness. Ittai showed a level of loyalty that David respected, so David let him come. This loyalty in the face of trouble is the same thing seen throughout Israel's story.

Zadok and all the Levites bare the ark of the covenant, and David told Zadok to carry it back into the city, saying if he found favour in the eyes of the Most High, he would be brought again to see it and its habitation; but if not, let the Most High do as seemed good. He also told Zadok the seer to return with his son Ahimaaz and Jonathan the son of Abiathar, and to send him word. So they carried the ark again to Jerusalem. David sent the ark back in faith: make sure it stays in the city, and if it is the Most High's will, I will return. That is how much faith David had. Many of the songs in the book of Psalms were written while David was on the run like this, and some of it is prophecy of Christ, because the spirit of Christ was in every prophet.

David went up the ascent of Mount Olivet weeping, barefoot, his head covered, and all the people with him weeping. When told that Ahithophel was among the conspirators, David prayed that the Most High turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness. Then Hushai the Archite met him with his coat rent, and David sent him back to the city to feign service to Absalom and defeat Ahithophel's counsel, reporting all he heard to Zadok and Abiathar by their two sons. Ahithophel was such a good counsellor that his counsel was said to be like inquiring at the oracle of God, like talking to an angel of the Most High. So David prayed the Most High would turn that counsel into foolishness, and sent his friend Hushai to act like Absalom's servant so he could listen to Ahithophel's counsel and intervene. This was a game of chess, not checkers, and that is how we have to treat this thing today.

David numbered the people and set captains of thousands and hundreds, sending a third part under Joab, a third under Abishai, and a third under Ittai the Gittite. He said he would surely go forth with them himself. The people answered that he should not go, for he was worth ten thousand of them and it was better that he support them out of the city. David hearkened to their counsel and said what seemed best to them he would do; he did not run a dictatorship. In a time when he could not trust his own flesh and blood, he trusted the proven men he had warred with for years. David charged Joab, Abishai, and Ittai to deal gently for his sake with the young man, even with Absalom, and all the people heard the charge. Even after Absalom defiled his concubines and stole the people's hearts, David still sought to make amends with his son.

The battle was in the wood of Ephraim, and Israel was slain before the servants of David in a great slaughter of twenty thousand men. The wood devoured more people that day than the sword devoured. Absalom, riding on a mule, went under the thick boughs of a great oak, and his head caught hold of the oak so that he was taken up between the heaven and the earth while the mule went on. He hung there yet alive. A man told Joab he had seen Absalom hanged in an oak. Joab asked why he had not smitten him to the ground for a reward of ten shekels and a girdle, but the man refused, saying he would not put forth his hand against the king's son for a thousand shekels, because he had heard the king charge them to beware that none touch the young man. The man told Joab that to have killed Absalom would have been to work falsehood against his own life, for nothing is hid from the king, and Joab himself would have set himself against him. Joab said he would not tarry, took three darts, and thrust them through the heart of Absalom while he was yet alive in the midst of the oak. Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder; he could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted. Ten young men that bore Joab's armor compassed Absalom and smote him and slew him, for a beast will consort to his own like.

Joab blew the trumpet and held back the people from pursuing Israel. They took Absalom, cast him into a great pit in the woods, and laid a very great heap of stones upon him, and all Israel fled everyone to his tent. In his lifetime Absalom had reared up a pillar for himself in the king's dale, saying he had no son to keep his name in remembrance, and he called it after his own name; it is called Absalom's place unto this day.

Ahimaaz wanted to run and bear the king the tidings that the Lord had avenged him of his enemies, but Joab first sent Cushi, since the king's son was dead and this was not good news to carry. Ahimaaz pressed again and was allowed to run, and he outran Cushi by way of the plain. David sat between the two gates while the watchman on the wall saw first Ahimaaz running alone, then another man. The king said a man running alone brings tidings, and he recognized the running of Ahimaaz as a good man coming with good news. Ahimaaz fell before the king and said all was well, blessing the Lord who had delivered up the men that lifted their hand against the king; the good news was that David was alive and had overcome. When David asked if the young man Absalom was safe, Ahimaaz said he saw a great tumult but knew not what it was. Cushi came and said the enemies of the king and all that rose against him should be as that young man is. David understood that his son was one of the casualties of war. He was much moved, went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept, crying, O my son Absalom, would God I had died for thee. David's whole life was war, slaughtering giants from his youth up, and now he mourned in heartache for his son.

name: Shimei son of Gera
charge: Cursing the king and casting stones at him
summary: As David fled Jerusalem, Shimei of Saul's house came out cursing and throwing stones and dust: come out, thou bloody man, thou man of Belial. David forbade Abishai to kill him and later swore he would not put him to death. Solomon inherited the case.
offense: As David fled from Absalom, Shimei came out cursing, casting stones, and calling him a bloody man. He claimed that the Lord had returned the blood of Saul's house upon David (2 Samuel 16:5-8). David had repeatedly refused to kill Saul and had judged men who expected reward for deaths within Saul's house. Shimei used David's present distress as proof of an accusation the record did not sustain. Abishai asked leave to take his head, but David restrained him. With his own son seeking his life, David would not make Shimei's abuse the occasion for another immediate killing. He left room for the Lord to look upon his affliction and return good for the cursing (2 Samuel 16:9-12). The restraint belonged to David; it did not turn the curse into lawful speech. Exodus 22:28 forbids cursing the ruler of the people.
judgment: Solomon confined him to Jerusalem on pain of death. Three years later Shimei went to Gath after runaway servants, and Solomon had Benaiah kill him: the Lord shall return thy wickedness upon thine own head.

Exodus 22:28 forbids cursing the ruler of the people.

As David came to Bahurim, a man of the house of Saul named Shimei the son of Gera came out, cursing and casting stones at David and all his servants. Shimei cursed, calling David a bloody man and a man of Belial, saying the Most High had returned upon him all the blood of the house of Saul, and delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom his son, and taken him in his mischief because he was a bloody man. Shimei was of the house of Saul, and Saul was the wicked one who tried to kill David; it was by the hand of the Most High that Saul did not succeed. Yet Shimei cursed David as if David were in the wrong, because word gets around, people gossip and blame, and he saw David at a low state and went to rub it in his face. That is the mindset of some people in Israel as well.

Abishai the son of Zeruiah asked why this dead dog should curse the king, and offered to go take off his head. But the king said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, because the Most High hath said unto him, Curse David; who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so? David rolled with mighty men of war, so Abishai was ready to take Shimei's head off his shoulders. But David said to let him curse, for if it was of the Most High, then let him do it. Just as the Most High brings people to our forums and classrooms who bicker and try to bring confusion, it is of the Most High, sometimes to test the patience of those who pray for patience.

David said to Abishai and all his servants, Behold, my own son who came forth out of my bowels seeketh my life, how much more now may this Benjamite do it? Let him alone and let him curse, for the Most High hath bidden him. It may be that the Most High will look on his affliction and requite him good for the cursing this day. David reasoned that if his own son sought his life, this Benjamite was nothing; the Most High was doing this, so let him curse. It may be the Most High will look on all that was done to David and bless him in front of them, the same as when people try to bring us down and the Most High blesses us before them, which is why this congregation has grown exponentially.

David and his men went by the way while Shimei went along the hillside cursing, throwing stones, and casting dust; and they came weary and refreshed themselves. Absalom and all the men of Israel came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him. When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom saying, God save the king, Absalom asked why he went not with his friend, and Hushai answered that he would serve whom the Most High and Israel chose, and would serve in the presence of the son as he served the father. Hushai put into action the plan he and David made. Absalom challenged him, asking, Is this thy kindness to thy friend? Why wentest thou not with thy friend? This is a real friend, not a friendish one; a true friend tells you when you are wrong and full of it, not the one who only strokes your head and pats your back like Absalom did to steal the people's hearts.

Absalom asked Ahithophel for counsel, and Ahithophel said, Go in unto thy father's concubines whom he left to keep the house, and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father, and the hands of all with thee shall be strong. So they spread Absalom a tent on the top of the house, and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel. The counsel of Ahithophel was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God. Ahithophel counselled Absalom to lie with the ten concubines David left, in the sight of all Israel, on the roof of the house. This is the exact fulfillment of what the Most High spoke in chapter 12, that David's wives would be taken and one would lie with them in the sight of the sun, and that what David did secretly would be done before all Israel. It was not coincidence or irony; it was prophesied to happen, and none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did. The Most High keeps mercy and forgives, but by no means clears the guilty, so even when we come in and repent, we still must remember the fear of the Most High, for there is but one step between us and death.

The victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, because they heard how the king grieved for his son, and they got them by stealth into the city as ashamed men steal away when they flee in battle. Joab came into the house and told David he had shamed the faces of all his servants who had saved his life and the lives of his sons, daughters, wives, and concubines, because he loved his enemies and hated his friends. Joab said if Absalom had lived and all of them had died, it would have pleased David well. No one else could speak to the king this way, but Joab knew David's skeletons. Joab charged David to arise and speak comfortably unto his servants, swearing that if he did not, not one man would tarry with him that night, and that would be worse than all the evil that had befallen him from his youth. Then the king arose and sat in the gate, and all the people came before him.

All the tribes of Israel were at strife, saying the king had saved them from the Philistines and their enemies but had fled the land because of Absalom, who was now dead, so why did they say nothing about bringing the king back. David sent to Zadok and Abiathar the priests to speak to the elders of Judah, asking why they were the last to bring the king back when they were his brethren, his bone and his flesh. He told Amasa that he would make him captain of the host in the room of Joab. David bowed the heart of all the men of Judah as the heart of one man, so they sent word for him to return with all his servants, and the king came again to Jordan while Judah came to Gilgal to meet him and conduct him over.

Shimei the son of Gera the Benjamite hastened down with a thousand men of Benjamin, along with Ziba the servant of Saul's house with his sons and servants, and fell down before the king at Jordan. Shimei begged the king not to impute iniquity unto him nor remember the day he did perversely when David went out of Jerusalem, confessing that he had sinned. This was the same Shimei who had cursed David, cast stones, and called him a bloody man and a man of Belial while David was in a low state surrounded by his mighty men. Abishai and the sons of Zeruiah said Shimei should be put to death for cursing the Lord's anointed, but David rebuked them as adversaries, asking whether any man should be put to death that day in Israel when he knew he was king. He swore Shimei would not die. David understood grace long before the New Testament, for grace has always been around.

Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king, having neither dressed his feet, trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes from the day the king departed until he returned in peace, showing his mourning for David. When asked why he had not gone with the king, Mephibosheth said his servant Ziba had deceived him and slandered him, since Mephibosheth was lame and could not saddle his own beast. He acknowledged that all his father's house were dead men before the king, yet David had set him to eat at his own table, so he had no further right to cry to the king. David told him to speak no more of the matter and said that he and Ziba should divide the land. Mephibosheth answered that Ziba could take it all, for it was enough that his lord the king had come again in peace to his own house.

Barzillai the Gileadite, a very aged man of fourscore years, came down from Rogelim to conduct the king over Jordan, having provided the king with sustenance at Mahanaim, for he was a very great man. When David invited him to come and be fed in Jerusalem, Barzillai asked how long he had to live that he should go up, saying at eighty years old he could no longer discern the taste of what he ate or drank nor hear the voice of singing men and women, so he would only go a little way over and asked to return and die in his own city by his parents' grave. He sent Chimham in his place, and the king kissed and blessed Barzillai, who returned to his own place. A quarrel then arose between the men of Israel and the men of Judah over who had the right to bring the king back. Judah claimed the king was near of kin to them, being of the tribe of Judah, while Israel claimed ten parts in the king and more right in David, and the words of Judah were fiercer than the words of Israel. This was the tribe strife that would later split the northern and southern kingdoms, though they were all Israel.

The days of David draw near that he should die, and he charges Solomon to be strong, to keep the charge of the Lord his God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes, commandments, and judgments as written in the law of Moses, that he may prosper. There was a stipulation for the throne to continue: if his children take heed to their way and walk before the Most High in truth with all their heart, the throne stands. Reading through the kings, we see many who broke the commandments, and among their children some were righteous and some unrighteous. -
Solomon thrusts out Abiathar from being priest unto the Lord, fulfilling the word the Most High spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh. The old judgment on Eli's line is carried out.

Joab, who had turned after Adonijah, flees to the tabernacle of the Lord and catches hold of the horns of the altar, but Solomon sends Benaiah to fall upon him. Joab dies for the innocent blood he shed when he slew Abner and Amasa, two men more righteous and better than he, without David's knowledge. The blood returns upon Joab's own head and upon his seed, while upon David and his seed and throne there shall be peace forever from the Lord. Benaiah is set over the host in his place.

Shimei is commanded to build a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, never crossing the brook Kidron on pain of death, and he agrees. After three years he goes to Gath after his runaway servants and breaks the oath, so Solomon has Benaiah put him to death, and the kingdom is established in Solomon's hand.

If a man steal an ox or a sheep and kill it or sell it, he restores five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep. We are in a different situation where we do not keep oxen and sheep, but the principle of restitution still applies among brothers and sisters in the body: if something is stolen, the law written here governs the payback. Do not be stealing.

If a thief be found breaking up means breaking in. He entered your home and you defended yourself and he died: that is what is called self-defense today, and no blood is shed for him, meaning there is no judgment. The judgment was already passed in the breaking in. If the sun be risen upon him, the thief got away, and there shall be blood shed for him means there shall be a judgment; then the verse gives the judgment. He makes full restitution, and if he have nothing he is sold for his theft: not sold into slavery, but into work servitude until he pays off the debt of what he stole. If the theft be found in his hand alive, he restores double. Verse three covers the thief who already got rid of what he stole; verse four covers the one still holding it.

These are self-explanatory: if a man lets his beast feed in another man's field or vineyard, he makes restitution of the best of his own field and vineyard; and he that kindles a fire that consumes another man's corn surely makes restitution.

If a man deliver money or stuff to his neighbor to keep and it be stolen, the thief found pays double. If the thief be not found, the master of the house is brought unto the judges, to see whether he put his hand unto his neighbor's goods, whether he was part of a scheme to deceive the owner out of his goods. For all manner of trespass, whether for ox, ass, sheep, raiment, or any lost thing, both parties come before the judges, and whom the judges condemn pays double unto his neighbor.

If a beast delivered to a neighbor to keep die or be hurt or driven away, no man seeing it, an oath of the Lord is between them both. In layman's terms he swears: I did not take the stuff, I did not set you up, I do not know where it is. The owner accepts the oath and the matter ends there; it is not to be spoken of again. Paul uses this civil law to show how the Most High is unchangeable. An oath for confirmation is the end of all strife; God confirmed his counsel by an oath, and by two immutable things, that it is impossible for God to lie and that he will not take back what went out of his mouth, we have strong consolation. The same way, once the oath of this law is applied, the matter is over.

If the thing kept be stolen from him, he makes restitution; if it be torn in pieces, he brings it for witness and does not make it good. If a man borrow ought of his neighbor, ought meaning anything, and it be hurt or die with the owner not present, he surely makes it good. You borrowed it, it got messed up, you owe the man. But if the owner be with it, or if it be an hired thing, it came for its hire. If you came to plow a man's field for ten shekels with your own donkey and your donkey breaks his leg, you cannot expect the owner to pay for your own faulty equipment; the same as a business loan today, the property owner is not liable when your own equipment breaks down.

If a man entice a maid that is not betrothed and lie with her, he shall surely endow her to be his wife; he has to sign the papers. He is at fault for not going through the proper channels of marriage, and she is at fault for being enticed and laying down. The proper channel was that the father married off the daughter. To marry thy daughter is to perform a weighty matter, for the father gives her over to that man for the rest of her life and is out of all watching over her; so she is to be given to a man of understanding, one keeping the commandments as a wise man. In our own land the daughter went from her father's house to a husband's house with the blessing of the father.

Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live: witchcraft goes into horoscopes, palm readings, and all things of that nature. Whosoever lieth with a beast, bestiality, shall surely be put to death. He that sacrificeth unto any god save unto the Lord only shall be utterly destroyed.

This is twofold, and first and foremost the stranger is your brother from a different area, our own people. [Leviticus 25](/bible/leviticus/25) shows it: if thy brother be waxen poor, though he be a stranger or a sojourner, sojourn meaning travel, thou shalt relieve him that he may live with thee. A brother of another tribe who falls on hard times and travels down to live with you is that stranger; neither vex him nor oppress him, for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.

Ye shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child. A wife without a husband already has a hard life, and a son or daughter without a father the same; do not make their life harder than it already is. If thou afflict them in any wise and they cry unto the Most High, he will surely hear their cry, and his wrath shall wax hot: he will kill you with the sword, and your own wives shall be widows and your children fatherless. That is the Lord's plain warning against mistreating those less fortunate.

Usury means interest. You cannot charge your brother or sister interest: if you lend twenty dollars, you get twenty dollars back, nothing more, nothing less; no little bit more off the top. This is the same law read in [Leviticus 25:36-37](/bible/leviticus/25#v36).

If thou take thy neighbor's raiment to pledge, deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down, for that is his covering only; wherein shall he sleep? The tunics and overcoats worn then were also sleeping garments to keep a man warm at night, especially the poor. A well-off man does not have to work for you; this speaks of the less fortunate who extend their services for money and give what is most valuable to them, their raiment, as the pledge. If he cries unto the Most High, he will hear, for he is gracious.

Thou shalt not revile the gods means do not hate or speak evil of your leaders. The word gods here is the leaders over you: the Most High says in the psalm, I have said, Ye are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High, speaking of us. [Acts 23](/bible/acts/23) is the example: when Paul spoke against the high priest, they that stood by said, Revilest thou God's high priest? And Paul answered, I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest: for it is written, Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people, quoting this very verse.

Thou shalt not delay to offer the first of thy ripe fruits and of thy liquors, and the firstborn of thy sons shalt thou give unto me. The firstborn sons that opened the matrix were consecrated unto the Lord, and the father redeemed them back from the priest with shekels. Likewise with the oxen and the sheep: seven days the firstling stayed with his dam, his mother, and on the eighth day it was given. The Lord did not want it too young, taken as soon as it popped out; it had to be its appointed time with the mother, then brought to the priest.

Ye shall be holy men unto me: neither shall ye eat any flesh that is torn of beasts in the field; ye shall cast it to the dogs. This is twofold, and the dogs are the strangers of other nations, the aliens and foreigners. Always get the context of the law, because sometimes the stranger is your brother and sometimes it is literally the other nations. [Deuteronomy 14:21](/bible/deuteronomy/14#v21) doubles this law: that which dieth of itself thou shalt give unto the stranger that is in thy gates, or sell it unto an alien, for thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God. Cast the torn flesh to the other nations; ye shall not eat it, because ye are holy people.

Dead flies make the apothecary's ointment stink; so a little folly ruins the man who holds a reputation for wisdom and honor. A wise man's heart is at his right hand, but a fool's heart at his left. Even as the fool walks by the way his wisdom fails him, and he shows everyone that he is a fool. If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, leave not your place, for yielding pacifies great offenses.

There is an evil under the sun, an error that proceeds from the ruler: folly is set in high dignity while the rich sit in a low place. He has seen servants riding upon horses and princes walking as servants upon the earth, the natural order turned upside down.

He that digs a pit shall fall into it, and whoever breaks a hedge a serpent shall bite; he that removes stones is hurt by them, and he that cleaves wood is endangered by it. If the iron is blunt and the edge is not whetted, more strength is needed, but wisdom is profitable to direct. The serpent bites without enchantment, and a babbler is no better.

The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious, but the fool is swallowed up by his own lips. His talk begins in foolishness and ends in mischievous madness. A fool is full of words, though no man can tell what shall be after him. The labor of the foolish wearies every one of them because he does not even know how to go to the city.

Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning; blessed is the land whose king is the son of nobles and whose princes eat in due season, for strength and not for drunkenness. Slothfulness lets the building decay and idleness makes the house drop through. A feast is made for laughter and wine makes merry, but money answers all things. Curse not the king, not even in your thought, nor the rich in your bedchamber, for a bird of the air shall carry the voice and tell the matter.

name: Barzillai the Gileadite
charge: Bringing beds, wheat, and honey to the king and his hungry men in the wilderness at Mahanaim
summary: When David fled from Absalom, an old man of Rogelim brought provision for the king and the people with him, saying, The people is hungry, and weary, and thirsty, in the wilderness. David wanted to keep him at court for life. Barzillai was eighty and asked only to die in his own city; David took his son instead, and charged Solomon on his deathbed to remember the house.
offense: When David came to Mahanaim during Absalom's rebellion, Barzillai joined Shobi and Machir in bringing beds, vessels, grain, pulses, honey, butter, sheep, and cheese for the people. They considered the people hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness (2 Samuel 17:27-29). Their service answered the actual condition of those who had fled. Barzillai was very aged and a very great man, and he sustained the king while David lay at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 19:32). Wealth became provision at a moment when the kingdom's outcome was not settled. He assisted the displaced king before the victory made that assistance safe or fashionable. After the rebellion, he came down to conduct David over Jordan. David offered to take him to Jerusalem and feed him there. Barzillai, eighty years old, answered concerning the limits of his age and asked to return to his own city near the burial place of his father and mother (2 Samuel 19:31-37). His service had not been a concealed demand for life at court.
judgment: The king said unto Barzillai, Come thou over with me, and I will feed thee with me in Jerusalem. Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do to him that which shall seem good unto thee: and whatsoever thou shalt require of me, that will I do for thee. And the king kissed Barzillai, and blessed him. David to Solomon: shew kindness unto the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be of those that eat at thy table: for so they came to me when I fled because of Absalom thy brother. Centuries later his family was still known by his name.
offenseFull: When David came to Mahanaim during Absalom's rebellion, Barzillai joined Shobi and Machir in bringing beds, vessels, grain, pulses, honey, butter, sheep, and cheese for the people. They considered the people hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness (2 Samuel 17:27-29). Their service answered the actual condition of those who had fled.

Barzillai was very aged and a very great man, and he sustained the king while David lay at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 19:32). Wealth became provision at a moment when the kingdom's outcome was not settled. He assisted the displaced king before the victory made that assistance safe or fashionable.

After the rebellion, he came down to conduct David over Jordan. David offered to take him to Jerusalem and feed him there. Barzillai, eighty years old, answered concerning the limits of his age and asked to return to his own city near the burial place of his father and mother (2 Samuel 19:31-37). His service had not been a concealed demand for life at court.

entries.commentary: Ahithophel had already given Absalom wicked counsel in the previous chapter, telling him to go in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel so that the hands of all that were with him would be made strong. Ahithophel was David's own counselor turned traitor, being the devil the Bible speaks of, working deceit and betrayal from inside the gates of Israel. His counsel in those days was regarded as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God. That tells you Ahithophel was very influential and had the gift of gab, so persuasive that his advice sounded almost biblical. Now he asks Absalom to let him choose out twelve thousand men to pursue David that same night while David was weary and weak handed, to smite the king only and bring back all the people. He wanted the victory and the bragging rights of being the one who killed King David.

Absalom wanted a second opinion, so he called Hushai the Archite to hear likewise what he would say. There is safety in a multitude of counselors, but only where the counsel is according to thus saith the Lord; a counselor who does not go to the scriptures is not one you should want. Hushai told Absalom that Ahithophel's counsel was not good at this time. He reminded him that his father and his mighty men were mighty and chafed in their minds as a bear robbed of her whelps, war ready and strategic, and that David would not lodge with the people but move by night. Hushai warned that if Absalom's men were overthrown at the first, even the most valiant warrior whose heart is as the heart of a lion would utterly melt, for all Israel knew David was a mighty man. This shows David and his mighty men were on another level; none of Absalom's thousands could compare to them. Instead Hushai counseled that all Israel be gathered from Dan to Beersheba as the sand by the sea, with Absalom going to battle in his own person. This deliberately inaccurate counsel would waste time gathering troops and give David room to escape; Hushai was a counterintelligence agent, a spy planted in righteousness, always siding with King David. Absalom and all the men of Israel said Hushai's counsel was better than Ahithophel's. The Lord had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that He might bring evil upon Absalom. The Lord was working with Hushai and David, while Satan was in the spirit of Absalom and Ahithophel.

Hushai reported both Ahithophel's counsel and his own to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, telling them to send quickly and warn David not to lodge in the plains of the wilderness that night but to pass over speedily, lest he be swallowed up. The messengers Jonathan and Ahimaaz waited by En-rogel; a maidservant carried the word to them, but a lad saw them and told Absalom. The Most High put His spirit on certain people to orchestrate His plan; often when a man tries to do evil to another, it falls back on him, for he that diggeth a pit shall fall therein. They fled to a man's house in Bahurim that had a well, and a woman spread a covering over the well's mouth and ground corn upon it to camouflage it. When Absalom's servants came asking, she told them the men had gone over the brook of water, and the pursuers returned to Jerusalem. The two came up out of the well and told David to arise and pass quickly over the water. David and all the people passed over Jordan by the morning light, and there lacked not one of them that was not gone over.

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he set his house in order and hanged himself. The evil counsel he devised reared its head around and bit its author; evil pursueth sinners, but to the righteous good shall be repaid. To be righteous is to observe to do all the commandments of the Lord; all unrighteousness is sin, and sin is the transgression of the law. David was righteous and did not want to war against his own son, yet good was repaid to him, while the sinner was pursued by his own evil.

He swore Shimei would not die. David understood grace long before the New Testament, for grace has always been around.

Judah claimed the king was near of kin to them, being of the tribe of Judah, while Israel claimed ten parts in the king and more right in David, and the words of Judah were fiercer than the words of Israel. This was the tribe strife that would later split the northern and southern kingdoms, though they were all Israel.

The days of David draw near that he should die, and he charges Solomon to be strong, to keep the charge of the Lord his God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes, commandments, and judgments as written in the law of Moses, that he may prosper. There was a stipulation for the throne to continue: if his children take heed to their way and walk before the Most High in truth with all their heart, the throne stands. Reading through the kings, we see many who broke the commandments, and among their children some were righteous and some unrighteous. -
Solomon thrusts out Abiathar from being priest unto the Lord, fulfilling the word the Most High spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh. The old judgment on Eli's line is carried out.

Joab, who had turned after Adonijah, flees to the tabernacle of the Lord and catches hold of the horns of the altar, but Solomon sends Benaiah to fall upon him. Joab dies for the innocent blood he shed when he slew Abner and Amasa, two men more righteous and better than he, without David's knowledge. The blood returns upon Joab's own head and upon his seed, while upon David and his seed and throne there shall be peace forever from the Lord. Benaiah is set over the host in his place.

Shimei is commanded to build a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, never crossing the brook Kidron on pain of death, and he agrees. After three years he goes to Gath after his runaway servants and breaks the oath, so Solomon has Benaiah put him to death, and the kingdom is established in Solomon's hand.

These are the children of the province who came up out of captivity, whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away, returning each man to his own city in Jerusalem and Judah. The first wave came led by Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, and the other chief men. Zerubbabel had been one of the bodyguards of the Persian Empire, the wisest guard granted a request in 1 Esdras. -
The men of the people of Israel are numbered family by family, house by house, showing exactly who returned. The record is precise because Israel kept careful count of who came back to the land.
The priests, Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants are all counted. Each service group is named so the temple work could be carried out by the proper lineages.

Some could not show their father's house or their seed, whether they were of Israel, and were set aside. The priests who could not find their register by genealogy were put from the priesthood as polluted, forbidden the most holy things until a priest stood up with Urim and Thummim. -
The whole congregation together numbered 42,360, beside their servants and maids. Their singing men and women, horses, mules, camels, and asses are all counted.

Some of the chief of the fathers, coming to the house of the Lord at Jerusalem, offer freely to set it up in its place. They give after their ability to the treasure of the work, and the priests, Levites, and people dwell in their cities.

Five were wise and five were foolish. The foolish took their lamps and took no oil with them; the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps. The oil is the wisdom of the scriptures. The foolish come afterward saying, Lord, Lord, open to us, and are answered, Verily I say unto you, I know you not. Calling on his name while breaking the commandments is exactly this. Men bless what the law calls an abomination and still say Lord, Lord.

Every man received according to his several ability, and the two who traded were told, Well done, thou good and faithful servant. The one who hid his talent blamed his lord and called him a hard man, and was answered, Thou wicked and slothful servant. That fearful spirit is not of the Most High, and a man should examine himself for it. Unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance; but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath. Knowledge that is not used is knowledge that is lost.

He separates them one from another, as a shepherd divideth his sheep from the goats, and says to those on the right hand, Inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me. Meeting the need of a brother or sister in the body is counted as done to Christ himself. Those on the left hand are answered with the same measure: inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me. --- Topics: [Clean and Unclean Meats](/encyclopedia/clean-and-unclean-meats) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

name: Sheba son of Bichri
charge: Insurrection: we have no part in David
summary: On the heels of Absalom's rebellion, Sheba the Benjamite blew a trumpet and cried, every man to his tents, O Israel, and all Israel went up after him. David judged him more dangerous than Absalom. He was besieged in Abel of Beth-maachah.
offense: The return of David was followed by strife between the men of Judah and the men of Israel over their share in bringing the king back (2 Samuel 19:41-43). Into that contention Sheba the son of Bichri blew a trumpet and declared that Israel had no part in David or inheritance in the son of Jesse. The men of Israel went up after him, while Judah clave to the king (2 Samuel 20:1-2). The rebellion drew strength from a quarrel that should not have governed the people's allegiance. Sheba offered separation as the answer to wounded tribal honour. The kingdom had scarcely emerged from Absalom's conspiracy when another man turned contention into a summons to depart. David saw that Sheba could do greater hurt if he gained fenced cities. The pursuit brought Joab's army to Abel of Beth-maachah, where it raised a bank and battered the wall (2 Samuel 20:6, 14-15). One man's cause now placed a whole city's life and inheritance beneath the danger of a siege.
judgment: A wise woman called to Joab from the city and asked why he would swallow up the inheritance of the Lord. She identified herself with those who were peaceable and faithful in Israel (2 Samuel 20:16-19). Her appeal distinguished the city's people from the rebellion of the man within it. Joab answered that he did not seek to destroy the city. Sheba had lifted his hand against David; if the city delivered him alone, the army would depart (2 Samuel 20:20-21). The demand narrowed the matter to the rebel instead of treating everyone behind the wall as equally guilty.

entries.commentary: A man of Belial, a devil, named Sheba the son of Bichri, blew a trumpet and cried that they had no part in David nor inheritance in the son of Jesse, and every man of Israel went up from David to follow Sheba, while the men of Judah clave unto the king from Jordan to Jerusalem. David came to his house in Jerusalem and took the ten concubines Absalom had defiled, put them in ward, and fed them but went not in unto them; they were shut up in widowhood until the day of their death because Absalom had gone in unto them.

David told Amasa to assemble the men of Judah within three days, but Amasa tarried longer than the set time. So David sent Abishai with Joab's men, the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men to pursue Sheba lest he escape into fenced cities. At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab came to Amasa with a sword secretly fastened, took him by the beard with his right hand as if to kiss him, and smote him in the fifth rib so that his bowels shed to the ground, and he died at one stroke. Joab was grimy and shady, murdering the man who had been named captain in his place. One of Joab's men stood by Amasa calling all who favored Joab and David to follow after Joab. Amasa wallowed in his blood in the midst of the highway, and when the people stood still to look, the man removed him into the field and cast a cloth over him, and then all the people went on after Joab to pursue Sheba.

Joab pursued Sheba through all the tribes to Abel of Beth-maachah, and they cast up a bank against the city and battered the wall to throw it down. A wise woman of the city called out to Joab, reminding him of the old saying that men would surely ask counsel at Abel, and asked why he would swallow up a city that was a mother in Israel and the inheritance of the Lord. Joab answered that he did not seek to destroy, but only wanted Sheba the son of Bichri, who had lifted up his hand against the king; deliver him and he would depart. The woman promised that Sheba's head would be thrown over the wall. She went to all the people in her wisdom, and they cut off Sheba's head and cast it out to Joab, who blew the trumpet and retired from the city, every man to his tent, and returned to Jerusalem unto the king.

Joab was over all the host of Israel, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada over the Cherethites and the Pelethites. Adoram was over the tribute, Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder, and Sheva was scribe. Zadok and Abiathar were the priests, and Ira the Jairite was a chief ruler about David. Thou shalt not sacrifice unto the Most High any bullock or sheep wherein is blemish, or any evilfavouredness, for that is an abomination unto the Lord thy God. Back then you could be put to death for sacrificing a bullock or sheep with a blemish, because doing an abominable thing carried death.

If there be found among you man or woman that hath wrought wickedness, transgressed the covenant, and gone and served other gods, the sun or moon or any of the host of heaven, which the Most High commanded not, the matter had to be established first. Whether it be told thee or thou hast heard of it, thou shalt enquire diligently, and behold, if it be true and the thing certain that such abomination is wrought in Israel, then judgment proceeds. Make sure you are certain of a thing before you bring somebody to judgment; only after diligent enquiry was the man or woman brought to the gates and stoned with stones till they die.

At the mouth of two witnesses or three witnesses shall he that is worthy of death be put to death; at the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death. The hands of the witnesses shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterward the hands of all the people. Wait till we go back to this: the ones who witnessed against you were the first to lay hands on you, so a false witness could not hide behind the crowd. So thou shalt put the evil away from among you.

If there arise a matter too hard for thee in judgment, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke, matters of controversy within thy gates, then thou shalt get thee up into the place which the Lord shall choose. Come unto the priests the Levites and unto the judge that shall be in those days, and they shall shew thee the sentence of judgment; thou shalt do according to all that they inform thee, according to the sentence of the law which they shall teach thee, declining neither to the right hand nor to the left. The man that will do presumptuously and will not hearken unto the priest that standeth to minister before the Most High, or unto the judge, even that man shall die; and all the people shall hear, and fear, and do no more presumptuously.

When thou art come unto the land and shalt say, I will set a king over me like as all the nations that are about me, thou shalt in any wise set him king whom the Lord thy God shall choose: one from among thy brethren; thou mayest not set a stranger over thee, which is not thy brother. These are the laws for a king that is to rule over Israel. He shall not multiply horses to himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt to multiply horses, for the Lord hath said, Ye shall henceforth return no more that way. Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away. You hear a lot of these dudes today saying king this and king that, and many of the same men pushing for multiple wives; the law of the king says do not multiply wives to thyself. Neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.

When he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites. It shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the Most High and keep all the words of this law and these statutes to do them. The purpose: that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, that he turn not aside from the commandment to the right hand or to the left, and that he prolong his days in his kingdom, he and his children, in the midst of Israel.

name: Rizpah
charge: Spreading sackcloth on the rock and suffering neither the birds by day nor the beasts by night to touch the bodies
summary: Seven of Saul's sons were given to the Gibeonites and hanged in the hill before the Lord in the beginning of barley harvest. Two of them were hers. She took sackcloth and spread it on the rock and stayed from the beginning of harvest until water dropped on them out of heaven, keeping the birds off by day and the beasts off by night. It was told David, and he took the bones of Saul and Jonathan and of those seven and buried them in the sepulchre of Kish.
offense: Two of Rizpah's sons were among the seven delivered to the Gibeonites in the judgment concerning Saul's bloody house. From the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon the bodies from heaven, she spread sackcloth upon the rock and kept the birds away by day and the beasts by night (2 Samuel 21:8-10). She could not restore her sons to life, but she would not abandon their bodies to be consumed. Her watch extended beyond an hour of mourning. Day and night brought different threats, and she remained attentive to both. The account records her action without placing a speech in her mouth. Her perseverance itself made the condition of the dead known. The law required care even for the body of a man put to death and hanged, forbidding it to remain upon the tree overnight and defile the land (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). The exposure in this account was prolonged; Rizpah's vigil did not substitute for burial. It preserved the bodies until the matter reached the king and burial followed.
judgment: David was told what Rizpah had done. He went to gather the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead and gathered the bones of those who had been hanged (2 Samuel 21:11-13). The response reached beyond her two sons to the earlier dead of Saul's house. The bones of Saul and Jonathan were buried in the sepulchre of Kish, and all that the king commanded was performed. Afterward God was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:14). The account closes not with the bodies exposed upon the hill, but with burial and the land's relief. Rizpah's sons were not returned to her. The good that followed her endurance was the care given to the dead and the completion of a matter affecting the whole land. Her vigil stands within the record of judgment as an act of steadfast attention to those who could no longer speak for themselves.

name: Saul's house and the Gibeonites
charge: Breaking Israel's sworn covenant by slaying the Gibeonites
summary: Three years of famine in David's reign were traced by inquiry of the Lord to Saul and his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites in his zeal for Israel, against the oath Joshua had sworn. David asked the Gibeonites what atonement they required.
offense: There was famine for three successive years, and David inquired of the Lord. The answer named Saul and his bloody house because he had slain the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:1). The land's distress had a cause beyond the conditions of a single harvest. The Gibeonites were a remnant of the Amorites with whom the children of Israel had sworn an oath. Joshua and the princes had made a league to let them live, and the princes refused to violate it after the deception by which it was obtained became known (Joshua 9:15-20). Israel's oath in the Lord's name remained binding when it became inconvenient. Saul nevertheless sought to slay them in his zeal for the children of Israel and Judah (2 Samuel 21:2). Zeal for one's people did not authorize breaking the word by which those people were bound. A purpose presented as national benefit could still bring bloodguilt upon the nation. When David asked what should be done, the Gibeonites refused silver and gold and did not demand an indiscriminate killing in Israel. They asked for seven men of Saul's sons from the house that had sought their destruction (2 Samuel 21:3-6). The injury could not be treated as an ordinary debt to be settled by wealth. Numbers 35:33 declares that blood pollutes the land.
judgment: David delivered seven men but spared Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, because of the Lord's oath between David and Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7-9). The same matter that exposed a broken national oath also recorded the keeping of a personal one. Judgment did not permit the king to forget every other obligation. The seven were hanged together at the beginning of barley harvest. Rizpah guarded the bodies until rain came, and her conduct was reported to David. He then gathered the remains of Saul, Jonathan, and those who had been hanged, and ordered burial (2 Samuel 21:9-14). After the king's command was carried out, God was entreated for the land. The resolution included reckoning with bloodshed, remembering the oath, and caring for the remains; the story does not stop at the execution itself. Saul had acted in a zeal that disregarded an obligation sworn before the Lord. His death did not make that breach disappear from the land. The king who followed him had to inquire into the cause and address what remained unresolved beneath the years of famine.

entries.commentary: There was a famine in the days of David, three years, year after year, and David inquired of the Lord. The Lord answered that it was for Saul and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites. Saul broke his word. The Gibeonites were not of the children of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites, and Israel had sworn unto them, yet Saul sought to slay them in his zeal. David asked the Gibeonites what he should do and wherewith he should make the atonement. The blessing was not truly coming from the Gibeonites who are of Ammon; it was coming from the Most High, who was teaching Israel a lesson through this famine. The Gibeonites would take no silver nor gold of Saul nor of his house, but asked for seven of Saul's sons to be hanged unto the Lord in Gibeah of Saul. The lesson the Most High is teaching Israel here is to pay what you vow. Let your yea be yea and your nay be nay; Saul went back on his word after he had given his yea to the Amorites, and the whole house paid for it.

The king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, because of the Lord's oath that was between David and Jonathan. David did not go back on his oath; earlier he had promised Jonathan that his seed would always eat at David's table as long as there was family of the lineage of Jonathan. But the king took the two sons of Rizpah and the five sons of Michal and delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them in the hill before the Lord. They fell all seven together and were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, in the beginning of barley harvest.

Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, took sackcloth and spread it upon the rock from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and she suffered neither the birds of the air by day nor the beasts of the field by night to touch them. When David was told, he went and took the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, which had stolen them from the street of Beth-shan where the Philistines had hanged them when Saul was slain in Gilboa. Jonathan's body had been hanged in the temple of Dagon, the fish god of the Hamites. David buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father, and performed all that the king commanded. After that the Most High was entreated for the land.

The Philistines had war again with Israel, and David went down and waxed faint. Ishbi-benob, of the sons of the giant, thought to slay him, but Abishai the son of Zeruiah succoured him and killed the Philistine. Then the men of David swore that he should go no more out with them to battle, that he quench not the light of Israel; he was getting up in age and it was time to sit on the throne. There were further battles at Gob and at Gath. Sibbechai slew Sippai, Elhanan slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite whose spear staff was like a weaver's beam, and Jonathan the son of Shimeah, David's brother, slew a man of great stature with six fingers on every hand and six toes on every foot. These four were born to the giant in Gath and fell by the hand of David and his servants. These giants were tall men, one about eight or nine feet, not the twenty foot giants of fairy tales. Goliath had kin, and eventually they were all served by David and his servants.

The kings on this side Jordan, in the hills, in the valleys, and in all the coasts of the great sea over against Lebanon: the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite. These are Hamites, better known as Nilotic Africans. When they heard what had been done, they gathered themselves together to fight with Joshua and with Israel with one accord.

The inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai, and they did work wilily: they made as if they had been ambassadors, with old sacks upon their asses, wine bottles old and rent and bound up, old shoes and old garments, and bread dry and mouldy. They came to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal saying, We be come from a far country: now therefore make ye a league with us. Israel was commanded to destroy all the inhabitants of the land, the very nations listed in verse 1, so the Gibeonites' only hope was to pretend they were not of the land.

The men of Israel were suspicious at first: peradventure ye dwell among us, and how shall we make a league with you? Joshua pressed them, Who are ye, and from whence come ye? The Gibeonites leaned on the fame of the Most High: we have heard all that he did in Egypt, and to Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites beyond Jordan. Their props sold the story. In ancient times wine did not come in bottles like ours; wine came in bags, sometimes made of leather, and they would rend through wear and tear over time.

The men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. That is the first mistake, and not asking counsel of the Most High at this moment ended up being a snare and a trap to us as a people, as the rest of the scriptures show. Let reason think on whether it is the right move, and even before you reason within yourself, the Most High says counsel, counsel, counsel before every action. This type of ordeal will play out again in the times when Christ returns: the sons of strangers shall come to build up Israel's walls, their kings shall minister unto Israel, and the nation and kingdom that will not serve thee shall perish. There is nothing new under the sun.

At the end of three days Israel heard that they were their neighbours, dwelling among them. The children of Israel smote them not, because the princes of the congregation had sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel. All the congregation murmured against the princes, but the princes held the line: we have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel, now therefore we may not touch them. Our forefathers were wrong in one situation, but they were upright men in holding up to their word.

We will even let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath which we sware unto them. A vow made before the Most High stands, even one gotten by guile. Let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation. Hewers of wood and drawers of water means slaves. This is according to the law of the Most High pertaining to other nations. If you just read the Old Testament, there was no equality among the nations, and there is still no equality among nations: they were made for a certain purpose. The reason they are not in that purpose now is because we have sinned and failed, and one day Israel will rise again to put them back in their rightful places.

Joshua called for them: wherefore have ye beguiled us, saying, We are very far from you, when ye dwell among us? Now therefore ye are cursed, and there shall none of you be freed from being bondmen, and hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God. They were servants all the way up and through.

The Gibeonites answered honestly: it was certainly told thy servants how the LORD thy God commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants, therefore we were sore afraid of our lives because of you. Behold, we are in thine hand. So did he unto them, and delivered them out of the hand of the children of Israel, that they slew them not; and Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day.

Moses commands the tribes to separate cities out of their own inheritance for the Levites to dwell in, with suburbs round about them. The Levites needed cities inside every tribe's territory because the Most High took them from among the children of Israel as a gift, to do the service of the tabernacle of the congregation. Every tribe needed that service done among them, so the Levites had to be spread out through all the children of Israel. The commandment was fulfilled when Israel came into the land: the heads of the fathers of the Levites came to Eleazar the priest and Joshua at Shiloh and claimed the cities the Lord commanded by the hand of Moses.

The cities were for the Levites to dwell in, and the suburbs were for their cattle, their goods, and all their beasts. The suburbs were measured out: a thousand cubits from the wall of the city round about, and two thousand cubits on the east, south, west, and north sides, with the city in the midst.

Among the Levite cities six were set apart for refuge, appointed for the manslayer to flee there, with forty and two more added: forty and eight cities in all, given from every tribe according to its inheritance, many from them that had many and few from them that had few. Why would the Lord permit a manslayer refuge? The Most High gave Moses the understanding of how to discern manslaughter from murder. For murder there was no refuge, but for manslaughter cities of refuge were given. The law itself was already instituted in [Exodus 21](/bible/exodus/21); [Numbers 35](/bible/numbers/35) answers where the manslayer goes: the Most High appointed him a place to flee.

Killeth any person unawares means he did not mean to do it; it was an accident that resulted in a death. Accidental deaths are of the Lord, beyond our control. Refuge means a condition of being safe or sheltered from pursuit, danger, or trouble. The cities of refuge exist because the manslayer is being pursued: someone has the right to avenge the death of the one who was killed. The city of refuge keeps the manslayer alive until he stands before the congregation in judgment, so the trial can discern between murder and manslaughter before the avenger reaches him.

Six cities of refuge stood, three on this side Jordan and three in the land of Canaan, and they served the children of Israel, the stranger, and the sojourner among them alike. The chapter lays out three categories when someone dies by the hand of another: he meant to hurt him but not kill him, yet he died, and that is murder; he hated him and killed him with premeditation, and that is murder; or he had no quarrel and never meant it, and that is manslaughter, not worthy of death.

Smite him with an instrument of iron, with a stone, or with a hand weapon of wood so that he die, and he is a murderer: even if the intent was only to hurt him and not to kill him, if he dies, the judgment is death. This is a precept for the street: the music culture glorifies slinging an iron, but the word says if you sling that iron and the brother dies, you are a murderer and your judgment is to die.

The revenger of blood himself slays the murderer when he meets him; there was no refuge and no mercy for murder. This is the law given to Israel at that time, an understanding of those judgments; it is not license for anyone to go about killing today.

Laying of wait means he was lurking and stalking, waiting to catch him slipping because of hatred between them; that is premeditated murder. Even without a weapon, smiting him in enmity with the hand so that he dies is murder; he that smote him shall surely be put to death.

The law repeats its key words on purpose, the way legal statutes do, because the details decide the case: suddenly, without enmity, without laying of wait, and seeing him not. Seeing him not matters because it is nearly impossible to kill a man by accident while looking straight at him; the victim was out of sight when the thing flew and struck him. He was not his enemy and sought not his harm: there could be no documented past hatred, and he could not even have been seeking to harm him, since seeking only to harm still makes the death murder. Then the congregation judges between the slayer and the revenger of blood according to these judgments.

Once the congregation clears him of murder, it delivers the slayer out of the hand of the revenger and restores him to his city of refuge; he still must abide there. He stays within the city until the death of the high priest which was anointed with the holy oil, whoever held that office when the incident happened.

If the slayer steps outside the borders of his city of refuge before that high priest dies and the revenger of blood finds him there and kills him, the revenger is not guilty of blood, because the slayer was instructed to remain within the borders. After the death of the high priest the slayer returns to the land of his possession, and the avenger can no longer touch him.

The murderer is put to death by the mouth of witnesses, plural: multiple people must testify, and their stories must match in the details for the murder to be established. One witness alone cannot cause a man to die, because a single witness could lie in the interest of the avenger and put an innocent man to death. The rule stood first for sins worthy of death and then had to become the principle for every matter: two or three witnesses establish any accusation of iniquity or sin.

The judges could take no satisfaction for the life of a murderer guilty of death, and no satisfaction for the manslayer to come home before the death of the high priest; a guilty man cannot buy himself off. No matter who stands before the judge or what money is offered, if they are guilty of death they are guilty of death; a gift blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous. Israel's judges later fell into exactly this: they became covetous and took bribes to clear the guilty and turn aside the poor in the gate.

Blood defileth the land, and the land cannot be cleansed of the blood shed in it but by the blood of him that shed it; the murderer who escapes his judgment leaves the land polluted. That judgment was instituted back in the days of Noah, and Moses carried it forward in the statutes given to Israel, for the Lord himself dwells among the children of Israel.

When a man hath taken a wife and she find no favour in his eyes because he hath found some uncleanness in her, then let him write her a bill of divorcement, give it in her hand, and send her out of his house. Christ magnified this law: when the Pharisees asked why Moses then commanded to give a writing of divorcement, he said, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery; and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery.

If the latter husband hate her and write her a bill of divorcement, or if the latter husband die, her former husband which sent her away may not take her again to be his wife after that she is defiled, for that is abomination before the Lord. The question is whether a woman who leaves her husband and becomes another man's wife can be joined to the first again; the prophet asks the same thing: shall he return unto her again? shall not that land be greatly polluted?

When a man hath taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, neither shall he be charged with any business; he shall be free at home one year and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken. Make it plain: the first year, stay at home and make a baby. Husband and wife render due benevolence to one another; benevolence means good, it is a good thing. The war laws give the same understanding: the man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her, for the Lord is the one that goeth with the host to fight against the enemies.

No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge, for he taketh a man's life to pledge. The millstone is a tool for grinding meal: the manna was gathered and ground in mills or beaten in a mortar and baked into cakes. Taking a man's tool takes away his living, like somebody stealing your tools so you cannot make a living. It is better that they steal your money, because with your tools you can go back and make more money.

Remember what the Lord thy God did unto Miriam by the way, after that ye were come forth out of Egypt: Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married, and Miriam was not supposed to be speaking against Moses. The anger of the Lord was kindled against them, the cloud departed from off the tabernacle, and behold, Miriam became leprous, white as snow. The Lord said, if her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? Had her father chastised her and rebuked her sharply, she would not have had that tongue. That is for a lot of our sisters today who do not have that understanding.

When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge; stand abroad, and let the man bring the pledge out unto thee. If the man be poor, thou shalt not sleep with his pledge; deliver him the pledge again when the sun goeth down, that he may sleep in his own raiment and bless thee, and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the Lord thy God. The law was already given: if thou at all take thy neighbour's raiment to pledge, deliver it by that the sun goeth down, for that is his covering only, and when he crieth unto the Most High, he will hear, for he is gracious. The history shows how wicked we were to each other: Israel laid themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar, stacking up people's raiment like pallets and drinking the wine of the condemned in the house of their god, instead of returning the pledge before the sun went down as righteousness. That is why the Lord was judging us.

The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin. The example: as soon as the kingdom was confirmed in Amaziah's hand, he slew his servants which had slain the king his father, but the children of the murderers he slew not, according unto that which is written in the book of the law of Moses. The soul that sinneth, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.

The word of the Most High asks what they mean by the proverb, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge. As the Most High lives, they shall no more use this proverb in Israel, for all souls are His; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is His. The soul that sinneth, it shall die, setting the theme of individual accountability.

If a man be just and do that which is lawful and right, has not eaten upon the mountains nor lifted his eyes to idols, nor defiled his neighbour's wife, nor oppressed any, but restored the debtor his pledge and given his bread to the hungry, he is just and shall surely live. He has not given forth upon usury nor taken increase, has withdrawn his hand from iniquity, executed true judgment between man and man, and walked in the Most High's statutes.

If that just man beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, who eats upon the mountains, defiles his neighbour's wife, oppresses the poor and needy, spoils by violence, and lifts his eyes to idols, committing abomination. Such a son who gives forth upon usury and takes increase shall not live; he has done all these abominations and shall surely die, and his blood shall be upon him.

If that wicked man beget a son that sees all his father's sins, considers, and does not do likewise, but gives his bread to the hungry, covers the naked, takes off his hand from the poor, and keeps the Most High's judgments and statutes. That son shall not die for the iniquity of his father; he shall surely live, but the father, because he cruelly oppressed and spoiled his brother, shall die in his own iniquity.

They ask why the son does not bear the iniquity of the father, when the son has done that which is lawful and right and kept the statutes; he shall surely live. The soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous is upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked upon him.

If the wicked turn from all his sins, keep all the Most High's statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live and not die; his transgressions shall not be mentioned unto him. The Most High has no pleasure that the wicked should die, but that he return from his ways and live; yet if the righteous turn away from his righteousness and commit iniquity, all his righteousness shall not be mentioned, and he shall die in his sin.

Yet the house of Israel says the way of the Lord is not equal; the Most High answers, Are not your ways unequal. When a righteous man turns from his righteousness and dies in his iniquity, it is for the iniquity he has done; when a wicked man turns from his wickedness and does that which is lawful and right, he shall save his soul alive.

Therefore the Most High will judge the house of Israel, everyone according to his ways; repent and turn yourselves from all your transgressions, so iniquity shall not be your ruin. Cast away all your transgressions and make you a new heart and a new spirit, the heart being the mind, for the Most High has no pleasure in the death of him that dies; wherefore turn yourselves and live. This reading taught repentance, how our enemies take the chief of our young men and women to leave the nation base, and that the Most High has a plan to use the lowly and base to confound the wise, so let your light shine rather than look for any slither of hope to unite with our oppressors. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant)
