name: David's numbering of the people
charge: Numbering Israel in pride; a plague on the nation
summary: David commanded Joab to number Israel and Judah. Joab objected; the king's word prevailed. When the count came in, David's heart smote him: I have sinned greatly. Gad offered three judgments, and David chose to fall into the hand of the Lord.
offense: The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and David was moved to number the people; Chronicles names Satan as the one who stood up against Israel and provoked him (2 Samuel 24:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1). The provocation did not make David an unwilling bystander. He gave the command and pressed it against objection. Joab wished that the Lord would multiply the people a hundredfold and asked why David delighted in this thing. Chronicles records his warning that the act would bring trespass upon Israel (1 Chronicles 21:3). The king's word prevailed, and the officers went through the land (2 Samuel 24:2-8). Authority could compel the count without making the purpose acceptable. Numbering itself was not absent from the law. Exodus 30:12 required a ransom for each man when Israel was numbered, that there be no plague among them. The people were the Lord's, not a measure of strength for a ruler to possess independently of him. Joab's protest and the prescribed warning both stood against treating the census as a harmless exercise of royal pleasure. Afterward David's heart smote him. He confessed that he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly (2 Samuel 24:10). He did not place the guilt upon the officers who had obeyed him. The recognition came after the command had already carried its work through the kingdom.
judgment: Pestilence: seventy thousand men died from Dan to Beersheba in three days. The angel stood at Araunah's threshingfloor with drawn sword when the Lord said, it is enough. David bought the floor and built an altar; it became the temple site.
offenseFull: The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and David was moved to number the people; Chronicles names Satan as the one who stood up against Israel and provoked him (2 Samuel 24:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1). The provocation did not make David an unwilling bystander. He gave the command and pressed it against objection.

Joab wished that the Lord would multiply the people a hundredfold and asked why David delighted in this thing. Chronicles records his warning that the act would bring trespass upon Israel (1 Chronicles 21:3). The king's word prevailed, and the officers went through the land (2 Samuel 24:2-8). Authority could compel the count without making the purpose acceptable.

Numbering itself was not absent from the law. Exodus 30:12 required a ransom for each man when Israel was numbered, that there be no plague among them. The people were the Lord's, not a measure of strength for a ruler to possess independently of him. Joab's protest and the prescribed warning both stood against treating the census as a harmless exercise of royal pleasure.

Afterward David's heart smote him. He confessed that he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly (2 Samuel 24:10). He did not place the guilt upon the officers who had obeyed him. The recognition came after the command had already carried its work through the kingdom.

entries.commentary: The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David to number Israel and Judah. This was the Most High wanting to judge Israel; he used David and used Satan to provoke him to do it. Joab objected, asking why the king delighted in this thing, for numbering the people was not the king's job but the work of the Levites. Notwithstanding, the king's word prevailed against Joab and the captains, and they went out to number the people. Joab did not understand that behind it all, verse one, the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel; it was of the Most High that this happened.

Joab and the captains passed over Jordan and went through all the land, from Aroer and Gad and Gilead, to Dan-jaan, to Zidon, to the stronghold of Tyre and the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites, and out to the south of Judah to Beersheba. It took them nine months and twenty days to count all of Israel. Joab gave the sum to the king: there were in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men that drew the sword, and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand men. This did not count the women and the children.

David's heart smote him after he had numbered the people, and he said unto the Lord, I have sinned greatly; take away the iniquity of thy servant, for I have done very foolishly. As soon as it was done it hit him, because it was not the king's job but the Levites' to number the people. In the morning the word of the Lord came to the prophet Gad, David's seer, offering David three things to choose one: seven years of famine, three months fleeing before his enemies, or three days of pestilence. David was in a great strait and said, Let us fall now into the hand of the Lord, for his mercies are great, and let me not fall into the hand of man. He had two prophets, Gad and Nathan, who ministered to him.

The Lord sent the pestilence upon Israel from the morning to the time appointed, and there died seventy thousand men from Dan to Beersheba. When the angel stretched out his hand upon Jerusalem to destroy it, the Lord repented him of the evil and said to the angel, It is enough, stay now thine hand; and the angel was by the threshing place of Araunah the Jebusite. David saw the angel that smote the people, something we cannot see today, for the Most High has blinded our eyes to it and this walk is by faith and the keeping of the commandments. David spoke unto the Lord, Lo, I have sinned and done wickedly, but these sheep, what have they done; let thine hand be against me and against my father's house. Remember the reason for the seventy thousand is verse one, the Most High was angry at Israel.

Gad told David to rear an altar unto the Lord in the threshing floor of Araunah, and David went up as the Lord commanded. Araunah bowed himself before the king and offered to give the floor, the oxen, and the instruments freely for the burnt sacrifice, saying, The Lord thy God accept thee. David refused to take it for nothing, saying he would not offer burnt offerings unto the Lord his God of that which cost him nothing, and bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. He built there an altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, so the Lord was entreated for the land and the plague was stayed from Israel. True worship costs us something. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

Satan stood up against Israel and provoked David to number the people; David commanded Joab to number Israel from Beersheba to Dan. Joab objected, asking why the king would require this thing and be a cause of trespass to Israel, but the king's word prevailed. Joab numbered the people: a thousand thousand and a hundred thousand men that drew sword in Israel, and four hundred threescore and ten thousand in Judah. Joab left Levi and Benjamin uncounted because the king's word was abominable to him.

The Most High was displeased with the numbering and smote Israel; David confessed he had sinned greatly and done very foolishly and begged that the iniquity be taken away. The Most High sent Gad the seer to offer David three choices: three years of famine, three months of destruction before his foes, or three days of pestilence with the destroying angel. David chose to fall into the hand of the Most High rather than the hand of man, saying very great are His mercies, for he knew man would not show him the mercy the Most High would.

The Most High sent pestilence, and seventy thousand men of Israel fell; the angel was sent to destroy Jerusalem, but the Most High beheld it, repented of the evil, and told the angel it was enough to stay his hand. David lifted up his eyes and saw the angel of the Most High standing between earth and heaven with a drawn sword stretched over Jerusalem, and he and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces. David pleaded that he alone had sinned by commanding the numbering, asking that the hand be on him and his father's house but not on the people, who as sheep had done nothing. Our forefathers had the pleasure of seeing such acts of the Most High in their midst; in these last days we walk by faith in what the scriptures say, for the war is now of a different kind.

The angel commanded Gad to tell David to set up an altar in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite, and David went up at the word spoken in the name of the Most High. Ornan, threshing wheat, turned and saw the angel and hid with his four sons, then saw David and bowed to the ground; David asked to buy the threshingfloor for the full price so the plague might be stayed. Ornan offered to give it all, the place, the oxen, the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat, but David refused to take what was another man's or to offer burnt offerings without cost. David paid six hundred shekels of gold, built the altar, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the Most High answered him by fire from heaven and commanded the angel to sheathe his sword. David paid the full price rather than take the offering for free, and this is a pattern for Israel today: what is given to the Most High should cost the giver something. -

When David saw that the Most High answered him at the threshingfloor of Ornan, he sacrificed there. The tabernacle Moses made and the altar of burnt offering were then at the high place in Gibeon. David could not go to Gibeon to inquire of the Most High because he was afraid of the sword of the angel, so he worshipped at the new altar instead. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

The altar to burn incense upon was made of shittim wood, a cubit in length and a cubit in breadth, foursquare, and two cubits high, with horns of the same. A cubit has been read to be about seventeen inches, so this stood about waist high. It was overlaid with pure gold, the top, the sides round about, and the horns, with a crown of gold round about, two golden rings under the crown, and staves of shittim wood overlaid with gold. The staves through the rings were how the priests bore it as Israel moved through the wilderness.

The altar was put before the vail that is by the ark of the testimony, before the mercy seat where the Most High would meet with Moses. Aaron burned sweet incense on it every morning when he dressed the lamps, and again at even when he lighted the lamps, a perpetual incense before the Lord throughout the generations; it burned continually, morning and evening. No strange incense went on it, and no burnt sacrifice, meat offering, or drink offering; this altar was for one specific incense only. The service had to be exactly as prescribed, and deviation carried death, which is a reason to thank the Lord for Christ.

Aaron made an atonement upon the horns of it once in a year with the blood of the sin offering of atonements; it is most holy unto the Lord. This altar served the day of atonement. On the tenth day of the seventh month Israel afflicted their souls and did no work at all, and the priest made an atonement for the sanctuary, the tabernacle, the altar, the priests, and all the people of the congregation, to cleanse them from all their sins before the Lord; an everlasting statute, once a year. The priests went always into the first tabernacle accomplishing the service of God, but into the second went the high priest alone once every year, not without blood. Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, so the day of atonement is still kept by afflicting the soul and doing no work, but without the animal sacrifice, because Christ took the place of the animal.

Numbering the children of Israel was not done lightly; when they were counted, every man gave a ransom for his soul unto the Lord, that there be no plague among them when they were numbered. The ransom was half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary, from every one that passed among them that were numbered, from twenty years old and above; the rich gave no more and the poor gave no less, to make an atonement for their souls. The atonement money was appointed for the service of the tabernacle of the congregation. The gold, the wood, the curtains, and the fabrics all had to be bought and kept up, and the tabernacle moved with the nation through the wilderness; that is the same reason offerings are gathered in the congregation today, because the house of the Most High cannot be built or kept without it.

The laver of brass, with his foot also of brass, stood between the tabernacle of the congregation and the altar, with water in it; a great brass bowl set on a brass base. Aaron and his sons washed their hands and their feet thereat when they went into the tabernacle of the congregation and when they came near to the altar to minister, that they die not; the priests could not go in unclean. It was a statute for ever to Aaron and to his seed throughout their generations.

The holy anointing oil was compounded of principal spices, pure myrrh five hundred shekels, sweet cinnamon two hundred and fifty, sweet calamus two hundred and fifty, cassia five hundred after the shekel of the sanctuary, and oil olive an hin, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary, which is a maker of perfume. With it were anointed the tabernacle of the congregation, the ark of the testimony, the table and all his vessels, the candlestick and his vessels, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering with all his vessels, and the laver and his foot, that they be most holy; whatsoever toucheth them shall be holy. Aaron and his sons were anointed and consecrated with it to minister in the priest's office. It was not poured upon man's flesh, and none was to be made like it after the composition of it; whosoever compounded any like it, or put any of it upon a stranger, was cut off from his people. The Most High gave specific orders down to the spices and the weights, and none could deviate from them or they would die. Our forefathers carried out that tedious, exact work, yet we complain about the smallest things set in place for order, the uniform, the new moon, and not cooking on the sabbath; the spirit has to get right.

The perfume was made of sweet spices, stacte, onycha, and galbanum, with pure frankincense, of each a like weight, tempered together, pure and holy, a confection after the art of the apothecary. Part of it was beaten very small and put before the testimony in the tabernacle of the congregation; unto you it shall be most holy. The Most High wanted the tabernacle anointed and smelling sweet, everything done one specific way. It was for the Lord alone; ye shall not make to yourselves according to the composition thereof, and whosoever made like unto it, to smell thereto, was cut off from his people. There were no knockoffs of the holy things; a copy carried death.

name: Adonijah
charge: Exalting himself to be king; asking for the king's concubine
summary: David's fourth son exalted himself, saying, I will be king, and gathered chariots, horsemen, Joab, and Abiathar for a coronation feast at En-rogel while David lay dying. Solomon was anointed the same day. Pardoned once, Adonijah then asked for Abishag the Shunammite.
offense: Adonijah exalted himself, saying that he would be king, and prepared chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. David had not displeased him by asking why he acted so (1 Kings 1:5-6). The display of succession grew without the father's correction, but display was not appointment. Joab and Abiathar supported him. He made a sacrificial feast and invited the king's sons and servants while leaving out Solomon, Nathan, Benaiah, and the mighty men (1 Kings 1:7-10). The invitations divided the house according to the claim he intended to establish. Religious sacrifice accompanied a decision made without the king's declaration. Nathan and Bathsheba brought the matter before David, who confirmed his oath that Solomon would reign. Solomon was placed upon the king's mule and anointed at Gihon by Zadok and Nathan (1 Kings 1:28-40). David also declared that the Lord had chosen Solomon to sit upon the throne (1 Chronicles 28:5). Adonijah's seniority among the surviving sons did not overrule that choice. When the news reached his feast, the guests rose in fear and departed. Adonijah caught hold of the horns of the altar and sought assurance that Solomon would not kill him (1 Kings 1:41-51). The man who had announced himself king now depended upon the king's mercy.
judgment: Solomon had spared him on condition of worthiness. The second offense was the end of it: Benaiah fell upon him and he died. Abiathar was banished and Joab executed in the same purge.
offenseFull: Adonijah exalted himself, saying that he would be king, and prepared chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. David had not displeased him by asking why he acted so (1 Kings 1:5-6). The display of succession grew without the father's correction, but display was not appointment.

Joab and Abiathar supported him. He made a sacrificial feast and invited the king's sons and servants while leaving out Solomon, Nathan, Benaiah, and the mighty men (1 Kings 1:7-10). The invitations divided the house according to the claim he intended to establish. Religious sacrifice accompanied a decision made without the king's declaration.

Nathan and Bathsheba brought the matter before David, who confirmed his oath that Solomon would reign. Solomon was placed upon the king's mule and anointed at Gihon by Zadok and Nathan (1 Kings 1:28-40). David also declared that the Lord had chosen Solomon to sit upon the throne (1 Chronicles 28:5). Adonijah's seniority among the surviving sons did not overrule that choice.

When the news reached his feast, the guests rose in fear and departed. Adonijah caught hold of the horns of the altar and sought assurance that Solomon would not kill him (1 Kings 1:41-51). The man who had announced himself king now depended upon the king's mercy.

entries.commentary: David is old and cannot stay warm, so his servants seek a fair young woman to lie in his bosom and give him heat. This is one of the things that happens with age, when the body no longer produces heat as it did in youth and strength. Abishag the Shunammite is found and ministers to the king, but he does not know her. That means he did not have relations with her; she was there only to keep him warm. -
Adonijah exalts himself, saying he will be king, and prepares chariots and horsemen to promote himself. He takes the throne to himself rather than receiving it from the Most High.
David repeats the oath he swore by the Lord God of Israel, that Solomon his son shall reign after him and sit upon his throne in his stead. The throne belongs to Solomon by that sworn word. -

David commands that Solomon be set on the king's own mule and brought to Gihon, where Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him king over Israel. The people come up rejoicing so that the earth rings with the sound.

The days of David draw near that he should die, and he charges Solomon to be strong, to keep the charge of the Lord his God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes, commandments, and judgments as written in the law of Moses, that he may prosper. There was a stipulation for the throne to continue: if his children take heed to their way and walk before the Most High in truth with all their heart, the throne stands. Reading through the kings, we see many who broke the commandments, and among their children some were righteous and some unrighteous. -
Solomon thrusts out Abiathar from being priest unto the Lord, fulfilling the word the Most High spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh. The old judgment on Eli's line is carried out.

Joab, who had turned after Adonijah, flees to the tabernacle of the Lord and catches hold of the horns of the altar, but Solomon sends Benaiah to fall upon him. Joab dies for the innocent blood he shed when he slew Abner and Amasa, two men more righteous and better than he, without David's knowledge. The blood returns upon Joab's own head and upon his seed, while upon David and his seed and throne there shall be peace forever from the Lord. Benaiah is set over the host in his place.

Shimei is commanded to build a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, never crossing the brook Kidron on pain of death, and he agrees. After three years he goes to Gath after his runaway servants and breaks the oath, so Solomon has Benaiah put him to death, and the kingdom is established in Solomon's hand.

David said, This is the house of the Lord God, and this is the altar of the burnt offering for Israel. He commanded to gather together the strangers that were in the land of Israel and set masons to hew wrought stones to build the house of God. These strangers were brought in to help with the building of the temple. David prepared iron in abundance for the nails and for the joinings, brass in abundance without weight, and cedar trees in abundance. The Zidonians and they of Tyre brought much cedar wood to David.

David said that Solomon his son was young and tender, and the house to be built for the Lord must be exceeding magnifical, of fame and glory throughout all countries, so he prepared abundantly before his death. He called for Solomon his son and charged him to build a house for the Lord God of Israel.

David told Solomon that it was in his mind to build a house unto the name of the Lord, but the word of the Lord came to him saying he should not build it because he had shed blood abundantly and made great wars. Because of all the wars and fighting David had done, the Most High did not allow him to build the temple. The Lord promised David a son who would be a man of rest, to whom he would give rest from all his enemies round about, whose name would be Solomon, and in whose days he would give peace and quietness unto Israel. This son would build the house for the Most High's name, and the Most High would establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever.

David charged Solomon that the Lord be with him and prosper him to build the house of the Lord his God, and asked that the Lord give him wisdom and understanding and charge concerning Israel that he might keep the law of the Lord. He said Solomon would prosper if he took heed to fulfill the statutes and judgments which the Lord charged Moses with concerning Israel. This is the same message the Most High gives us today: we will prosper as long as we obey the commandments. Be strong and of good courage; dread not, nor be dismayed.

In his trouble David prepared for the house of the Lord a hundred thousand talents of gold and a thousand thousand talents of silver, and brass and iron without weight, and timber and stone in abundance, telling Solomon he might add thereto. Without weight means they gave in such abundance they were not counting it. There were workmen with him in abundance, hewers and workers of stone and timber and all manner of cunning men for every kind of work. David told Solomon to arise and be doing, and the Lord be with him.

David commanded all the princes of Israel to help Solomon his son, asking whether the Lord their God was not with them and had not given them rest on every side, for he had given the inhabitants of the land into David's hand and the land was subdued before the Lord. This is what David was there to do: he subdued all the nations by the power of the Most High. He charged them to set their heart and soul to seek the Lord their God, to arise and build the sanctuary of the Lord God, and to bring the ark of the covenant and the holy vessels of God into the house that was to be built. Earlier David had moved the ark from place to place, and that is when he desired to build a house for it before the Lord.

*1 And David assembled all the princes of Israel, the princes of the tribes, and the captains of the companies that ministered to the king by course, and the captains over the thousands, and captains over the hundreds, and the stewards over all the substance and possession of the king, and of his sons, with the officers, and with the mighty men, and with all the valiant men, unto Jerusalem. 2 Then David the king stood up upon his feet, and said, Hear me, my brethren, and my people: As for me, I had in mine heart to build an house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and for the footstool of our God, and had made ready for the building: 3 But God said unto me, Thou shalt not build an house for my name, because thou hast been a man of war, and hast shed blood. 4 Howbeit the LORD God of Israel chose me before all the house of my father to be king over Israel for ever: for he hath chosen Judah to be the ruler; and of the house of Judah, the house of my father; and among the sons of my father he liked me to make me king over all Israel: 5 And of all my sons, (for the LORD hath given me many sons,) he hath chosen Solomon my son to sit upon the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel. 6 And he said unto me, Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father. 7 Moreover I will establish his kingdom for ever, if he be constant to do my commandments and my judgments, as at this day. 8 Now therefore in the sight of all Israel the congregation of the LORD, and in the audience of our God, keep and seek for all the commandments of the LORD your God: that ye may possess this good land, and leave it for an inheritance for your children after you for ever. 9 And thou, Solomon my son, know thou the God of thy father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind: for the LORD searcheth all hearts, and understandeth all the imaginations of the thoughts: if thou seek him, he will be found of thee; but if thou forsake him, he will cast thee off for ever. 10 Take heed now; for the LORD hath chosen thee to build an house for the sanctuary: be strong, and do it. 11 Then David gave to Solomon his son the pattern of the porch, and of the houses thereof, and of the treasuries thereof, and of the upper chambers thereof, and of the inner parlours thereof, and of the place of the mercy seat, 12 And the pattern of all that he had by the spirit, of the courts of the house of the LORD, and of all the chambers round about, of the treasuries of the house of God, and of the treasuries of the dedicated things: 13 Also for the courses of the priests and the Levites, and for all the work of the service of the house of the LORD, and for all the vessels of service in the house of the LORD. 14 He gave of gold by weight for things of gold, for all instruments of all manner of service; silver also for all instruments of silver by weight, for all instruments of every kind of service: 15 Even the weight for the candlesticks of gold, and for their lamps of gold, by weight for every candlestick, and for the lamps thereof: and for the candlesticks of silver by weight, both for the candlestick, and also for the lamps thereof, according to the use of every candlestick. 16 And by weight he gave gold for the tables of shewbread, for every table; and likewise silver for the tables of silver: 17 Also pure gold for the fleshhooks, and the bowls, and the cups: and for the golden basons he gave gold by weight for every bason; and likewise silver by weight for every bason of silver: 18 And for the altar of incense refined gold by weight; and gold for the pattern of the chariot of the cherubims, that spread out their wings, and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD. 19 All this, said David, the LORD made me understand in writing by his hand upon me, even all the works of this pattern. 20 And David said to Solomon his son, Be strong and of good courage, and do it: fear not, nor be dismayed: for the LORD God, even my God, will be with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee, until thou hast finished all the work for the service of the house of the LORD. 21 And, behold, the courses of the priests and the Levites, even they shall be with thee for all the service of the house of God: and there shall be with thee for all manner of workmanship every willing skilful man, for any manner of service: also the princes and all the people will be wholly at thy commandment.*

When David was past the top of the hill, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him with saddled asses, two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a bottle of wine. When David asked where his master's son was, Ziba said Mephibosheth abode in Jerusalem, saying the house of Israel would restore him the kingdom of his father. So David gave Ziba all that pertained to Mephibosheth. Ziba came with gifts, and when David asked about Mephibosheth, Ziba claimed Mephibosheth thought the kingdom was about to be restored to him, which was not true. On that word David handed Ziba everything that belonged to Mephibosheth.

As David came to Bahurim, a man of the house of Saul named Shimei the son of Gera came out, cursing and casting stones at David and all his servants. Shimei cursed, calling David a bloody man and a man of Belial, saying the Most High had returned upon him all the blood of the house of Saul, and delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom his son, and taken him in his mischief because he was a bloody man. Shimei was of the house of Saul, and Saul was the wicked one who tried to kill David; it was by the hand of the Most High that Saul did not succeed. Yet Shimei cursed David as if David were in the wrong, because word gets around, people gossip and blame, and he saw David at a low state and went to rub it in his face. That is the mindset of some people in Israel as well.

Abishai the son of Zeruiah asked why this dead dog should curse the king, and offered to go take off his head. But the king said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, because the Most High hath said unto him, Curse David; who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so? David rolled with mighty men of war, so Abishai was ready to take Shimei's head off his shoulders. But David said to let him curse, for if it was of the Most High, then let him do it. Just as the Most High brings people to our forums and classrooms who bicker and try to bring confusion, it is of the Most High, sometimes to test the patience of those who pray for patience.

David said to Abishai and all his servants, Behold, my own son who came forth out of my bowels seeketh my life, how much more now may this Benjamite do it? Let him alone and let him curse, for the Most High hath bidden him. It may be that the Most High will look on his affliction and requite him good for the cursing this day. David reasoned that if his own son sought his life, this Benjamite was nothing; the Most High was doing this, so let him curse. It may be the Most High will look on all that was done to David and bless him in front of them, the same as when people try to bring us down and the Most High blesses us before them, which is why this congregation has grown exponentially.

David and his men went by the way while Shimei went along the hillside cursing, throwing stones, and casting dust; and they came weary and refreshed themselves. Absalom and all the men of Israel came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him. When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom saying, God save the king, Absalom asked why he went not with his friend, and Hushai answered that he would serve whom the Most High and Israel chose, and would serve in the presence of the son as he served the father. Hushai put into action the plan he and David made. Absalom challenged him, asking, Is this thy kindness to thy friend? Why wentest thou not with thy friend? This is a real friend, not a friendish one; a true friend tells you when you are wrong and full of it, not the one who only strokes your head and pats your back like Absalom did to steal the people's hearts.

Absalom asked Ahithophel for counsel, and Ahithophel said, Go in unto thy father's concubines whom he left to keep the house, and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father, and the hands of all with thee shall be strong. So they spread Absalom a tent on the top of the house, and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel. The counsel of Ahithophel was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God. Ahithophel counselled Absalom to lie with the ten concubines David left, in the sight of all Israel, on the roof of the house. This is the exact fulfillment of what the Most High spoke in chapter 12, that David's wives would be taken and one would lie with them in the sight of the sun, and that what David did secretly would be done before all Israel. It was not coincidence or irony; it was prophesied to happen, and none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did. The Most High keeps mercy and forgives, but by no means clears the guilty, so even when we come in and repent, we still must remember the fear of the Most High, for there is but one step between us and death.

name: Solomon at Gibeon
charge: Asking for an understanding heart to judge the people, and not for long life, riches, or the life of his enemies
summary: Offered anything he wanted, the young king asked for wisdom to judge a great people. The speech pleased the Lord, who gave him the wisdom and added the riches and honour he had not asked. The kingdom he built on it was the greatest Israel ever had. What he did with his wives afterward is another case.
offense: Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad: for who is able to judge this thy so great a people? And the speech pleased the Lord, that Solomon had asked this thing. In Wisdom: I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came to me; I preferred her before sceptres and thrones, and esteemed riches nothing in comparison of her.
judgment: Because thou hast asked this thing, and hast not asked for thyself long life; neither hast asked riches for thyself, nor hast asked the life of thine enemies; but hast asked for thyself understanding to discern judgment; behold, I have done according to thy words: lo, I have given thee a wise and an understanding heart; so that there was none like thee before thee, neither after thee shall any arise like unto thee. And I have also given thee that which thou hast not asked, both riches, and honour. All the earth sought to Solomon, to hear his wisdom, which God had put in his heart.

entries.commentary: Solomon makes affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt and takes his daughter, while building his own house, the house of the Lord, and the wall of Jerusalem. He loves the Lord and walks in the statutes of David his father, though the people still sacrifice in high places because no house was yet built to the name of the Lord.

At Gibeon the Most High appears to Solomon in a dream and says, ask what I shall give thee. Solomon, calling himself a little child who knows not how to go out or come in, asks for an understanding heart to judge the great people, to discern between good and bad. This is what we still need to pray for. We should pray that the Most High endows our leadership with wisdom, and that we ourselves learn wisdom in these scriptures and how to judge matters among one another. -

Because Solomon asked for understanding to discern judgment and not for long life, riches, or the life of his enemies, the Most High gives him a wise and understanding heart like no other before or after. He also gives what Solomon did not ask, riches and honor, and promises length of days if he walks in his ways.

Two harlots come before the king, each claiming the living child, after one woman's child died in the night and she exchanged it. Solomon calls for a sword and commands the living child divided in two, and gives half to each. The true mother pleads that the child be given alive to the other rather than slain, and by this the king discerns her, for her bowels yearned upon her son. All Israel hears the judgment and fears the king, for they see the wisdom of God is in him to do judgment.

Solomon is king over all Israel, and these are the princes he set: priests, scribes, a recorder, one over the host, one over the officers, one over the household, and one over the tribute. Twelve officers provide victuals for the king and his household, each man his month in the year. This is the establishment of government, showing order. There is the king, then ranking men, each with a position of order, the same pattern of captains and officers set up in the days of Moses.

Judah and Israel are as many as the sand by the sea, eating, drinking, and making merry, and Solomon reigns over all the kingdoms from the river to the border of Egypt, who bring presents and serve him. Every man dwells safely under his vine and fig tree from Dan to Beersheba. Israel dwells safely because of the wars of King David, who put down all the surrounding nations and put them to tribute. That is why Solomon is able to rule in a time of peace.

The Most High gives Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, largeness of heart as the sand on the seashore, so that his wisdom excels all the children of the east country and all the wisdom of Egypt. He is wiser than all men, speaks three thousand proverbs, and his songs are a thousand and five, which is why we have Proverbs and the Song of Songs. He speaks of trees, beasts, fowl, creeping things, and fishes, and people of all nations come to hear his wisdom. Since his wisdom already excelled Egypt's, we have no need to dabble in Egyptology or any doctrine outside the scriptures given to us. -

When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the Most High, she came to prove him with hard questions, and came to Jerusalem with a great train, camels bearing spices, much gold, and precious stones. She communed with him of all that was in her heart, and Solomon answered all her questions; there was nothing hid from the king that he told her not.

When the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon's wisdom, the house he built, the meat of his table, the sitting of his servants, their apparel, his cupbearers, and his ascent to the house of the Most High, there was no more spirit in her. Everything in the kingdom was in order, the servants in uniform, the cupbearers in place; this is why order matters in the body today, so that those who come in are astonished and the worldly spirit of disorder leaves them, seeing the discipline and love for the people.

She told the king the report she heard in her own land was true, that she had not believed it until her eyes had seen it, and behold the half was not told her; his wisdom and prosperity exceeded the fame she heard. She said happy are his men and servants that stand continually before him and hear his wisdom; they were happy to be in order, serving with joyfulness and not complaining, because Solomon ruled wisely and took care of his people. She blessed the Most High who delighted in Solomon to set him on the throne of Israel, because the Most High loved Israel forever; even the nations understood that the Most High chose Israel above all people.

She gave the king a hundred and twenty talents of gold, and spices in great store, and precious stones; and the navy of Hiram brought from Ophir great plenty of almug trees and precious stones, of which Solomon made pillars for the house of the Most High and harps and psalteries for singers. Solomon knew how to entertain the people, providing for singing and joyfulness in the house of the Most High, for he had vision for the house and wanted Israel to enjoy the feasts and serve with gladness of heart. Solomon gave the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatever she asked. People assume this was sexual, but her desire was to know his wisdom and see his order; the word desire in scripture does not always mean what people think, as the law shows the tithe money could be spent on whatever the soul lusted after, meaning oxen, sheep, wine, and food. Nothing is said of her being pregnant. The Ethiopian tradition claims Solomon fathered a son with her and founded a dynasty, but the scripture gives no such thing; she turned and went to her own country with her servants.

The weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred sixty-six talents, besides that of the merchants and the kings of Arabia and the governors. He made two hundred targets and three hundred shields of beaten gold, and a great throne of ivory overlaid with the best gold. The throne had six steps, a round top, stays on either side, and two lions by the stays with twelve lions on the six steps, such as was not made in any kingdom. These standing lions were not graven images to bow down to; the law forbids images set up to worship, but these were not worshipped. All Solomon's drinking vessels were gold, and the vessels of the house of the forest of Lebanon were pure gold; silver was nothing accounted of in his days. Once in three years the navy of Tarshish brought gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.

Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth for riches and wisdom, and all the earth sought him to hear the wisdom the Most High put in his heart, bringing presents year by year. No king reigned like Solomon or was richer than him. He gathered a thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, placed in the cities and at Jerusalem; these were of his own people, so he provided jobs for them rather than making them slaves. He made silver in Jerusalem as stones, and had horses and linen yarn brought out of Egypt; a chariot came up for six hundred shekels of silver and a horse for a hundred and fifty. Solomon bought the best of everything, but there comes a point where riches and power can pervert the mind if a man is not grounded, and that is what begins to happen.

Solomon the son of David was strengthened in his kingdom, and the Lord his God was with him and magnified him exceedingly. The Most High established Solomon before he ever built the house. Solomon spake to all Israel, to the captains of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges and to every governor, the chief of the fathers, and went with all the congregation to the high place at Gibeon, where the tabernacle of the congregation that Moses had made in the wilderness was. The ark of God had already been brought up by David from Kirjathjearim to the place he had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it at Jerusalem. To read that history, go back to Second Samuel 6, and to First Chronicles 15.

The brasen altar that Bezaleel the son of Uri had made was set before the tabernacle of the Lord, and Solomon and the congregation sought unto it. Solomon went up to that brasen altar before the Lord and offered a thousand burnt offerings upon it. In that night the Most High appeared unto Solomon and said, Ask what I shall give thee. This same account is told in First Kings chapter 3, where the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night; reading it there gives more detail of what was said. Solomon answered that the Lord had shewed great mercy unto David his father and made him to reign in his stead, and asked that the promise unto David be established, for the Lord had made him king over a people like the dust of the earth in multitude. Solomon asked for wisdom and knowledge that he might go out and come in before the people, for who could judge so great a people. When you read between Kings and Chronicles and line up the history, you get the full detail of what went on with Solomon and David.

The Most High said to Solomon that because this was in his heart, and he had not asked riches, wealth, honor, the life of his enemies, nor long life, but wisdom and knowledge to judge the people, wisdom and knowledge were granted unto him. The Lord also gave Solomon riches, wealth, and honor such as no king before him had, and none after him would have the like. When a man seeks the things of the Most High first, the other things are added unto him. Solomon returned from the high place at Gibeon to Jerusalem and reigned over Israel. He gathered chariots and horsemen, having a thousand and four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, which he placed in the chariot cities and with the king at Jerusalem. The king made silver and gold at Jerusalem as plenteous as stones, and cedars as the sycomore trees in the valley for abundance. Horses were brought out of Egypt, and the merchants received the linen yarn at a price and fetched up horses and chariots for all the kings of the Hittites and of Syria.

name: The two women before Solomon
charge: Conflicting claims to a living child
summary: Two women brought competing claims to a living infant before Solomon. One alleged that the other had exchanged their children after her own child died. Solomon tested their responses to a proposed division of the child and identified his mother.
offense: The account first presents the exchange of the children as one woman's testimony. Both women claimed the surviving child. The narrator identifies the mother through her compassion: she preferred to surrender the child rather than see him killed.
judgment: Solomon ordered that the living child be given to his mother and not killed. Israel recognized the wisdom of God in his judgment. The custody decision is explicit; no punishment of the false claimant is recorded. The unrecorded classification refers only to that punishment, not to an absence of a judicial decision.

entries.commentary: Solomon makes affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt and takes his daughter, while building his own house, the house of the Lord, and the wall of Jerusalem. He loves the Lord and walks in the statutes of David his father, though the people still sacrifice in high places because no house was yet built to the name of the Lord.

At Gibeon the Most High appears to Solomon in a dream and says, ask what I shall give thee. Solomon, calling himself a little child who knows not how to go out or come in, asks for an understanding heart to judge the great people, to discern between good and bad. This is what we still need to pray for. We should pray that the Most High endows our leadership with wisdom, and that we ourselves learn wisdom in these scriptures and how to judge matters among one another. -

Because Solomon asked for understanding to discern judgment and not for long life, riches, or the life of his enemies, the Most High gives him a wise and understanding heart like no other before or after. He also gives what Solomon did not ask, riches and honor, and promises length of days if he walks in his ways.

Two harlots come before the king, each claiming the living child, after one woman's child died in the night and she exchanged it. Solomon calls for a sword and commands the living child divided in two, and gives half to each. The true mother pleads that the child be given alive to the other rather than slain, and by this the king discerns her, for her bowels yearned upon her son. All Israel hears the judgment and fears the king, for they see the wisdom of God is in him to do judgment.

name: King Solomon
charge: Multiplying foreign wives; building high places to their gods
summary: The wisest king loved many strange women, seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, from the very nations the Lord had said, ye shall not go in to them. When he was old they turned his heart, and he built high places for Chemosh and Molech in the hill before Jerusalem.
offense: Solomon received wisdom, riches, honour, and the work of building the Lord's house. Yet he loved many strange women of the nations concerning whom the Lord had warned Israel, and he clave to them in love. In his old age his wives turned his heart after other gods (1 Kings 11:1-4). The warning concerned the very influence he allowed nearest his heart. The law for a king had forbidden multiplying horses, wives, silver, and gold, and required him to read the law all the days of his life so that his heart would not be lifted above his brethren (Deuteronomy 17:16-20). Royal greatness was to remain under instruction. Solomon's abundance did not place him beyond the dangers the command had named in advance. He went after Ashtoreth and Milcom and built high places for Chemosh and Molech. He did likewise for his strange wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods (1 Kings 11:5-8). The man who had built the temple in Jerusalem also established places of forbidden worship. Providing for the practice of those around him made the compromise part of the kingdom's life. The Lord had appeared to him twice and commanded him concerning this very matter (1 Kings 11:9-10). His failure was not a lack of access to wisdom. Nehemiah later remembered that even Solomon, beloved of God and made king over all Israel, was caused to sin by such marriages (Nehemiah 13:26). The greatness of the beginning deepened the warning of the end.
judgment: The Lord was angry, and told him the kingdom would be rent from his son and given to his servant, leaving one tribe for David's sake. Adversaries were raised up in his own lifetime; Jeroboam received the ten tribes at his death. So the kingdom was divided.

Yet he loved many strange women of the nations concerning whom the Lord had warned Israel, and he clave to them in love. In his old age his wives turned his heart after other gods (1 Kings 11:1-4). entries.commentary: Solomon loved many strange women besides the daughter of Pharaoh, women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Zidonians, and Hittites, nations the Most High had said Israel should not join with, for surely they would turn their heart after their gods; and Solomon clave to these in love. He had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines, and his wives turned away his heart. It happened exactly as the Most High said it would, for the law had warned that intermarriage would turn the heart to serve other gods, and it was not a maybe but a will.

When Solomon was old his wives turned his heart after other gods, and his heart was not perfect with the Most High as David his father's was; he went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians and Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites, and did evil in the sight of the Most High. David also sinned, but when David sinned he repented and turned back, while Solomon kept going into sin; this is why a righteous man falls seven times and rises again. Solomon built high places for Chemosh the abomination of Moab and for Molech the abomination of Ammon, and did likewise for all his strange wives who burnt incense and sacrificed to their gods. The six-pointed star called the star of David is in truth the star of Molech, an idol, and has nothing to do with righteousness.

The Most High was angry with Solomon because his heart was turned from him who had appeared to him twice and commanded him not to go after other gods, but he kept not the commandment. Therefore the Most High said he would surely rend the kingdom from Solomon and give it to his servant, but not in Solomon's days for David's sake; he would rend it out of the hand of his son. This is the pivotal moment in the history of Israel, for this sin divided the kingdom under Jeroboam and Rehoboam. The Most High said he would not rend all the kingdom but would give one tribe to the son of David for David's sake and for Jerusalem's sake.

The Most High stirred up an adversary to Solomon, Hadad the Edomite, of the king's seed in Edom, for when David was in Edom, Joab remained six months until he had cut off every male, and Hadad fled as a child to Egypt where Pharaoh gave him favor, a house, and a wife. Esau was always the first hater and enemy of Israel, comforting himself in the thought of killing us. When Hadad heard David and Joab were dead, he sought to return to his own country. The Most High also stirred up Rezin the son of Eliadah, who gathered men, reigned in Damascus, and was an adversary to Israel all the days of Solomon. There was peace under Solomon while he kept the commandments, but when he broke them the Most High gave strength to his enemies.

Jeroboam the son of Nebat, Solomon's servant, a mighty man of valor, lifted up his hand against the king. Solomon had made him ruler over the charge of the house of Joseph, which was the two tribes Ephraim and Manasseh. The prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met Jeroboam in the way, took his new garment, rent it in twelve pieces, and gave Jeroboam ten, saying the Most High would rend ten tribes from Solomon's hand and give them to him. One tribe would remain for David's servant's sake and for Jerusalem, because Israel had forsaken the Most High and worshipped Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom. The house of David held Judah and Benjamin, with Levi, so that ten tribes went to Jeroboam. If Jeroboam would walk in the ways of the Most High and keep his statutes, the Most High would build him a sure house as he built for David. Solomon then sought to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam fled to Shishak king of Egypt until Solomon died.

The rest of the acts of Solomon and his wisdom are written in the book of the acts of Solomon; he reigned in Jerusalem over Israel forty years, then slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, and Rehoboam his son reigned in his stead.

Thou shalt not sacrifice unto the Most High any bullock or sheep wherein is blemish, or any evilfavouredness, for that is an abomination unto the Lord thy God. Back then you could be put to death for sacrificing a bullock or sheep with a blemish, because doing an abominable thing carried death.

If there be found among you man or woman that hath wrought wickedness, transgressed the covenant, and gone and served other gods, the sun or moon or any of the host of heaven, which the Most High commanded not, the matter had to be established first. A lot of people do not know how to apply [Leviticus 5:1](/bible/leviticus/5#v1); the precept for [Leviticus 5:1](/bible/leviticus/5#v1) is [Deuteronomy 17:4](/bible/deuteronomy/17#v4). Whether it be told thee or thou hast heard of it, thou shalt enquire diligently, and behold, if it be true and the thing certain that such abomination is wrought in Israel, then judgment proceeds. Make sure you are certain of a thing before you bring somebody to judgment; only after diligent enquiry was the man or woman brought to the gates and stoned with stones till they die.

At the mouth of two witnesses or three witnesses shall he that is worthy of death be put to death; at the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death. The hands of the witnesses shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterward the hands of all the people. Wait till we go back to this: the ones who witnessed against you were the first to lay hands on you, so a false witness could not hide behind the crowd. So thou shalt put the evil away from among you.

If there arise a matter too hard for thee in judgment, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke, matters of controversy within thy gates, then thou shalt get thee up into the place which the Lord shall choose. Come unto the priests the Levites and unto the judge that shall be in those days, and they shall shew thee the sentence of judgment; thou shalt do according to all that they inform thee, according to the sentence of the law which they shall teach thee, declining neither to the right hand nor to the left. The man that will do presumptuously and will not hearken unto the priest that standeth to minister before the Most High, or unto the judge, even that man shall die; and all the people shall hear, and fear, and do no more presumptuously.

When thou art come unto the land and shalt say, I will set a king over me like as all the nations that are about me, thou shalt in any wise set him king whom the Lord thy God shall choose: one from among thy brethren; thou mayest not set a stranger over thee, which is not thy brother. These are the laws for a king that is to rule over Israel. He shall not multiply horses to himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt to multiply horses, for the Lord hath said, Ye shall henceforth return no more that way. Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away. You hear a lot of these dudes today saying king this and king that, and many of the same men pushing for multiple wives; the law of the king says do not multiply wives to thyself. Neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.

When he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites. It shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the Most High and keep all the words of this law and these statutes to do them. The purpose: that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, that he turn not aside from the commandment to the right hand or to the left, and that he prolong his days in his kingdom, he and his children, in the midst of Israel.

On that day they read in the books of Moses and found written that the Ammonite and the Moabite should not come into the congregation of God for ever, because they met not Israel with bread and water but hired Balaam against them to curse them, and the Most High turned the curse into a blessing. When the people heard the law, they separated from Israel all the mixed multitude. The reading of the law produced immediate obedience, cutting off what the law said to cut off. -

Eliashib the priest, having oversight of the chambers of the house of God, was allied to Tobiah and had prepared him a great chamber where the offerings, tithes, and vessels had formerly been laid. Nehemiah was away in the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon, and when he returned and understood the evil, he cast all Tobiah's household stuff out of the chamber, cleansed the chambers, and brought back the vessels of the house of God with the meat offering and the frankincense.

Nehemiah found that the portions of the Levites had not been given, so the Levites and singers had fled every one to his field, and he contended with the rulers and set the Levites back in their place. He made treasurers over the treasuries, faithful men, to distribute unto their brethren, and prayed, Remember me, O my God, concerning this, and wipe not out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God.

Nehemiah saw men in Judah treading wine presses on the Sabbath, bringing in sheaves, lading asses, and bringing wine, grapes, and figs into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, and men of Tyre selling fish and all manner of ware on the Sabbath. He contended with the nobles of Judah and asked what evil thing this was to profane the Sabbath day, reminding them that their fathers did the same and the Most High brought this evil upon the city, and now they brought more wrath upon Israel. Buying and selling on the Sabbath is breaking the commandment. -

When the gates of Jerusalem began to be dark before the Sabbath, Nehemiah commanded them shut and set his servants at the gates so no burden would be brought in on the Sabbath, and the merchants lodged outside Jerusalem once or twice. He testified against them and warned that if they came again he would lay hands on them, and from that time they came no more on the Sabbath. This laying on of hands is not a blessing but a serious warning, and the merchants knew he was not joking. He then commanded the Levites to cleanse themselves and keep the gates to sanctify the Sabbath day.

Nehemiah saw Jews that had married wives of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab, and their children spake half in the speech of Ashdod and could not speak the Jews' language, but according to the language of each people. Because the fathers were not truly in the house, the children learned their mother's tongue and customs instead of Hebrew and the law. Nehemiah contended with them, cursed them, smote certain of them, plucked off their hair, and made them swear not to give or take daughters in marriage with those nations, reminding them that Solomon himself, though beloved of his God, was caused to sin by outlandish women. -

One of the sons of Joiada, son of Eliashib the high priest, was son in law to Sanballat the Horonite, so Nehemiah chased him away because he had defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites. Thus Nehemiah cleansed the people from all strangers, appointed the wards of the priests and Levites every one in his business, and provided for the wood offering and the firstfruits, closing the book with the prayer, Remember me, O my God, for good. This is the book of records, and to see it as history rather than religion is to understand who these people are. -

Solomon makes affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt and takes his daughter, while building his own house, the house of the Lord, and the wall of Jerusalem. He loves the Lord and walks in the statutes of David his father, though the people still sacrifice in high places because no house was yet built to the name of the Lord.

This is what we still need to pray for. He also gives what Solomon did not ask, riches and honor, and promises length of days if he walks in his ways.

name: Rehoboam
charge: Forsaking the counsel of the old men; forsaking the law of the Lord
summary: Solomon's son rejected the elders' advice to serve the people and took his young companions' line: my little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins. Ten tribes left him that day. Later, when the kingdom was established, he forsook the law of the Lord and all Israel with him.
offense: The people came to Rehoboam at Shechem asking that he lighten the grievous service and heavy yoke laid upon them under Solomon. They offered to serve him if he would hear their burden (1 Kings 12:1-5). The new king asked for three days before answering. Taking time for counsel was sound; the failure came in choosing which counsel would govern him. The elders who had stood before Solomon told him to serve the people that day and answer with good words. His companions told him to announce a heavier yoke and scorpions in place of whips (1 Kings 12:6-11). One answer sought an enduring bond through service. The other treated the people's distress as an opportunity to display superiority. Proverbs 15:1 sets a soft answer against grievous words that stir up anger. Rehoboam chose the rough answer. Possession of the throne had not given him the understanding by which it could be held. Later, after he established and strengthened the kingdom, he forsook the law, and the people followed him (2 Chronicles 12:1). The repeated failure was a heart that had not prepared itself to seek the Lord (2 Chronicles 12:14). Neither inherited position nor strengthened cities supplied that preparation.
judgment: The northern tribes rejected the house of David, stoned Adoram, and made Jeroboam king. Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:16-20). His answer fulfilled the division already declared through Ahijah, yet the prophecy did not make his pride wise. The Lord accomplished his word through a king responsible for the answer he chose. When Rehoboam assembled Judah and Benjamin to recover the kingdom, Shemaiah forbade them to fight their brethren because the division was from the Lord. They obeyed and returned (1 Kings 12:21-24). He could still hearken to correction after refusing sound counsel at Shechem. Shishak afterward took Judah's fortified cities and threatened Jerusalem. Shemaiah named the cause: because they had forsaken the Lord, he had left them in Shishak's hand. The king and princes humbled themselves and confessed that the Lord was righteous (2 Chronicles 12:2-6). The Lord granted some deliverance, but they would serve Shishak and learn the difference between his service and the service of earthly kingdoms (2 Chronicles 12:7-8). Egypt carried away the treasures and Solomon's golden shields; Rehoboam replaced the gold with brass. Humbling preserved him from utter destruction without restoring everything his departure had cost.

The other treated the people's distress as an opportunity to display superiority. Proverbs 15:1 sets a soft answer against grievous words that stir up anger.

Rehoboam chose the rough answer. Possession of the throne had not given him the understanding by which it could be held. Later, after he established and strengthened the kingdom, he forsook the law, and the people followed him (2 Chronicles 12:1). His answer fulfilled the division already declared through Ahijah, yet the prophecy did not make his pride wise. The Lord accomplished his word through a king responsible for the answer he chose.

When Rehoboam assembled Judah and Benjamin to recover the kingdom, Shemaiah forbade them to fight their brethren because the division was from the Lord. They obeyed and returned (1 Kings 12:21-24). He could still hearken to correction after refusing sound counsel at Shechem.

Shishak afterward took Judah's fortified cities and threatened Jerusalem. Shemaiah named the cause: because they had forsaken the Lord, he had left them in Shishak's hand. The king and princes humbled themselves and confessed that the Lord was righteous (2 Chronicles 12:2-6).

The Lord granted some deliverance, but they would serve Shishak and learn the difference between his service and the service of earthly kingdoms (2 Chronicles 12:7-8). Egypt carried away the treasures and Solomon's golden shields; Rehoboam replaced the gold with brass. Humbling preserved him from utter destruction without restoring everything his departure had cost.

Rehoboam told them to depart three days and return, which was wisdom, for it is right to take time and get counsel before giving an answer.

Solomon was the wisest man on earth and still had counselors, yet Rehoboam forsook the counselors of the wisest man for his peers. The problem is getting counsel from those on your own level rather than from elders. The young men told him to say his little finger would be thicker than his father's loins, and that where his father chastised them with whips he would chastise them with scorpions, which was disrespectful.

When Jeroboam and the people came the third day, Rehoboam answered roughly, forsaking the old men's counsel, and told them he would add to their yoke and chastise them with scorpions. The king hearkened not to the people, for the cause was from the Most High, that he might perform the saying he spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam; the prophecy had to come to pass.

When all Israel saw the king would not hearken, they said, What portion have we in David? To your tents, O Israel. So Israel departed and rebelled against the house of David to this day, and only over those in the cities of Judah did Rehoboam reign. Rehoboam sent Adoram who was over the tribute, and all Israel stoned him with stones, so the king fled in his chariot to Jerusalem. This is the split, the northern tribes rebelling against the house of David until this day. When Israel heard Jeroboam had returned, they called him to the congregation and made him king over Israel; none followed the house of David but the tribe of Judah only. That is how Jeroboam got the ten tribes.

Rehoboam assembled the house of Judah with Benjamin, a hundred and eighty thousand chosen warriors, to fight against the house of Israel and bring the kingdom back to himself. But the word of the Most High came to Shemaiah the man of God, telling Rehoboam and the house of Judah and Benjamin not to fight against their brethren the children of Israel, for this thing was from the Most High; and they hearkened and returned home.

Jeroboam built Shechem in mount Ephraim and Penuel, and feared in his heart that if the people went up to sacrifice at Jerusalem their hearts would turn again to Rehoboam king of Judah and they would kill him. Jeroboam took counsel and made two calves of gold, telling Israel it was too much to go up to Jerusalem, and setting one calf in Bethel and the other in Dan, and this thing became a sin. He made a house of high places and priests of the lowest of the people, not of the sons of Levi. Jeroboam ordained a feast in the eighth month on the fifteenth day, a feast he devised of his own heart, and offered on the altar at Bethel sacrificing to the calves he made. Devising your own holy days and throwing off the days of the Most High is the same error men make today, and after forty years of peace under Solomon the nation of Israel began to decline even more.

When Rehoboam establishes the kingdom and strengthens himself, he forsakes the law of the Lord, and all Israel with him. One who leads goes astray and carries many others with him; this is why the people must be examples to one another in righteousness, of one mind and one spirit in the rebuilding of the kingdom.

In the fifth year of Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt comes up against Jerusalem because Rehoboam transgressed against the Lord. Shishak comes with twelve hundred chariots, threescore thousand horsemen, and people without number out of Egypt, the Lubims, the Sukkiims, and the Ethiopians. He takes the fenced cities of Judah and comes to Jerusalem; the invasion is the direct result of forsaking the law.

Shemaiah the prophet comes to Rehoboam and the princes of Judah gathered at Jerusalem and declares the word of the Lord: because they have forsaken him, he has left them in the hand of Shishak. The princes and the king humble themselves and say the Lord is righteous. When correction comes, the right response is to confess that the Most High is righteous in what he does, acknowledging the punishment as just.

When the Lord sees that they humble themselves, his word comes to Shemaiah saying he will not destroy them but grant them some deliverance, and his wrath will not be poured on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak. Nevertheless they will be Shishak's servants, that they may know the difference between serving the Most High and serving the kingdoms of the countries. The people today must likewise humble themselves, relearn to obey the commandments, and accept their condition as righteous judgment from the hand of the Most High. -

Shishak takes away the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king's house, carrying off all the shields of gold Solomon had made. Rehoboam makes shields of brass in their place and commits them to the guard that keeps the entrance of the king's house. Whenever the king enters the house of the Lord the guard fetches the shields and returns them to the guard chamber.

Because Rehoboam humbles himself, the wrath of the Lord turns from him so that he is not utterly destroyed, and in Judah things go well. Deliverance and the destruction of enemies come to the people when they humble themselves before the Most High.

Rehoboam strengthens himself in Jerusalem and reigns; he is forty and one years old when he begins to reign and reigns seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the Lord chose to put his name there. His mother's name is Naamah an Ammonitess. He does evil because he prepares not his heart to seek the Lord; the failure is a heart never set on the Most High.

The acts of Rehoboam are written in the book of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer concerning genealogies, and there were wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually. Rehoboam sleeps with his fathers, is buried in the city of David, and his son Abijah reigns in his place. The moment he hears her feet at the door, Ahijah calls her by name and says he is sent to her with heavy tidings.

The message declares that though the Most High exalted Jeroboam from among the people and rent the kingdom from the house of David to give it to him, he did not walk as David who kept the commandments. Jeroboam reigned twenty-two years, then slept with his fathers, and Nadab his son reigned in his place. They built high places, images, and groves on every hill, and there were also sodomites in the land, doing according to the abominations of the nations cast out before them. -

name: Jeroboam son of Nebat
charge: Two golden calves; priests of the lowest of the people; a feast devised of his own heart
summary: Given ten tribes by the Lord, Jeroboam feared the people would return to Jerusalem to worship, so he set calves in Bethel and Dan, saying, behold thy gods, O Israel, made priests of any who were not Levites, and moved the feast to a month of his own choosing. His sin became a recurring measure of the kings who followed him.
offense: The Lord gave Jeroboam ten tribes and promised an established house if he would hearken, walk in his ways, and keep his commandments (1 Kings 11:37-38). The kingdom came with a charge to obey, not permission to construct a religion suited to its preservation. Jeroboam reasoned that worship at Jerusalem would turn the people's hearts toward Rehoboam and lead to his own death. Instead of trusting the promise, he made two golden calves, set them at Bethel and Dan, and told Israel that going to Jerusalem was too much for them (1 Kings 12:26-30). Convenience offered to the people concealed the king's fear for himself. The words announcing their gods repeated the language of the calf in the wilderness (Exodus 32:4). He also made priests who were not sons of Levi and appointed a feast in the eighth month, a month devised from his own heart (1 Kings 12:31-33). He altered the objects, ministers, place, and time of worship to secure his rule. The priests and Levites who would not serve his arrangement left their possessions and came to Judah; others from the tribes followed to seek the Lord at Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:13-17). A man of God cried against the altar at Bethel. Jeroboam's hand dried up when he reached to seize him, and the altar was rent. The king asked for his hand to be restored, and it was healed (1 Kings 13:1-6). Yet relief from the immediate judgment did not produce a turning from the system that had occasioned it.
judgment: After these things Jeroboam continued making priests for the high places. This became sin to his house, to cut it off from the earth (1 Kings 13:33-34). The warning, sign, and restoration of his hand left him without cause to treat the matter as unknown. When his son Abijah fell sick, Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise to Ahijah. The blind prophet was told who was coming and addressed her before the disguise could serve its purpose (1 Kings 14:1-6). Concealment from men's eyes could not conceal the household from the Lord.
