name: Obadiah, who hid the prophets
charge: Taking a hundred prophets and hiding them by fifty in a cave, and feeding them with bread and water, while serving in Ahab's house
summary: The governor of Ahab's house feared the Lord greatly. When Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord he took a hundred of them, hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water through a famine. Sent out by the king to look for grass, he met Elijah, and was afraid to carry the message that would summon Ahab, in case the Spirit carried the prophet away and he was killed for it. Elijah swore he would shew himself, and he went.
offense: Obadiah governed Ahab's house and feared the Lord greatly. When Jezebel cut off the Lord's prophets, he hid a hundred of them, fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water (1 Kings 18:3-4). Service within the royal household did not require him to join its persecution. The fear of the Lord governed what he would do with the position he held. The famine made this sustained care costly. Ahab himself went out seeking grass to preserve horses and mules, dividing the search with Obadiah (1 Kings 18:5-6). While the kingdom struggled to find provision, Obadiah maintained people the queen intended to destroy. His service was measured in lives sheltered and food supplied, not merely in a private refusal to approve her deeds. When Elijah met him and sent him to announce his presence to Ahab, Obadiah named his fear. Ahab had searched kingdoms and nations for the prophet. If Obadiah reported that Elijah was there and the Spirit carried him away before Ahab arrived, the king would kill the messenger (1 Kings 18:7-12). His concern was not imaginary, nor did he conceal it beneath a claim of fearlessness. He reminded Elijah that he had feared the Lord from his youth and had hidden the prophets. Elijah swore that he would show himself to Ahab that day. Obadiah then went to meet the king and told him (1 Kings 18:12-16). He received the assurance and performed the errand. Courage was seen in his obedience with the danger understood.
judgment: A hundred prophets had been preserved when Jezebel sought to cut them off. Obadiah's provision kept their hiding places from becoming places of starvation. His fear of God bore fruit in the continuing lives of other servants, even while he occupied a post beneath a king who had forsaken the commandments. His message also brought Ahab to Elijah, preparing the meeting from which the summons to Carmel followed (1 Kings 18:16-19). The hidden work of feeding and sheltering was followed by an errand that served a public confrontation. Different duties required the same fidelity. Hebrews 6:10 declares that God does not forget work and labour of love shown in ministering to the saints. Obadiah's account does not conclude with a new title or an estate bestowed upon him. The good already accomplished was substantial: servants were alive, and the required message was delivered. Elijah would later speak of being left alone, but the Lord's work in Israel had never been limited to what one prophet could see (1 Kings 19:10, 18). Obadiah's caves belonged to that larger history of preservation. A man inside Ahab's house had feared the Lord more than he agreed with the house's evil.

verses.text: 3And Ahab called Obadiah, which was the governor of his house. (Now Obadiah feared the Lord greatly: 4For it was so, when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, that Obadiah took an hundred prophets, and hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water.)

entries.commentary: After many days the word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year: Go show thyself unto Ahab, and I will send rain upon the earth. There was a sore famine in Samaria. Ahab called Obadiah, governor of his house, who feared the Lord greatly; when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah took an hundred prophets and hid them by fifty in a cave and fed them with bread and water, putting his own life in danger to save them. The famine was so sore it was hitting the animals, so Ahab and Obadiah divided the land between them, each going his own way to seek fountains and brooks to find grass to save the horses and mules alive. This was the fruit of the drought Elijah had pronounced.

As Obadiah went his way, Elijah met him; Obadiah fell on his face and said, Art thou my lord Elijah? Elijah told him to go tell Ahab that Elijah is here. Obadiah was afraid, for Ahab had searched every nation and kingdom to find and slay Elijah; that is how badly Jezebel wanted him dead, so she got Ahab to do her bidding. This is why Elijah had been on the run, first by Jordan, then years with the widow. Obadiah feared that the spirit of the Lord would carry Elijah away and Ahab would slay him for a false report, so he pleaded his own record: he feared the Lord from his youth and had hidden a hundred of the Lord's prophets by fifty in a cave. Elijah swore by the Lord of hosts that he would surely show himself to Ahab that day, and so Obadiah went to Ahab, and Ahab came to meet Elijah.

When Ahab saw Elijah he said, Art thou he that troubleth Israel? That is the mind of a wicked person: he blamed the trouble on the ordained prophet of God rather than on his own wickedness. When the spirit is gone, wisdom cannot enter a malicious soul, so Ahab had thoughts without understanding. Elijah answered, I have not troubled Israel, but thou and thy father's house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the Lord and thou hast followed Baalim. It was Ahab following the sin of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, worshipping the golden calves, that brought the trouble. Elijah commanded that all Israel be gathered to Mount Carmel with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the groves that eat at Jezebel's table. Jezebel was the one feeding these eight hundred and fifty false prophets and encouraging them, and Ahab never checked her.

Ahab gathered the prophets and all Israel to Mount Carmel, and Elijah said unto the people, How long halt ye between two opinions? If the Lord be God, follow him, but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word. That is a call for all of us to examine ourselves: cast away every burden and sin and follow the Most High and his son fully, keeping the commandments, and do not keep one foot in and one foot out. Being lukewarm, playing the middle ground, ends with Christ spewing a man out of his mouth, and the next step after that is death. Elijah proposed the test: let each side dress a bullock, lay it on wood, and put no fire under, and the God that answereth by fire, let him be God. All the people said, It is well spoken.

The prophets of Baal dressed their bullock first and called on the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, O Baal, hear us, but there was no voice nor any that answered, and they leaped upon the altar. Picture the scene: eight hundred and fifty men doing this, running wild, while Elijah sat back watching the madness. At noon Elijah mocked them, saying, Cry aloud, for he is a god; either he is talking, or pursuing, or on a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth and must be awaked. They cried aloud and cut themselves with knives and lancets till the blood gushed out, for cutting themselves was part of their false worship whenever they called on Baal. From midday past the time of the evening sacrifice there was neither voice nor any to answer nor any that regarded. No one answered because the Most High will not give his glory to another, and the gods of the nations are idols that are not real; they are made up by people who have no God, so when they call on them the idols cannot answer.

Elijah repaired the altar of the Lord with twelve stones according to the twelve tribes of the sons of Jacob, made a trench about it, laid the wood and the bullock in order, and had them drench the sacrifice with four barrels of water three times until the water filled the trench. At the time of the evening sacrifice Elijah prayed, Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel, let it be known this day that thou art God in Israel and that I am thy servant. As the law appointed a sacrifice in the morning and in the evening, this was the evening sacrifice as the sun went down. Elijah prayed, Hear me, O Lord, that this people may know that thou art the Lord God and that thou hast turned their heart back again. Then the fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water in the trench. When all the people saw it they fell on their faces and cried, The Lord, he is the God; the Lord, he is the God. Elijah commanded, Take the prophets of Baal, let not one of them escape, and they were brought down to the brook Kishon and slain there. In the last days it will be the same: when the Most High rains down fire again by the hands of Christ, no false prophet of Baal will escape, for they that feed the sheep of God lies will not be able to flee.

Elijah told Ahab to get up and eat and drink, for there was a sound of abundance of rain. Ahab went up to eat while Elijah went to the top of Carmel, cast himself down upon the earth, and put his face between his knees to pray. Elijah sent his servant seven times to look toward the sea; at the seventh time he reported a little cloud out of the sea like a man's hand. Elijah sent word to Ahab to prepare his chariot and get down before the rain stopped him, for the hand of the Lord was coming. The heaven grew black with clouds and wind and there was a great rain; Ahab rode to Jezreel, a city in the north in Samaria, and the hand of the Lord was on Elijah so that he girded up his loins and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.

name: The prophets of Baal at Carmel
charge: Prophesying in the name of other gods
summary: Four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal cried from morning to noon and cut themselves with knives until the blood gushed out, and there was neither voice nor any to answer. Elijah's bullock, drenched three times, was consumed by fire from heaven with the water and the stones.
offense: At Carmel Elijah asked Israel how long they would halt between two opinions. If the Lord was God, they were to follow him; if Baal, then Baal. The people answered nothing (1 Kings 18:21). The contest exposed a divided service that could not be made right by refusing to decide. Four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal stood against Elijah. They chose a bullock, dressed it, and called upon Baal from morning until noon. There was no voice and no answer. They leaped upon the altar and, after Elijah challenged them, cried aloud and cut themselves with knives and lancets until the blood flowed (1 Kings 18:22-28). Increasing noise and injury did not give their god power to answer. The law forbade a prophet to speak in the name of other gods (Deuteronomy 18:20). Deuteronomy 13:1-5 also required Israel to reject a teacher who led them after other gods, even if a sign accompanied his words. Here no answer came at all, yet the servants of Baal continued until the time of the evening sacrifice (1 Kings 18:29). Zeal for the practice could not make the practice obedience. Elijah repaired the Lord's altar, drenched the offering, and prayed that the people know the Lord and turn back to him (1 Kings 18:30-37). The difference was not merely between two methods of conducting worship. It was between calling upon the living God according to his word and persisting in a service he had forbidden.
judgment: The Lord's fire consumed the offering, wood, stones, dust, and water. The people fell upon their faces and confessed that the Lord was God (1 Kings 18:38-39). The answer left the assembly no reason to maintain its earlier silence. What the prophets of Baal could not obtain through hours of crying was accomplished when the Lord answered his servant. Elijah commanded that none of the prophets of Baal escape. They were taken to the brook Kishon and slain (1 Kings 18:40). The sentence belonged to the covenant law against leading Israel into the service of other gods; the crowd's earlier acceptance and the worship's royal standing did not remove that charge. Rain followed after Elijah prayed upon Carmel (1 Kings 18:41-45). The drought had not been ended by Baal's servants, their multitude, their cries, or their wounds. The return of rain confirmed the same distinction as the fire: the Lord who had withheld it was the one who could send it again.
offenseFull: At Carmel Elijah asked Israel how long they would halt between two opinions. If the Lord was God, they were to follow him; if Baal, then Baal. The people answered nothing (1 Kings 18:21). The contest exposed a divided service that could not be made right by refusing to decide.

Four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal stood against Elijah. They chose a bullock, dressed it, and called upon Baal from morning until noon. There was no voice and no answer. They leaped upon the altar and, after Elijah challenged them, cried aloud and cut themselves with knives and lancets until the blood flowed (1 Kings 18:22-28). Increasing noise and injury did not give their god power to answer.

The law forbade a prophet to speak in the name of other gods (Deuteronomy 18:20). Deuteronomy 13:1-5 also required Israel to reject a teacher who led them after other gods, even if a sign accompanied his words. Here no answer came at all, yet the servants of Baal continued until the time of the evening sacrifice (1 Kings 18:29). Zeal for the practice could not make the practice obedience.

Elijah repaired the Lord's altar, drenched the offering, and prayed that the people know the Lord and turn back to him (1 Kings 18:30-37). The difference was not merely between two methods of conducting worship. It was between calling upon the living God according to his word and persisting in a service he had forbidden.

verses.text: 19Now therefore send, and gather to me all Israel unto mount Carmel, and the prophets of Baal four hundred and fifty, and the prophets of the groves four hundred, which eat at Jezebel’s table.
22Then said Elijah unto the people, I, even I only, remain a prophet of the Lord; but Baal’s prophets are four hundred and fifty men.

entries.commentary: After many days the word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year: Go show thyself unto Ahab, and I will send rain upon the earth. There was a sore famine in Samaria. Ahab called Obadiah, governor of his house, who feared the Lord greatly; when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah took an hundred prophets and hid them by fifty in a cave and fed them with bread and water, putting his own life in danger to save them. The famine was so sore it was hitting the animals, so Ahab and Obadiah divided the land between them, each going his own way to seek fountains and brooks to find grass to save the horses and mules alive. This was the fruit of the drought Elijah had pronounced.

As Obadiah went his way, Elijah met him; Obadiah fell on his face and said, Art thou my lord Elijah? Elijah told him to go tell Ahab that Elijah is here. Obadiah was afraid, for Ahab had searched every nation and kingdom to find and slay Elijah; that is how badly Jezebel wanted him dead, so she got Ahab to do her bidding. This is why Elijah had been on the run, first by Jordan, then years with the widow. Obadiah feared that the spirit of the Lord would carry Elijah away and Ahab would slay him for a false report, so he pleaded his own record: he feared the Lord from his youth and had hidden a hundred of the Lord's prophets by fifty in a cave. Elijah swore by the Lord of hosts that he would surely show himself to Ahab that day, and so Obadiah went to Ahab, and Ahab came to meet Elijah.

When Ahab saw Elijah he said, Art thou he that troubleth Israel? That is the mind of a wicked person: he blamed the trouble on the ordained prophet of God rather than on his own wickedness. When the spirit is gone, wisdom cannot enter a malicious soul, so Ahab had thoughts without understanding. Elijah answered, I have not troubled Israel, but thou and thy father's house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the Lord and thou hast followed Baalim. It was Ahab following the sin of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, worshipping the golden calves, that brought the trouble. Elijah commanded that all Israel be gathered to Mount Carmel with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the groves that eat at Jezebel's table. Jezebel was the one feeding these eight hundred and fifty false prophets and encouraging them, and Ahab never checked her.

Ahab gathered the prophets and all Israel to Mount Carmel, and Elijah said unto the people, How long halt ye between two opinions? If the Lord be God, follow him, but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word. That is a call for all of us to examine ourselves: cast away every burden and sin and follow the Most High and his son fully, keeping the commandments, and do not keep one foot in and one foot out. Being lukewarm, playing the middle ground, ends with Christ spewing a man out of his mouth, and the next step after that is death. Elijah proposed the test: let each side dress a bullock, lay it on wood, and put no fire under, and the God that answereth by fire, let him be God. All the people said, It is well spoken.

The prophets of Baal dressed their bullock first and called on the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, O Baal, hear us, but there was no voice nor any that answered, and they leaped upon the altar. Picture the scene: eight hundred and fifty men doing this, running wild, while Elijah sat back watching the madness. At noon Elijah mocked them, saying, Cry aloud, for he is a god; either he is talking, or pursuing, or on a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth and must be awaked. They cried aloud and cut themselves with knives and lancets till the blood gushed out, for cutting themselves was part of their false worship whenever they called on Baal. From midday past the time of the evening sacrifice there was neither voice nor any to answer nor any that regarded. No one answered because the Most High will not give his glory to another, and the gods of the nations are idols that are not real; they are made up by people who have no God, so when they call on them the idols cannot answer.

Elijah repaired the altar of the Lord with twelve stones according to the twelve tribes of the sons of Jacob, made a trench about it, laid the wood and the bullock in order, and had them drench the sacrifice with four barrels of water three times until the water filled the trench. At the time of the evening sacrifice Elijah prayed, Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel, let it be known this day that thou art God in Israel and that I am thy servant. As the law appointed a sacrifice in the morning and in the evening, this was the evening sacrifice as the sun went down. Elijah prayed, Hear me, O Lord, that this people may know that thou art the Lord God and that thou hast turned their heart back again. Then the fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water in the trench. When all the people saw it they fell on their faces and cried, The Lord, he is the God; the Lord, he is the God. Elijah commanded, Take the prophets of Baal, let not one of them escape, and they were brought down to the brook Kishon and slain there. In the last days it will be the same: when the Most High rains down fire again by the hands of Christ, no false prophet of Baal will escape, for they that feed the sheep of God lies will not be able to flee.

Elijah told Ahab to get up and eat and drink, for there was a sound of abundance of rain. Ahab went up to eat while Elijah went to the top of Carmel, cast himself down upon the earth, and put his face between his knees to pray. Elijah sent his servant seven times to look toward the sea; at the seventh time he reported a little cloud out of the sea like a man's hand. Elijah sent word to Ahab to prepare his chariot and get down before the rain stopped him, for the hand of the Lord was coming. The heaven grew black with clouds and wind and there was a great rain; Ahab rode to Jezreel, a city in the north in Samaria, and the hand of the Lord was on Elijah so that he girded up his loins and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.

The prophet or dreamer of dreams who speaks to turn you away from the Lord your God was put to death under the kingdom. Today Israel is in the land of its oppressors and cannot exact that judgment, and no kind of violence is advocated; the deceived and the deceiver are his, and the judgment belongs to the Most High. What is done today: mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned, and avoid them. The doctrine learned is the law, for I give you good doctrine, forsake ye not my law. Going contrary to the laws of marriage, of the sabbath, of raising children righteously, or of going to thy brother alone when there is an ought between you, and secretly enticing others to follow, is how one turns people away from the Lord; those men and those women have to be put out from among the body.

If thy brother, thy son, thy daughter, the wife of thy bosom, or thy friend which is as thine own soul entice thee secretly to serve other gods: these are the people closest to you, the ones that can have influence on you. Thou shalt not consent, nor hearken, nor pity, nor spare, neither shalt thou conceal him, meaning hide him; when wickedness is concealed, the whole nation is put in jeopardy. Trust in a person is no cover for your soul: when someone you love and trust has the devil on them, they will lead you astray. Nobody can make you do anything, but they can influence you; do not give anyone that credit and let them cause you to lose your crown. This is why [Leviticus 5:1](/bible/leviticus/5#v1) is opened at the start of class: if you know of anything, you are supposed to utter it. Many grew up on snitches get stitches, but in repentance we have to understand that concealing sin is part of why Israel is in the condition it is in, and we have to teach righteousness. It is that simple.

If certain men, the children of Belial, withdraw the inhabitants of a city, saying, let us go and serve other gods: inquire, make search, and ask diligently, and if it be truth and the thing certain, that city was smitten with the edge of the sword, gathered into the midst of the street, and burnt with fire, an heap for ever, not to be built again. Achan is the example of this kind of judgment: Israel committed a trespass in the accursed thing, and one man's folly kindled the anger of the Lord against all Israel. Wars Israel had been winning without losing a man began to be lost, and Joshua had to search and seek out who had committed the crime in Israel. All Israel stoned Achan with stones and burned him with fire in the valley of Achor, and the Lord turned from the fierceness of his anger; righteous judgment lifted the wrath and the people were able to move forward.

The priests the Levites, and all the tribe of Levi, shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel; they shall eat the offerings of the Lord made by fire, and his inheritance. Therefore shall they have no inheritance among their brethren: the Lord is their inheritance, as he hath said unto them.

This shall be the priest's due from the people, from them that offer a sacrifice, whether ox or sheep: they shall give unto the priest the shoulder, and the two cheeks, and the maw. The firstfruit also of thy corn, of thy wine, and of thine oil, and the first of the fleece of thy sheep, shalt thou give him. For the Most High hath chosen him out of all thy tribes to stand to minister in the name of the Lord, him and his sons for ever.

If a Levite come from any of thy gates out of all Israel, and come with all the desire of his mind unto the place which the Lord shall choose, then he shall minister in the name of the Lord his God, as all his brethren the Levites do which stand there before the Lord. They shall have like portions to eat, beside that which cometh of the sale of his patrimony.

When thou art come into the land, thou shalt not learn to do after the abominations of those nations: there shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer. These things actually existed and they are all real: wizards, necromancers, divination, observers of times, people that consult with familiar spirits. If they were not real, they would not be in the Bible with the Most High telling us not to do them. All that do these things are an abomination unto the Lord, and because of these abominations the Most High driveth those nations out from before thee. Thou shalt be perfect with the Lord thy God, meaning upright; the nations hearken unto observers of times and unto diviners, but as for thee, the Most High hath not suffered thee so to do.

The Lord thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken. This is talking about Christ, Yeshua. This answers what Israel desired of the Most High in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, Let me not hear again the voice of the Lord my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I die not; and the Lord said, They have well spoken that which they have spoken. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak unto them all that I shall command him; and whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him. If we do not follow Christ and do what Christ says, that judgment falls on us.

The prophet which shall presume to speak a word in the name of the Most High which he hath not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die. By this law a lot of these pastors stand condemned: they say things and claim Christ said them, when the Most High never commanded Christ to say it and Christ is not telling them to say it. How shall we know the word which the Lord hath not spoken? Ye shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy; this word went to all the congregation of the children of Israel. Fear every man his mother and his father goes back to the commandment, honour thy father and thy mother. Honour can be kept even at a distance: show respect, and do nothing that would bring shame on your mother. But there is a balance; if she asks for what is against the commandments of the Most High, the commandments come first. Keep my sabbaths: the feast days are Sabbaths also. The Passover, the first and last days of the feast of Tabernacles, the day of atonement, and the memorial of blowing of trumpets are all Sabbaths; no servile work, no buying and selling, though cooking is permitted on the feast days.
Turn not unto idols, nor make molten gods; this is the commandment against making any graven image.

The peace offering was eaten the same day it was offered or on the morrow; whatever remained to the third day was burnt. Eaten on the third day it is abominable, and the eater bears his iniquity, for he has profaned the hallowed thing of the Lord.

The corners of the field, the gleanings of the harvest, and the leavings of the vineyard belonged to the poor and the stranger. The Most High is teaching, do not be selfish; love thy neighbour as thyself and look out for the poor of your people. He that provides not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, has denied the faith. Those of his own house are his wife and children; his own is his nation. Care for your people. Charge them that are rich that they be not highminded, but ready to distribute, willing to communicate. Most of us today have no fields or vineyards, but some have good jobs and blessed incomes; you cannot take it with you, so give of your substance. The scriptures also say no good can come to him that gives no alms.

Dealing falsely is any dishonesty: skewing the truth to get your way, or cheating. Be honest. Have an honest job so you do not steal; run an honest business so you do not cheat people with foul practices, selling goods you know will fail or charging a customer for repairs he does not need. That honesty is owed even to the other nations.

Do not swear by His name falsely. Saying I swear to God over a lie profanes the name of the Most High. Christ said swear not at all, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by thy head; let your communication be yea, yea and nay, nay. The only reason a man swears is that he has lied before and no one believes him; in your repentance take swearing out of your speech, and do not put oaths on your own head or your family either.

The wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning: when a man works for you, pay him that same day. Holding back the wage is defrauding thy neighbour, so businesses in Israel should pay their people the way the scriptures say. If both parties agree beforehand to payment the next day, that agreement is between you, the Lord, and that man; the scripture states the standard.

Curse not the deaf, put no stumblingblock before the blind, but fear thy God. Do no unrighteousness in judgment; respect not the person of the poor nor honour the person of the mighty. The courts of this land do the opposite: our people receive far harsher sentences than others for the same crime with the same priors, sometimes before the very same judge.

A talebearer revealeth secrets, but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter. What a brother or sister tells you in confidence is not yours to spread; carrying it to the next person is talebearing, and it happens even in this truth. Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: much strife and contention comes from messy people. Repent of that messy spirit; it has no place in Israel.

Hate not thy brother in thine heart; rebuke thy neighbour and suffer not sin upon him. If you love your brother or sister you correct them when they are going off into sin; that is real love. Love thy neighbour as thyself: thy neighbour is the children of thy people. Get that right, against the teaching that makes the neighbour everybody.
Keep the statutes: no gendering cattle with a diverse kind, no sowing the field with mingled seed, and no garment mingled of linen and woollen; that is the law against mixed fabrics.

The bondmaid betrothed to an husband and not redeemed was scourged, not put to death, because she was not free; the man brought a ram for a trespass offering, and the priest made atonement, and the sin was forgiven him.

Fruit of a newly planted tree was counted as uncircumcised for three years and not eaten; in the fourth year all the fruit was holy to praise the Lord withal; only in the fifth year could the fruit be eaten, that it might yield its increase.

Eat nothing with the blood: cook the blood out of the meat. No rare or bloody meat, none of the raw-meat customs of the other nations. Use no enchantments nor observe times; that goes into the horoscopes, astrology, and the rest of that nonsense. Leave it alone.

Round not the corners of your head, meaning do not bald your head; mar not the corners of thy beard, meaning do not shave off the beard. This is written to all the children of Israel, not to the priests only.

No cuttings in the flesh for the dead, nor any marks printed upon you: that is the tattoo. The RIP tattoo for a dead family member is both a cutting in the flesh for the dead and a mark printed upon you. If you came into this truth already carrying tattoos, repent, ask the Most High for forgiveness, and get no more. Ear and nose piercings are not forbidden by this verse; the cutting forbidden here is the cutting in the flesh for the dead.

Prostituting your daughter to cause her to be a whore takes several forms: letting her dress immodestly, letting a little girl wear makeup and grown attire, and letting her have a boyfriend. There are no boyfriends and girlfriends in the scriptures. The father waketh for the daughter: his charge is to watch over her, know her clothes, her phone, her friends and their parents, and keep her under supervision, lest she pass away the flower of her age, which is her virginity being taken. Keeping a sure watch over her is not being too hard on her; it is the commandment, lest she make thee a laughingstock to thine enemies. Many daughters go the way of the mother, as the proverb says, as is the mother, so is her daughter; but Israel is teaching the sisters self-respect again, with the scriptures on modest apparel and on not wearing that which pertaineth to a man. When daughters are left without watch, the land falls into whoredom and fills with wickedness; the state of the community today shows the fruit of neglecting this law.

Keep my sabbaths and reverence my sanctuary. Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards to be defiled by them. Rise up before the hoary head and honour the face of the old man: show respect unto your elders.

Vex not the stranger that sojourns with thee in the land; he shall be as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself, for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt. The stranger of this law is an Israelite of another tribe sojourning outside the allotment of his own tribe: a man of Judah dwelling in the land of Benjamin is a stranger to that land, because that was not the allotment the Most High gave him. When your brother the stranger falls into decay, relieve him and let him sojourn with you; give him work to deliver him out of his low state until he can stand again. The bondmen laws show the contrast in how the word stranger is used. The bondmen and bondmaids were to be of the heathen round about, and in that context the children of the strangers sojourning among you are the heathen, a possession and an inheritance; but over your brethren the children of Israel ye shall not rule with rigour. Then the sojourner or stranger that waxeth rich by thee returns to the Israelite stranger, for the bondservant of the heathen did not wax rich.

Just balances, just weights, a just ephah and a just hin. Falsifying the balance is rigging the scale so that one pound weighs out as two and the buyer pays double; our people were doing that wickedness, and the Most High requires honest measure. Therefore observe all my statutes and all my judgments and do them: the Lord which brought Israel out of the land of Egypt requires it.

name: Elisha
charge: Asking a double portion of the spirit; leaving the oxen and following, and refusing Naaman's reward
summary: Called from ploughing, Elisha fed the people and followed Elijah. He asked a double portion of his spirit and continued the ministry after his master was taken. He supplied households, restored the Shunammite’s son, refused Naaman’s reward, and fed the Syrians delivered into Samaria. After his death, a man revived upon touching his bones.
offense: Elisha was ploughing when Elijah cast his mantle upon him. He left the oxen, asked to kiss his father and mother, and returned to prepare a farewell meal. He slew a yoke of oxen, boiled the flesh with their instruments, fed the people, and arose to minister to Elijah (1 Kings 19:19-21). The call was answered by a change of service, not merely an expression of admiration for the prophet. When Elijah's departure approached, Elisha would not leave him at Gilgal, Bethel, or Jericho. He crossed Jordan with him and asked for a double portion of his spirit. Elijah called it a hard thing and gave the condition that Elisha see him taken (2 Kings 2:1-10). The request concerned the power required to continue the work, not wealth or a place at the king's table. After Naaman's cleansing, Elisha refused the gift pressed upon him, swearing by the Lord before whom he stood that he would receive none (2 Kings 5:15-16). Gehazi afterward pursued what his master refused. The same opportunity distinguished service from covetousness. The healing was not to be turned into a private bargain by a servant who had not supplied its power. At Dothan, surrounded by the Syrian host, Elisha answered his servant's fear by praying that his eyes be opened. The mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15-17). Elisha did not deny the surrounding army; he knew it was not the only host present. He sought that his servant see the protection already there.
judgment: Elisha saw Elijah taken and received the mantle that fell. Returning to Jordan, he struck the water and called upon the Lord God of Elijah. The waters divided, and the sons of the prophets recognised that Elijah's spirit rested upon him (2 Kings 2:11-15). The departed master was not the source exhausted by his departure. The Lord remained with the servant appointed to continue. His ministry supplied households and preserved life: the widow's oil paid her debt, the Shunammite received her son alive, harmful pottage was made safe, and a hundred men ate from twenty barley loaves and left food remaining (2 Kings 4:1-7, 32-44). The wonders were not detached displays. They answered debt, bereavement, hunger, and danger among the people. When the Syrians sent to seize him were led into Samaria, the king asked whether to kill them. Elisha commanded that food and water be set before them and that they return to their master. They ate and departed (2 Kings 6:18-23). Power to deliver an enemy into the city did not require that power to be used for slaughter. The prophet who announced judgments also directed mercy where the Lord had given that charge. Elisha eventually became sick and died, but the Lord's power was not buried with him. A dead man cast into his sepulchre touched his bones, revived, and stood upon his feet (2 Kings 13:20-21). Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 48:12-14 remembers both the wonders of his life and the marvel after his death. His strength had never resided in possessions gathered from those he helped, but in the Lord whose word he served.

Elisha eventually became sick and died, but the Lord's power was not buried with him. A dead man cast into his sepulchre touched his bones, revived, and stood upon his feet (2 Kings 13:20-21). Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 48:12-14 remembers both the wonders of his life and the marvel after his death. His strength had never resided in possessions gathered from those he helped, but in the Lord whose word he served.

name: Ben-hadad and the Syrians at Aphek
charge: Saying the Lord is a god of the hills and not of the valleys
summary: Beaten at Samaria, the Syrians told their king the God of Israel was a hill god and would lose on level ground. The Lord heard it. A prophet told Ahab the outcome before the battle: that ye may know that I am the Lord.
offense: After defeat before Samaria, the Syrian servants attributed Israel's strength to the hills. They proposed replacing the kings with captains and fighting on the plain, where they supposed Israel's God could not give the same victory (1 Kings 20:23-25). They changed the ground without changing the presumption beneath the war. Ben-hadad gathered another host at Aphek. Israel appeared like two little flocks while the Syrians filled the country (1 Kings 20:26-27). The visible imbalance encouraged confidence in numbers, but the Lord's answer addressed the claim about his power. He would deliver the multitude so Israel would know that he was the Lord (1 Kings 20:28). Neither terrain nor a larger army marked the limit of his dominion.
judgment: After seven days facing one another, Israel struck a hundred thousand Syrian footmen in one day. The survivors fled into Aphek, where a wall fell upon twenty-seven thousand; Ben-hadad hid in an inner chamber (1 Kings 20:29-30). The place chosen to reverse the first defeat became the place of a greater overthrow. Ahab afterward received Ben-hadad and released him under a covenant. That release was charged against Ahab: he had let go a man appointed to destruction (1 Kings 20:31-42). The Syrian king's escape did not prove his claim about the Lord or make the agreement righteous. Victory given to Israel still required obedience from Israel's king.

verses.text: 23And the servants of the king of Syria said unto him, Their gods are gods of the hills; therefore they were stronger than we; but let us fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they. 24And do this thing, Take the kings away, every man out of his place, and put captains in their rooms: 25And number thee an army, like the army that thou hast lost, horse for horse, and chariot for chariot: and we will fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they. And he hearkened unto their voice, and did so.

26And it came to pass at the return of the year, that Ben–hadad numbered the Syrians, and went up to Aphek, to fight against Israel. 27And the children of Israel were numbered, and were all present, and went against them: and the children of Israel pitched before them like two little flocks of kids; but the Syrians filled the country. 28And there came a man of God, and spake unto the king of Israel, and said, Thus saith the Lord, Because the Syrians have said, The Lord is God of the hills, but he is not God of the valleys, therefore will I deliver all this great multitude into thine hand, and ye shall know that I am the Lord. 29And they pitched one over against the other seven days. And so it was, that in the seventh day the battle was joined: and the children of Israel slew of the Syrians an hundred thousand footmen in one day. 30But the rest fled to Aphek, into the city; and there a wall fell upon twenty and seven thousand of the men that were left. And Ben–hadad fled, and came into the city, into an inner chamber.

13And, behold, there came a prophet unto Ahab king of Israel, saying, Thus saith the Lord, Hast thou seen all this great multitude? behold, I will deliver it into thine hand this day; and thou shalt know that I am the Lord.

entries.commentary: Ben-hadad the king of Syria gathered all his hosts, with thirty-two kings, horses, and chariots, and besieged Samaria. He sent to Ahab demanding his silver, gold, wives, and children, even the goodliest, and Ahab answered, My lord, O king, I am thine, and all that I have. Ben-hadad sent again, saying that his servants would come and search Ahab's house and take away whatsoever was pleasant in his eyes. This siege was Ahab's judgment from the Lord for trying to kill Elijah, for serving Baal, and for letting Jezebel run him and kill the prophets.

Ahab called the elders of the land, who told him not to hearken nor consent to Ben-hadad's demand, so Ahab sent word that he would grant the first demand but not the second. Ben-hadad swore by his gods to reduce Samaria to dust for handfuls among his people. Ahab answered, Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off. When Ben-hadad heard this while drinking with the kings in the pavilions, he commanded his servants to set themselves in array against the city; Ahab's boast had provoked him to prepare for battle.

A prophet came unto Ahab saying, Thus saith the Lord, Hast thou seen all this great multitude? I will deliver it into thine hand this day, and thou shalt know that I am the Lord. Asked by whom, the prophet answered, By the young men of the princes of the provinces, and that Ahab himself should order the battle. Two hundred and thirty-two young men of the princes of the provinces went out first, followed by the children of Israel, being seven thousand; they went out at noon while Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk with the thirty-two kings, taking Israel lightly. The young men slew every one his man and the Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them; Ben-hadad escaped on a horse, and the king of Israel smote the horses and chariots and slew the Syrians with a great slaughter. The Most High gave the victory though Israel's numbers were small.

The prophet warned Ahab to strengthen himself and mark, for at the return of the year the king of Syria would come up against him again. The servants of Ben-hadad counseled that Israel's gods were gods of the hills, so they should fight in the plain, replace the kings with captains, and number a fresh army horse for horse and chariot for chariot; Ben-hadad hearkened and did so. At the return of the year Ben-hadad came up to fight, and the children of Israel pitched before them like two little flocks of kids while the Syrians filled the country; Israel's army was small compared to the great Syrian host. A man of God told Ahab, Because the Syrians have said the Lord is God of the hills but not of the valleys, I will deliver all this great multitude into thine hand, and ye shall know that I am the Lord. Here the Most High was giving Ahab a chance to repent, redeeming him by showing his power with fewer numbers; yet Ahab still did not repent, did not check Jezebel, and did not destroy the idols of Baal, for his sin had blinded him. Israel and Syria pitched one against the other seven days, and on the seventh day the battle was joined, and the children of Israel slew of the Syrians a hundred thousand footmen in one day. The rest fled to Aphek, where a wall fell upon twenty-seven thousand of the men left. Seven thousand against a hundred thousand, and the numbers did not matter because the Lord was with Israel; but Ahab still did not repent.

Ben-hadad fled into an inner chamber, and his servants, having heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful, put sackcloth on their loins and ropes on their heads and went to plead for his life. Ahab, hearing that Ben-hadad lived, called him his brother and had him brought up into his chariot. Look at Ahab's wickedness: this was a Syrian who was just trying to kill him last year, and he brought him up into the king's chariot. Ben-hadad offered to restore the cities his father had taken and give Ahab streets in Damascus, and Ahab said, I will send thee away with this covenant, and he made a covenant with the heathen and sent him away.

A son of the prophets told his neighbor to smite him in the word of the Lord; the man refused, and the prophet said a lion would slay him for not obeying the voice of the Lord, and a lion found him and slew him. Another man smote and wounded him, and the prophet disguised himself with ashes on his face and waited for the king, hiding the certain look that prophets carry, the same way we carry a certain look today. The prophet cried to the king a parable of a soldier charged to keep a prisoner on pain of his own life, who let the man escape; the king of Israel judged, So shall thy judgment be, thou thyself hast decided it. Then the prophet took the ashes away and Ahab discerned he was one of the prophets. The prophet declared, Thus saith the Lord, because thou hast let go a man whom I appointed to utter destruction, thy life shall go for his life and thy people for his people. Ben-hadad was supposed to die at war with Ahab, tied to the word that Hazael would move into the kingship of Syria, but Ahab made a covenant with him instead of killing him. The king of Israel went to his house heavy and displeased and came to Samaria, crying again over a just judgment because he would not obey the voice of the Lord. The lesson for us is the same: as it is written, so shall we do, that we may be justified and our life not be taken from us for rebellion against the Lord. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

name: The man who refused the prophetic command
charge: Refusing a command delivered in the word of the Lord
summary: A man of the sons of the prophets asked his neighbour to strike him in the word of the Lord. The neighbour refused. The prophet announced that a lion would kill him, and the stated judgment followed.
offense: A son of the prophets commanded his neighbour, in the word of the Lord, to smite him. The man refused (1 Kings 20:35). The command belonged to the prophetic action by which Ahab would be confronted, and the prophet expressly identified the refusal as not obeying the Lord's voice (1 Kings 20:36). The act must be understood within that commission. The prophet needed to appear wounded before the king and present the case of a prisoner allowed to escape. The neighbour was asked to participate in a particular sign, not to decide whether the message against Ahab should proceed. His refusal did not cancel the work the Lord had appointed.
judgment: After the man departed, a lion found and killed him. Another man then struck and wounded the prophet, who used his disguise in the encounter with Ahab that follows. This event is distinct from the death of the man of God from Judah in 1 Kings 13.

name: Jezebel and Naboth's vineyard
charge: Judicial murder to seize an inheritance
summary: Ahab coveted Naboth's vineyard; Naboth would not sell his fathers' inheritance. Jezebel arranged false witnesses to accuse him of blaspheming God and the king, had him stoned, and handed the land to Ahab.
offense: Naboth refused to sell or exchange his vineyard because it was the inheritance of his fathers (1 Kings 21:1-3). Ahab's desire for a garden did not extinguish the obligation by which Naboth held the land. The king withdrew in displeasure, and Jezebel promised to obtain what he had been refused. She wrote in Ahab's name, sealed the letters with his seal, and ordered a fast, an accusation by two false witnesses, and Naboth's execution (1 Kings 21:8-14). The elders obeyed. The outward form of judgment was made to serve a conclusion already chosen. Exodus 23:7 forbids slaying the innocent and righteous; the number of witnesses could not cleanse testimony known to be false.
judgment: Ahab went down to take possession, and Elijah met him there with the question joining the crimes: had he killed and also taken possession (1 Kings 21:16-19)? The benefit of the murder stood beside the murder itself. Jezebel's management of the plot did not remove the king's responsibility for receiving its fruit. The Lord pronounced judgment upon Ahab, Jezebel, and their house. Ahab's humbling delayed the destruction of his house, but did not restore Naboth or approve the seizure (1 Kings 21:20-29). Later Joram's body was cast into Naboth's portion, and Jehu recalled the blood of Naboth and his sons (2 Kings 9:25-26). The stolen inheritance remained a witness against the royal house.

verses.text: 1And it came to pass after these things, that Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard, which was in Jezreel, hard by the palace of Ahab king of Samaria. 2And Ahab spake unto Naboth, saying, Give me thy vineyard, that I may have it for a garden of herbs, because it is near unto my house: and I will give thee for it a better vineyard than it; or, if it seem good to thee, I will give thee the worth of it in money. 3And Naboth said to Ahab, The Lord forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee. 4And Ahab came into his house heavy and displeased because of the word which Naboth the Jezreelite had spoken to him: for he had said, I will not give thee the inheritance of my fathers. And he laid him down upon his bed, and turned away his face, and would eat no bread.

8So she wrote letters in Ahab’s name, and sealed them with his seal, and sent the letters unto the elders and to the nobles that were in his city, dwelling with Naboth. 9And she wrote in the letters, saying, Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people: 10And set two men, sons of Belial, before him, to bear witness against him, saying, Thou didst blaspheme God and the king. And then carry him out, and stone him, that he may die. 11And the men of his city, even the elders and the nobles who were the inhabitants in his city, did as Jezebel had sent unto them, and as it was written in the letters which she had sent unto them. 12They proclaimed a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people. 13And there came in two men, children of Belial, and sat before him: and the men of Belial witnessed against him, even against Naboth, in the presence of the people, saying, Naboth did blaspheme God and the king. Then they carried him forth out of the city, and stoned him with stones, that he died.

17And the word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying, 18Arise, go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, which is in Samaria: behold, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, whither he is gone down to possess it. 19And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the Lord, Hast thou killed, and also taken possession? And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the Lord, In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine.

entries.commentary: Naboth had a vineyard next to Ahab's palace in Jezreel, and Ahab asked to trade or buy it, offering a better vineyard or its worth in money. Naboth refused because the land was the inheritance of his fathers. He could not simply hand off an inheritance that was given to him. -

Ahab went home heavy and displeased, laid down on his bed, turned away his face, and would eat no bread. He threw a fit and sulked because he could not get his way, angry that a subject would not surrender his inheritance.

Jezebel came to Ahab and asked why his spirit was so sad that he would not eat, and he told her Naboth's refusal. Jezebel mocked his weakness, telling him he was king and should let his heart be merry, and she promised to get the vineyard of Naboth for him.

Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name and sealed them with his seal, sending them to the elders and nobles of Naboth's city. The seal was a signet, an official mark of the king's authority, so the letters carried royal weight as if Ahab himself had written them. She commanded them to proclaim a fast, set Naboth on high, and set two sons of Belial before him to bear false witness that he blasphemed God and the king, then stone him. This was evil counsel and a murderous plot. -

The elders and nobles obeyed Jezebel's letters, proclaimed a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people. Two children of Belial, children of the devil, sat before Naboth and falsely witnessed that he had blasphemed God and the king. They carried Naboth out and stoned him to death, then sent word to Jezebel that he was dead.

When Jezebel heard Naboth was dead, she told Ahab to arise and take possession of the vineyard he had been refused. Ahab rose up and went down to take the vineyard. This is extortion, seizing what another has by violence and force. Ahab shares the guilt. He sat by and let Jezebel commit the crime because he coveted the field, then turned his face from the evil and went to claim the reward. -

The word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishbite to go down and meet Ahab in the vineyard of Naboth. Elijah was to declare, Thus saith the Lord, hast thou killed and also taken possession, and in the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, dogs would lick Ahab's own blood.

Ahab called Elijah his enemy, and Elijah answered that he had found him because Ahab had sold himself to work evil in the sight of the Lord. The Most High would bring evil on Ahab, cut off every male of his house, and make his house like the house of Jeroboam and the house of Baasha because of the provocation by which he made Israel to sin. The phrase him that pisseth against the wall refers to the males, whom the Most High said he would cut off entirely. -

The Most High declared that the dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel. Any of Ahab's house dying in the city the dogs would eat, and any dying in the field the fowls of the air would eat, matching the curses spoken in the law. -

There was none like Ahab, who sold himself to work wickedness in the sight of the Lord, stirred up by Jezebel his wife. He did very abominably in following idols, as did the Amorites whom the Most High cast out before the children of Israel.

When Ahab heard these words he rent his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted, and went softly, humbling himself before the Most High. Because Ahab humbled himself, the Most High told Elijah he would not bring the evil in Ahab's own days but would bring it upon his house in his son's days. The judgment was not cancelled but delayed and transferred to the next generation, showing that genuine humbling before the Most High moves his hand. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement)

Elisha sends one of the children of the prophets to Ramoth-gilead to anoint Jehu king over Israel, pour the oil on his head, and flee. Jehu is charged to smite the house of Ahab to avenge the blood of the prophets and of the servants of the Most High shed at the hand of Jezebel, whose work was to kill the prophets while weak Ahab let it continue. The word declares the whole house of Ahab shall perish, and the dogs shall eat Jezebel in the portion of Jezreel with none to bury her.

Jehu's fellow captains ask why the mad fellow came, and when he tells them the prophet anointed him king, they hasten to put their garments under him and blow the trumpets, proclaiming Jehu king. Jehu conspires against Jehoram and charges that none escape the city to carry the news to Jezreel. He rides toward Jezreel where Jehoram lay wounded, and Ahaziah king of Judah had come down to see him.

A watchman spies Jehu's company, and two horsemen sent to ask if it is peace are each told to turn behind him and do not return, for the driving is furious like the driving of Jehu. Jehoram himself goes out and asks if it is peace, and Jehu answers that there can be no peace while the whoredoms and witchcrafts of his mother Jezebel are so many. Jehu draws his bow with full strength and smites Jehoram through the heart, then casts him into the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite according to the word of the Most High.

Ahaziah king of Judah flees but Jehu pursues and has him smitten in his chariot; he flees to Megiddo and dies there. His servants carry him to Jerusalem and bury him in the sepulchre of his fathers in the city of David.

Jezebel paints her face and tires her head, returning to her seductive ways as Jehu enters the gate. Jehu calls out for who is on his side, and two or three eunuchs look out. At Jehu's word they throw her down, her blood is sprinkled on the wall and the horses, and he treads her under foot. When they go to bury her they find only the skull, the feet, and the palms of her hands, fulfilling the word spoken by Elijah that dogs would eat the flesh of Jezebel and her carcass would be as dung upon the field.

name: Micaiah the son of Imlah
charge: What the Lord saith unto me, that will I speak; against four hundred prophets and two kings
summary: Two kings sat in their robes at the gate of Samaria and four hundred prophets told them to go up and prosper. Jehoshaphat asked whether there was not one more. There was one, whom Ahab hated because he never prophesied good. The messenger who fetched him coached him to agree. He said he would speak what the Lord said, told them the truth, was struck on the face and sent to prison on bread and water until the king came back in peace. The king did not come back.
offense: Four hundred prophets encouraged the expedition to Ramoth-gilead, and the messenger sent for Micaiah urged him to agree. His answer was settled before he entered the court: what the Lord said, he would speak (1 Kings 22:6, 13-14). Agreement with a multitude was not his commission. Before the enthroned kings he declared that Israel would be scattered like sheep without a shepherd. He also disclosed the vision of the lying spirit sent to persuade Ahab through his prophets (1 Kings 22:17-23). The warning reached the king before the battle. Ahab was not left without testimony against the pleasant answer he preferred.

name: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah, and the four hundred prophets
charge: Prophesying victory at Ramoth-gilead by a lying spirit; smiting Micaiah on the cheek
summary: Four hundred prophets told Ahab to go up and prosper. One, Micaiah, saw the Lord on his throne and a lying spirit sent into the mouths of the rest. Zedekiah struck him for it and asked which way the Spirit had gone. The battle answered for Ahab; scripture leaves Zedekiah hiding in an inner chamber.
offense: Zedekiah made horns of iron and announced, in the Lord's name, that Ahab would push the Syrians until he consumed them. The other prophets agreed (1 Kings 22:11-12). The visible sign and united approval presented certainty without establishing that the Lord had sent the word. When Micaiah exposed the contrary purpose, Zedekiah struck him and demanded how the Spirit had passed from himself to Micaiah (1 Kings 22:24). He treated his own standing as proof against correction. The blow defended a claim of authority; it supplied no answer to the prophecy.
judgment: Micaiah told him he would see when he went into an inner chamber to hide (1 Kings 22:25). The confidence displayed before the kings was set against an approaching need for concealment. Ahab died at Ramoth-gilead rather than consuming the Syrians as promised. Deuteronomy 18:22 identifies the unfulfilled word as one the Lord has not spoken. The failure of Zedekiah's promise exposed his presumption, although no subsequent account of his personal punishment is given. Iron horns, agreement, and violence could not make a false assurance stand against the Lord's judgment.

entries.commentary: After three years without war between Syria and Israel, Jehoshaphat king of Judah comes down to the king of Israel. Ahab reminds his servants that Ramoth in Gilead belongs to Israel, yet they sit still and do not take it out of the hand of the king of Syria. Ahab asks Jehoshaphat to go with him to battle, and Jehoshaphat answers that he is as Ahab is, his people and horses as Ahab's, but first asks that they inquire at the word of the Lord. Ahab gathers about four hundred prophets, who all say with one mouth, go up, for the Lord shall deliver it into the hand of the king. This is the setting for a division that ran between the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom. After the split, the northern kingdom fell into idolatry and forsook the Levites, so a prophet of the Most High would want nothing to do with their manner of worship. -

Jehoshaphat is not moved by four hundred prophets speaking the same thing, and asks whether there is not yet a prophet of the Lord that they may inquire of him. He wants to hear from a true prophet of the Most High, not from prophets who serve the king. Ahab answers that there is one man, Micaiah the son of Imlah, but he hates him because Micaiah does not prophesy good concerning him, but evil. Jehoshaphat rebukes him, saying, let not the king say so.

The king of Israel calls an officer to hasten Micaiah, while Ahab and Jehoshaphat sit each on his throne in their robes at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets prophesy before them. Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah makes horns of iron and says, thus saith the Lord, with these shalt thou push the Syrians until thou have consumed them. Here again a man claims to speak for the Most High while the whole company presses Ahab to go up and prosper.

The messenger tells Micaiah that all the prophets declare good to the king with one mouth, and urges him to speak likewise. Micaiah answers that whatever the Lord saith unto him, that will he speak, and at first he echoes the others, prompting the king to adjure him to tell nothing but the truth. Micaiah then reveals what he saw, all Israel scattered on the hills as sheep having no shepherd, and the Lord saying these have no master. He saw the Lord on his throne with all the host of heaven, and a spirit that offered to be a lying spirit in the mouth of all Ahab's prophets to persuade him to fall at Ramoth-gilead. The Most High put a lying spirit in the mouth of these prophets and spoke evil concerning Ahab. The deceiver as well as the deceived are under the hand of the Most High, who uses the lie to bring the judgment he has already declared. -

Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah smites Micaiah on the cheek and asks which way the spirit of the Lord went from him to speak to Micaiah, defending his own false prophecy. The king of Israel orders Micaiah taken back and put in prison, fed with bread and water of affliction until Ahab returns in peace. Micaiah answers that if Ahab returns at all in peace, the Lord has not spoken by him, and calls all the people to hearken. His word stands as the test of who truly spoke for the Most High.

The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat go up to Ramoth-gilead. Ahab disguises himself and tells Jehoshaphat to wear his robes, hoping to escape the word spoken against him, while the king of Syria commands his captains to fight only against the king of Israel. The captains pursue Jehoshaphat until they perceive he is not the king of Israel and turn back. A certain man draws a bow at a venture and smites Ahab between the joints of the harness, and the king is held up in his chariot until he dies at even, the blood running into the chariot. When they wash the chariot in the pool of Samaria, the dogs lick up his blood according to the word of the Lord. The judgment pronounced earlier against Ahab and his house begins to be fulfilled exactly as spoken.

The rest of the acts of Ahab, the ivory house he made and the cities he built, are written in the book of the Chronicles of the kings of Israel. Ahab sleeps with his fathers, and Ahaziah his son reigns in his stead.

Jehoshaphat the son of Asa begins to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab, at thirty-five years old, and reigns twenty-five years in Jerusalem. He walks in the ways of Asa his father, doing right in the eyes of the Lord, though the high places are not taken away and the people still burn incense there. Jehoshaphat makes peace with the king of Israel and puts the remnant of the sodomites out of the land. There is then no king in Edom but a deputy, because Edom had been subdued and had not yet revolted. -

Ahaziah the son of Ahab begins to reign over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat and reigns two years. He does evil in the sight of the Lord and walks in the way of his father and his mother and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin. He serves Baal and worships him and provokes the Lord God of Israel to anger, according to all that his father had done. The sin of the house of Ahab continues into the next generation. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

The priests the Levites, and all the tribe of Levi, shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel; they shall eat the offerings of the Lord made by fire, and his inheritance. Therefore shall they have no inheritance among their brethren: the Lord is their inheritance, as he hath said unto them.

This shall be the priest's due from the people, from them that offer a sacrifice, whether ox or sheep: they shall give unto the priest the shoulder, and the two cheeks, and the maw. The firstfruit also of thy corn, of thy wine, and of thine oil, and the first of the fleece of thy sheep, shalt thou give him. For the Most High hath chosen him out of all thy tribes to stand to minister in the name of the Lord, him and his sons for ever.

If a Levite come from any of thy gates out of all Israel, and come with all the desire of his mind unto the place which the Lord shall choose, then he shall minister in the name of the Lord his God, as all his brethren the Levites do which stand there before the Lord. They shall have like portions to eat, beside that which cometh of the sale of his patrimony.

When thou art come into the land, thou shalt not learn to do after the abominations of those nations: there shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer. These things actually existed and they are all real: wizards, necromancers, divination, observers of times, people that consult with familiar spirits. If they were not real, they would not be in the Bible with the Most High telling us not to do them. All that do these things are an abomination unto the Lord, and because of these abominations the Most High driveth those nations out from before thee. Thou shalt be perfect with the Lord thy God, meaning upright; the nations hearken unto observers of times and unto diviners, but as for thee, the Most High hath not suffered thee so to do.

The Lord thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken. This is talking about Christ, Yeshua. This answers what Israel desired of the Most High in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, Let me not hear again the voice of the Lord my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I die not; and the Lord said, They have well spoken that which they have spoken. I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak unto them all that I shall command him; and whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him. If we do not follow Christ and do what Christ says, that judgment falls on us.

The prophet which shall presume to speak a word in the name of the Most High which he hath not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die. By this law a lot of these pastors stand condemned: they say things and claim Christ said them, when the Most High never commanded Christ to say it and Christ is not telling them to say it. How shall we know the word which the Lord hath not spoken? When a prophet speaketh in the name of the Lord, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the Lord hath not spoken; the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously, and thou shalt not be afraid of him. --- Topics: [Clean and Unclean Meats](/encyclopedia/clean-and-unclean-meats) · [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood) · [The Sabbath](/encyclopedia/the-sabbath)

Woe is pronounced on the pastors that destroy and scatter the sheep of the Most High's pasture and have not visited them, so He will visit upon them the evil of their doings. He will gather the remnant of His flock out of the countries where He drove them, bring them again to their folds, and set up shepherds who will feed them so they fear no more and none are lacking.

The Most High promises to raise unto David a righteous Branch, a King who shall reign, prosper, and execute judgment and justice, in whose days Judah shall be saved and Israel dwell safely. His name is called THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS; this is plainly referring to Christ. The day comes when they will no longer swear by the Most High who brought Israel out of Egypt, but by Him who led the seed of the house of Israel out of the north country and all the countries where He had driven them, back to their own land.

Jeremiah's heart is broken and his bones shake like a drunken man because of the prophets and the words of the Most High's holiness, for the land is full of adulterers and mourns under swearing. Both prophet and priest are profane, and the Most High has found their wickedness even in His house, so their way shall be as slippery ways in the darkness where they are driven and fall. The prophets of Samaria prophesied in Baal and caused Israel to err, and the prophets of Jerusalem commit adultery, walk in lies, and strengthen the hands of evildoers so that none return from wickedness, becoming as Sodom and Gomorrah before Him.

The people are told not to hearken to the prophets who make them vain and speak a vision of their own heart, not out of the mouth of the Most High, telling those who despise Him that they shall have peace and no evil shall come. This is like the pastor who says, let me tell you what God told me to tell you, when it is a lie. None of these prophets has stood in the counsel of the Most High; had they stood there and caused the people to hear His words, they would have turned them from their evil way, but instead the whirlwind of His anger will fall grievously upon the head of the wicked in the latter days.

The Most High asks whether He is a God only near and not far off, when He fills heaven and earth and no one can hide in secret places where He cannot see him. He has heard the prophets who prophesy lies in His name saying, I have dreamed, thinking to cause His people to forget His name by their dreams as their fathers forgot it for Baal. Let the prophet with a dream tell a dream, but let him that has His word speak it faithfully, for His word is like a fire and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces; He is against those who steal His words and use their own tongues to lie on the Most High.

When the people, prophet, or priest ask what is the burden of the Most High, Jeremiah is to answer, What burden? for He will forsake them, and every man who claims the burden of the Most High He will punish in his house. Instead of saying the burden of the Most High, they are to ask one another what the Most High has answered and spoken, for they have perverted the words of the living God. Because they keep saying the burden of the Most High after being told not to, He will utterly forget them, forsake them, and cast them out of His presence with an everlasting reproach and perpetual shame that shall not be forgotten. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

name: Ahaziah of Israel
charge: Inquiring of Baal-zebub the god of Ekron
summary: Ahab's son fell through a lattice in Samaria and sent messengers to ask Baal-zebub whether he would recover. Elijah met them on the road: is it not because there is not a God in Israel that ye go to inquire of Baal-zebub? Two captains of fifty sent to arrest the prophet were consumed by fire.
offense: After falling through a lattice and becoming sick, Ahaziah sent to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron. Elijah intercepted the messengers with the question whether there was no God in Israel that the king sought this answer elsewhere (2 Kings 1:2-4). The inquiry exposed whom he trusted when his own life became uncertain. Recognising Elijah from the messengers' description, Ahaziah sent soldiers to summon him. Two captains addressed the man of God with the king's demand, and fire consumed their companies (2 Kings 1:9-12). Royal force did not give the king command over the word already pronounced against him.
judgment: The third captain knelt and pleaded that his life and his men's lives be precious. The angel told Elijah to go with him and not fear (2 Kings 1:13-15). The change from command to humble petition distinguished this company from those before it. Before Ahaziah, Elijah repeated the sentence: because he had sent to Ekron, he would not come down from his bed but would die. He died according to the word, and Jehoram succeeded him because he had no son (2 Kings 1:16-17). Bringing the prophet before the throne had not brought the judgment under the throne's control.
offenseFull: After falling through a lattice and becoming sick, Ahaziah sent to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron. Elijah intercepted the messengers with the question whether there was no God in Israel that the king sought this answer elsewhere (2 Kings 1:2-4). The inquiry exposed whom he trusted when his own life became uncertain.

Recognising Elijah from the messengers' description, Ahaziah sent soldiers to summon him. Two captains addressed the man of God with the king's demand, and fire consumed their companies (2 Kings 1:9-12). Royal force did not give the king command over the word already pronounced against him.
