name: The Shunammite woman
charge: Constraining the man of God to eat bread; building him a little chamber on the wall, with a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick
summary: A great woman of Shunem noticed that a holy man of God passed by continually and made him a room. She asked nothing. She was given a son; when he died on her knees she laid him on the prophet's bed, saddled the ass, and said, It is well. He was raised. Years later, back from a famine, she got her whole house and land restored by the king in one morning.
offense: She said unto her husband, Behold now, I perceive that this is an holy man of God, which passeth by us continually. Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick. Asked what could be done for her, she answered, I dwell among mine own people. When the child was dead she said to her husband and to Gehazi, It is well, and did not stop until she caught the prophet by the feet.
judgment: About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son. And the woman conceived, and bare a son at that season. The child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes; and Elisha said, Take up thy son. Then she went in, and fell at his feet, and bowed herself to the ground, and took up her son. After seven years' famine she came to cry to the king for her house and land at the very moment Gehazi was telling him how Elisha had restored a dead body to life; and the king appointed an officer: Restore all that was hers, and all the fruits of the field since the day that she left the land, even until now.

entries.commentary: A certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets cries to Elisha that her husband is dead, that her husband feared the Lord, and that the creditor has come to take her two sons to be bondmen. Because the husband died in debt, the creditor comes to take the sons to work off what is owed. Elisha asks what she has in the house, and she says nothing but a pot of oil. He tells her to borrow empty vessels from all her neighbors, not a few, then shut the door upon herself and her sons and pour oil into all the vessels. She pours out, and the oil continues until every vessel is full, and only then does the oil stay. Elisha tells her to sell the oil, pay her debt, and live with her children on the rest. The empty vessels she borrowed from her people, the children of Israel, were filled through the spirit of the Lord.

Elisha passes through Shunem, where a great woman constrains him to eat bread, and as often as he passes by he turns in there to eat. She perceives that he is a holy man of God and tells her husband to make a little chamber on the wall with a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick, so he may turn in whenever he comes. On a day when he rests in the chamber, Elisha wants to bless her and sends Gehazi to ask what may be done for her, whether she would be spoken for to the king or the captain of the host. She answers that she dwells among her own people. Gehazi tells Elisha the woman has no child and her husband is old. Elisha tells her that about this season, according to the time of life, she shall embrace a son. Like our mother Sarah, she does not believe it and tells the man of God not to lie to his handmaid, yet she conceives and bears a son at that season. -

When the child is grown, he goes out to his father to the reapers and cries, my head, my head. His father has a lad carry him to his mother, and he sits on her knees till noon and then dies, from what seemed only a headache. She carries the child up and lays him on the bed of the man of God, the bed in the chamber she had made for Elisha, shuts the door, and goes out. She calls to her husband for a young man and an ass so she may run to the man of God, and though he asks why, since it is neither new moon nor sabbath, she answers, it shall be well. She rides to Elisha at Carmel, and when the man of God sees her afar off, he sends Gehazi to ask whether it is well with her, her husband, and the child, and she answers, it is well.

When she comes to Elisha at the hill, she catches him by the feet, and Gehazi comes near to thrust her away, but the man of God says let her alone, for her soul is vexed within her and the Lord has hid it from him. She says, did I desire a son of my lord, did I not say do not deceive me. Elisha tells Gehazi to gird up his loins, take his staff, greet no man on the way, and lay the staff on the face of the child. The mother says, as the Lord liveth and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee, so Elisha rises and follows her. Gehazi goes on before them and lays the staff on the face of the child, but there is neither voice nor hearing. He returns to tell Elisha the child is not awake.

When Elisha comes to the house, the child is dead, laid upon his bed. He goes in, shuts the door upon them both, and prays to the Lord. He goes up and lies upon the child, putting his mouth on his mouth, his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands, and stretches himself upon the child, and the flesh of the child grows warm. He walks in the house to and fro, goes up and stretches himself upon him again, and the child sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. Elisha calls Gehazi to call the Shunammite, and when she comes he tells her to take up her son. She falls at his feet, bows to the ground, takes up her son, and goes out. This is another act of the Most High through Elisha, restoring the child to life.

Elisha comes again to Gilgal, where there is a dearth in the land, and the sons of the prophets sit before him. He tells his servant to set on the great pot and seethe pottage for them. One goes out into the field to gather herbs, finds a wild vine, and gathers his lap full of wild gourds, shredding them into the pot, for they knew them not. As the men eat, they cry out, O thou man of God, there is death in the pot, and they cannot eat. Elisha tells them to bring meal, casts it into the pot, and says pour out for the people that they may eat, and there is no harm in the pot. He cures the poisoned food so the men may eat safely.

A man comes from Baal-shalisha and brings the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley and full ears of corn in the husk. Elisha says, give to the people that they may eat. His servant asks how he should set this before a hundred men, but Elisha says again, give to the people, for thus saith the Lord, they shall eat and shall leave thereof. He sets it before them, and they eat and leave some, according to the word of the Lord.

Elisha warns the Shunammite woman whose son he restored to flee the coming seven year famine, and she sojourns in the land of the Philistines. When she returns to appeal to the king for her house and land, Gehazi is at that moment telling the king how Elisha restored a dead body to life. The timing is of the Most High, so the king restores all that was hers and the fruits of the field from the day she left.

Ben-hadad king of Syria, sick, sends Hazael to inquire of Elisha whether he will recover, for the word of a prophet, also called a seer, was precious in those days. Elisha tells Hazael the king may recover but the Most High has shown that he shall surely die, then weeps because he sees the evil Hazael will do to Israel: burning strongholds, slaying young men, and ripping up women with child. Elisha tells Hazael he will be king over Syria, revealing that leadership can discern spirits at work in a man that the man does not see in himself. Hazael returns and smothers the king with a wet cloth and reigns in his place.

Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat begins to reign over Judah and walks in the way of the kings of Israel because the daughter of Ahab was his wife. He does evil in the sight of the Most High, yet Judah is not destroyed for David his servant's sake, according to the promise.

In Jehoram's days Edom revolts from under the hand of Judah and makes a king over itself, breaking the subjection Edom had been under from the days of David and Solomon. This revolt fulfills the word spoken to Esau, that when he gained the dominion he would break the yoke from off his neck, a pattern reaching to Edom's later rise. Jehoram sleeps with his fathers and is buried in the city of David, and Ahaziah his son reigns in his place. -

Ahaziah son of Jehoram begins to reign over Judah and walks in the way of the house of Ahab, being the son-in-law of that house, a picture of the generational curse passed from father to son. He goes with Jehoram son of Ahab to war against Hazael king of Syria, and the Syrians wound Jehoram at Ramah. Jehoram returns to Jezreel to be healed, and Ahaziah goes down to see him, setting the stage for both kings to meet Jehu's judgment.

name: Naaman the Syrian
charge: Going down and dipping himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God, after his anger
summary: Captain of the host of Syria, a mighty man of valour, and a leper. He came with horses and chariots and a letter from his king, and was sent to wash in Jordan by a messenger who did not come to the door. He went away in a rage, was talked round by his servants, obeyed, and came up with the flesh of a little child. He went home with two mules' burden of earth and a vow to sacrifice to no other god.
offense: Naaman had rank, victories, and honour, but he was a leper. The witness that directed him toward help came from a captive maid serving his wife (2 Kings 5:1-4). A great commander had to receive useful counsel from one with little power in his house. He arrived with wealth and a royal letter, but the king of Israel could not heal him. Elisha sent a messenger requiring him to wash seven times in Jordan. Naaman became angry because he expected the prophet to appear and perform the healing in the manner he had imagined (2 Kings 5:5-12). His objection was not that the command was impossible, but that it did not honour his expectation. His servants reasoned that he would have attempted a great thing if commanded; how much more should he wash and be clean. He hearkened and dipped seven times according to the word (2 Kings 5:13-14). Humility made room for the obedience his first anger had refused.
judgment: His flesh became like a child's, and he returned with his company confessing that there was no God in all the earth but in Israel (2 Kings 5:14-15). Cleansing was followed by an acknowledgment beyond the cure itself. Elisha refused payment. Naaman declared that he would no longer offer sacrifice to other gods and asked pardon concerning his attendance upon his master in Rimmon's house (2 Kings 5:16-19). The exchange turned from purchasing a remedy to ordering future worship. Christ later named Naaman when warning hearers who would not receive a prophet among their own people (Luke 4:27). The man who first resisted a simple command became a witness to what followed when he finally obeyed it.

verses.text: 1Now Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the Lord had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper. 2And the Syrians had gone out by companies, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maid; and she waited on Naaman’s wife. 3And she said unto her mistress, Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy. 4And one went in, and told his lord, saying, Thus and thus said the maid that is of the land of Israel. 5And the king of Syria said, Go to, go, and I will send a letter unto the king of Israel. And he departed, and took with him ten talents of silver, and six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of raiment.

9So Naaman came with his horses and with his chariot, and stood at the door of the house of Elisha. 10And Elisha sent a messenger unto him, saying, Go and wash in Jordan seven times, and thy flesh shall come again to thee, and thou shalt be clean. 11But Naaman was wroth, and went away, and said, Behold, I thought, He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of the Lord his God, and strike his hand over the place, and recover the leper. 12Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean? So he turned and went away in a rage.

entries.commentary: Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, is a great man with his master and honorable, because by him the Lord had given deliverance to Syria. He is a mighty man of valor, but he is a leper. The Syrians had gone out by companies and brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maid, and she waits on Naaman's wife. This maid is an Israelite sister serving in a foreign house. She tells her mistress that if only her lord were with the prophet in Samaria, he would recover him of his leprosy. Naaman goes and tells his lord what the maid of Israel said.

The king of Syria sends Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel, and Naaman takes ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of raiment. The letter asks the king of Israel to recover Naaman of his leprosy. When the king of Israel reads the letter, he rends his clothes and asks, am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends to me to recover a man of his leprosy. He thinks the king of Syria is seeking a quarrel against him, knowing he has no such power.

When Elisha the man of God hears that the king of Israel has rent his clothes, he sends to the king asking why, and says let the man come to him, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel. Naaman comes with his horses and chariot and stands at the door of Elisha's house. Elisha sends a messenger out to him, saying go and wash in Jordan seven times, and thy flesh shall come again to thee, and thou shalt be clean.

Naaman is wroth and goes away, saying he thought the prophet would surely come out to him, stand, call on the name of the Lord his God, strike his hand over the place, and recover the leper. He complains in his pride that this was not the process he expected. He asks whether Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, are not better than all the waters of Israel, and turns away in a rage, thinking of a physical cleansing rather than a spiritual one. His mind is carnal, not thinking as the prophet thinks. His servants come near and reason with him, that if the prophet had bidden him do some great thing he would have done it; how much rather then when he says only wash and be clean. Taking heed, Naaman goes down and dips himself seven times in Jordan according to the saying of the man of God, and his flesh comes again like the flesh of a little child, and he is clean.

Naaman returns to the man of God with all his company and stands before him, saying, behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. He asks Elisha to take a blessing of his servant. Elisha says, as the Lord liveth before whom I stand, I will receive none, and though Naaman urges him, he refuses. Naaman asks that he be given two mules' burden of earth, for from now on he will offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice to other gods but to the Lord. He asks that the Lord pardon him in one thing, that when his master goes into the house of Rimmon to worship and leans on his hand, and he bows there, the Lord pardon his servant. Elisha says, go in peace, and Naaman departs a little way.

Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, reasons that his master has spared Naaman the Syrian by not receiving what he brought, and swears, as the Lord liveth, he will run after him and take somewhat of him. When Naaman sees him running, he lights down from the chariot to meet him and asks whether all is well. Gehazi lies, saying his master has sent him, that two young men of the sons of the prophets have come from mount Ephraim, and asks for a talent of silver and two changes of garments. Naaman urges him to take two talents, binds them in two bags with two changes of garments, and lays them on two of his servants to carry before Gehazi. When Gehazi comes to the tower, he takes the goods from their hand, bestows them in the house, and sends the men away, hiding what he took like a thief.

Gehazi goes in and stands before his master, and Elisha asks where he has come from, and Gehazi says his servant went nowhere. Elisha says, went not my heart with thee when the man turned from his chariot to meet thee; is it a time to receive money, garments, oliveyards, vineyards, sheep, oxen, menservants, and maidservants. Because Gehazi took in a time that was not the time to receive, the leprosy of Naaman shall cleave to him and to his seed forever, and he goes out from Elisha's presence a leper as white as snow. This shows how Israel thought then and how the nation still thinks now, hasty to grasp things by unjust means. -

Being full of the Holy Ghost he is led by the Spirit into the wilderness, forty days tempted of the devil, and in those days he did eat nothing. He answers with the law: man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.

The devil shows him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. No man can do that, which settles who was standing there. All this power will I give thee, for that is delivered unto me, and to whomsoever I will I give it. The offer is real, and the price is worship. Get thee behind me, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve. Again the answer is a commandment.

Set on a pinnacle of the temple and answered with scripture, he replies, It is said, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. When the devil had ended all the temptation, he departed from him for a season. The whole battle was fought with the word, and that is the only way it is won.

As his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read. He reads from Esaias: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor, to preach deliverance to the captives. This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.

They wonder at the gracious words, and then ask, Is not this Joseph's son? No prophet is accepted in his own country. He names the widow of Sarepta and Naaman the Syrian, and they are filled with wrath, thrust him out of the city, and lead him to the brow of the hill to cast him down headlong, but he passes through the midst of them.

In the synagogue there was a man which had a spirit of an unclean devil, and it cried out, I know thee who thou art; the Holy One of God. That spirit was sitting in the house of worship, and it knew exactly who he was. Knowing who he is and doing what he says are two different things.

He rebukes the fever in Simon's wife's mother and it leaves her, and he lays his hands on every one of the sick brought to him. I must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also: for therefore am I sent. He went where the people were, and some received the word and some did not.

This is the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing. The leper stays outside the camp; the priest goes forth out of the camp to him and looks whether the plague of leprosy be healed in the leper. The priest does not heal the plague; he examines the man after the healing and carries out the cleansing the Most High commanded.

For him that is to be cleansed the priest commands two birds alive and clean, cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop. One bird is killed in an earthen vessel over running water. The living bird, with the cedar wood, the scarlet, and the hyssop, is dipped in the blood of the bird that was killed over the running water; the priest sprinkles him that is to be cleansed seven times, pronounces him clean, and lets the living bird loose into the open field.

He that is to be cleansed washes his clothes, shaves off all his hair, and washes himself in water, and comes into the camp; but he tarries abroad out of his tent seven days. On the seventh day he shaves all his hair off his head, his beard, and his eyebrows, washes his clothes and his flesh in water, and is clean.

On the eighth day he brings two he lambs without blemish, one ewe lamb of the first year without blemish, three tenth deals of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering, and one log of oil. The priest that makes him clean presents him with these things before the Most High at the door of the tabernacle. One he lamb is offered for a trespass offering with the log of oil, waved for a wave offering, and slain in the holy place: as the sin offering is the priest's, so is the trespass offering; it is most holy.

The priest takes of the blood of the trespass offering and puts it upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed, upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot. Of the log of oil the priest pours into his own left hand, sprinkles of it with his finger seven times before the Lord, and puts oil upon the ear, the thumb, and the toe, upon the blood of the trespass offering; the remnant of the oil he pours upon the head of him that is to be cleansed, to make an atonement for him before the Lord.

The priest then offers the sin offering to make an atonement for him that is to be cleansed from his uncleanness, kills the burnt offering, and offers the burnt offering and the meat offering upon the altar; the priest makes an atonement for him, and he shall be clean.

If he be poor and cannot get so much, the law makes provision: one lamb for a trespass offering to be waved, one tenth deal of fine flour mingled with oil, a log of oil, and two turtledoves or two young pigeons, such as he is able to get, the one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. The same order is kept for the poor man: the blood of the trespass offering upon the right ear, the right thumb, and the right great toe, the oil sprinkled seven times and put upon the same places, and the rest of the oil upon his head. This is the law of him in whom is the plague of leprosy, whose hand is not able to get that which pertaineth to his cleansing.

The Most High tells Moses and Aaron that when Israel comes into the land of Canaan, and he puts the plague of leprosy in a house of the land of their possession, the owner shall come and tell the priest, saying, It seemeth to me there is as it were a plague in the house. The priest commands that the house be emptied before he goes in, that all that is in it be not made unclean; then he looks on the plague, and if it be in the walls with hollow strakes, greenish or reddish, in sight lower than the wall, he shuts up the house seven days. If at the seventh day the plague be spread in the walls, the stones in which the plague is are taken away and cast into an unclean place without the city; the house is scraped within round about, the dust poured out without the city into an unclean place, and other stones and other mortar are put in their place.

If the plague come again and break out in the house after the stones were taken away and the house scraped and plastered, the priest looks, and if the plague be spread, it is a fretting leprosy in the house: it is unclean. He breaks down the house, the stones of it, the timber, and all the mortar, and carries them forth out of the city into an unclean place. He that goes into the house while it is shut up is unclean until the even, and he that lies or eats in the house washes his clothes.

If the priest comes in and looks, and the plague hath not spread in the house after it was plastered, the priest pronounces the house clean, because the plague is healed. The house is cleansed the same way as the leper: two birds, cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop; one bird killed in an earthen vessel over running water, the house sprinkled seven times, and the living bird let go out of the city into the open fields; so he makes an atonement for the house, and it shall be clean.

The chapter closes the summary: this is the law for all manner of plague of leprosy and scall, for the leprosy of a garment and of a house, for a rising, a scab, and a bright spot, to teach when it is unclean and when it is clean. This is the law of leprosy.

name: Gehazi
charge: Greed and lying to a prophet
summary: Elisha refused payment from the healed Syrian Naaman. His servant Gehazi ran after Naaman, invented a story to collect silver and garments, then lied to Elisha's face about where he had been.
offense: Elisha refused Naaman's gift after his cleansing, but Gehazi resolved to run after the departing company and take something. He claimed that his master had sent him because two young men of the prophets had arrived in need (2 Kings 5:20-22). Covetousness borrowed both Elisha's authority and the appearance of care for others. Naaman gave silver and garments, and Gehazi concealed the goods before returning to his master. Asked where he had been, he said he had gone nowhere (2 Kings 5:23-25). One lie acquired the property; another attempted to preserve it. His nearness to prophetic service had not kept his heart from trading upon its reputation.
judgment: Elisha disclosed his knowledge of the encounter and asked whether this was a time to receive money, garments, and the possessions they could purchase (2 Kings 5:26). The question returned Gehazi to the discernment expressed in the refusal he had disregarded. Naaman's leprosy was pronounced upon Gehazi and his seed, and he went out a leper (2 Kings 5:27). The servant had pursued the healed man's wealth and received the affliction from which that man had been delivered. Hidden goods could not conceal a deed known to the Lord, and an appeal to his master's name could not make private gain faithful ministry.

entries.commentary: Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, is a great man with his master and honorable, because by him the Lord had given deliverance to Syria. He is a mighty man of valor, but he is a leper. The Syrians had gone out by companies and brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maid, and she waits on Naaman's wife. This maid is an Israelite sister serving in a foreign house. She tells her mistress that if only her lord were with the prophet in Samaria, he would recover him of his leprosy. Naaman goes and tells his lord what the maid of Israel said.

The king of Syria sends Naaman with a letter to the king of Israel, and Naaman takes ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of raiment. The letter asks the king of Israel to recover Naaman of his leprosy. When the king of Israel reads the letter, he rends his clothes and asks, am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends to me to recover a man of his leprosy. He thinks the king of Syria is seeking a quarrel against him, knowing he has no such power.

When Elisha the man of God hears that the king of Israel has rent his clothes, he sends to the king asking why, and says let the man come to him, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel. Naaman comes with his horses and chariot and stands at the door of Elisha's house. Elisha sends a messenger out to him, saying go and wash in Jordan seven times, and thy flesh shall come again to thee, and thou shalt be clean.

Naaman is wroth and goes away, saying he thought the prophet would surely come out to him, stand, call on the name of the Lord his God, strike his hand over the place, and recover the leper. He complains in his pride that this was not the process he expected. He asks whether Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, are not better than all the waters of Israel, and turns away in a rage, thinking of a physical cleansing rather than a spiritual one. His mind is carnal, not thinking as the prophet thinks. His servants come near and reason with him, that if the prophet had bidden him do some great thing he would have done it; how much rather then when he says only wash and be clean. Taking heed, Naaman goes down and dips himself seven times in Jordan according to the saying of the man of God, and his flesh comes again like the flesh of a little child, and he is clean.

Naaman returns to the man of God with all his company and stands before him, saying, behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. He asks Elisha to take a blessing of his servant. Elisha says, as the Lord liveth before whom I stand, I will receive none, and though Naaman urges him, he refuses. Naaman asks that he be given two mules' burden of earth, for from now on he will offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice to other gods but to the Lord. He asks that the Lord pardon him in one thing, that when his master goes into the house of Rimmon to worship and leans on his hand, and he bows there, the Lord pardon his servant. Elisha says, go in peace, and Naaman departs a little way.

Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, reasons that his master has spared Naaman the Syrian by not receiving what he brought, and swears, as the Lord liveth, he will run after him and take somewhat of him. When Naaman sees him running, he lights down from the chariot to meet him and asks whether all is well. Gehazi lies, saying his master has sent him, that two young men of the sons of the prophets have come from mount Ephraim, and asks for a talent of silver and two changes of garments. Naaman urges him to take two talents, binds them in two bags with two changes of garments, and lays them on two of his servants to carry before Gehazi. When Gehazi comes to the tower, he takes the goods from their hand, bestows them in the house, and sends the men away, hiding what he took like a thief.

Gehazi goes in and stands before his master, and Elisha asks where he has come from, and Gehazi says his servant went nowhere. Elisha says, went not my heart with thee when the man turned from his chariot to meet thee; is it a time to receive money, garments, oliveyards, vineyards, sheep, oxen, menservants, and maidservants. Because Gehazi took in a time that was not the time to receive, the leprosy of Naaman shall cleave to him and to his seed forever, and he goes out from Elisha's presence a leper as white as snow. This shows how Israel thought then and how the nation still thinks now, hasty to grasp things by unjust means. -

name: The lord on whose hand the king leaned
charge: Scoffing at the word of the Lord by Elisha in the famine of Samaria
summary: In a siege so hard that women ate their children, Elisha said that by the next day fine flour would sell for a shekel in the gate. The king's officer answered that it could not happen if the Lord opened windows in heaven. He saw it, and was trampled in the gate by the crowd rushing to buy.
offense: Samaria's famine had reached extremity when Elisha declared that flour and barley would be sold cheaply at the gate the next day. The officer upon whose hand the king leaned answered by asking whether such a thing could happen even if the Lord made windows in heaven (2 Kings 7:1-2). Present scarcity became his measure of what the Lord could provide. The promise did not require him to explain the means before believing the word. His answer treated the announcement as impossible at the moment it was expressly given in the Lord's name. A trusted position beside the king did not supply understanding of a deliverance neither man had arranged.
judgment: Elisha told him that he would see the abundance but not eat it. The Lord caused the Syrians to hear a host approaching, and they fled, leaving their provisions behind. Four leprous men discovered the empty camp and reported it (2 Kings 7:3-11). Relief came through a means the officer had not included in his objection. The people spoiled the camp, and the prices fell as announced. Appointed to oversee the gate, the officer was trampled there and died (2 Kings 7:16-20). The place where the promised provision became publicly available was the place where his exclusion was fulfilled. He witnessed the answer his unbelief had dismissed, but did not share its food.
offenseFull: Samaria's famine had reached extremity when Elisha declared that flour and barley would be sold cheaply at the gate the next day. The officer upon whose hand the king leaned answered by asking whether such a thing could happen even if the Lord made windows in heaven (2 Kings 7:1-2). Present scarcity became his measure of what the Lord could provide.

The promise did not require him to explain the means before believing the word. His answer treated the announcement as impossible at the moment it was expressly given in the Lord's name. A trusted position beside the king did not supply understanding of a deliverance neither man had arranged.
judgmentFull: Elisha told him that he would see the abundance but not eat it. The Lord caused the Syrians to hear a host approaching, and they fled, leaving their provisions behind. Four leprous men discovered the empty camp and reported it (2 Kings 7:3-11). Relief came through a means the officer had not included in his objection.

The people spoiled the camp, and the prices fell as announced. Appointed to oversee the gate, the officer was trampled there and died (2 Kings 7:16-20). The place where the promised provision became publicly available was the place where his exclusion was fulfilled. He witnessed the answer his unbelief had dismissed, but did not share its food.

entries.commentary: Elisha declares the word of the Most High that within a day the famine will break and fine flour and barley will sell cheaply in the gate of Samaria. The lord on whose hand the king leaned doubts the word, asking if the Most High would make windows in heaven. Elisha tells him he will see it with his eyes but not eat of it. The prophet speaks the word of the Most High plainly, without fear and without doubting, whether the message is blessing or judgment.

Four leprous men at the gate reason that they will die either way, so they go over to the camp of the Syrians hoping to be spared. The Most High had made the host of the Syrians hear the noise of chariots and horses, so they fled in the twilight and left everything behind. The lepers eat and drink and carry off silver, gold, and raiment, hiding the spoil for themselves.

The lepers realize this is a day of good tidings and that they should not hold their peace, so they report to the king's household. The king suspects a trap, thinking the Syrians are hiding in the field to catch Israel coming out of the city. Messengers sent to investigate find the way to Jordan full of garments and vessels cast away in the Syrians' haste, and the people go out and spoil the tents, so the food is sold cheaply exactly as the word said.

The king sets the doubting lord in charge of the gate, and the people trod upon him there and he died, just as the man of God had spoken. The lord saw the plenty with his eyes but did not eat of it, so the word of the Most High fell out to the letter. The trampling in the gate stands as a picture of a crowd stampeding after goods, hating one another over things, and here it became the judgment on a man who doubted the word.

name: Hazael king of Syria
charge: Smothering his master to take the throne, and doing to Israel the evil Elisha wept over
summary: Elisha looked at Hazael and wept, and told him why: he knew the evil he would do to the children of Israel. Hazael said, Is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing? He went home, lied to his master about the prophet's word, and smothered him with a wet cloth the next morning.
offense: Ben-hadad sent Hazael to ask Elisha whether he would recover. Elisha spoke of recovery yet disclosed that the Lord had shown him the king would surely die. He then wept over the violence Hazael would bring upon Israel (2 Kings 8:7-12). Knowledge of an approaching reign did not turn its cruelties into good deeds. Hazael returned with the assurance of recovery but withheld the disclosure of death. The next day he spread a water-soaked cloth over the king's face, killed him, and reigned in his place (2 Kings 8:14-15). The messenger's access to a sick master became the means of taking his throne.
judgment: Hazael afterward struck Israel and reduced its territory (2 Kings 10:32-33). The Lord used Syrian power in chastening Israel, but that use did not place Syria beyond judgment for its violence. Elisha's tears had already distinguished the coming suffering from something to celebrate. Amos charged Damascus with threshing Gilead with iron instruments and pronounced fire upon the house of Hazael and the palaces of Ben-hadad, with Syria carried to Kir (Amos 1:3-5). The house that made others suffer was itself named for overthrow. Being an instrument in another people's punishment did not give its ruler ownership of their lives or immunity from the Lord's reckoning.

verses.text: 7And Elisha came to Damascus; and Ben–hadad the king of Syria was sick; and it was told him, saying, The man of God is come hither. 8And the king said unto Hazael, Take a present in thine hand, and go, meet the man of God, and enquire of the Lord by him, saying, Shall I recover of this disease? 9So Hazael went to meet him, and took a present with him, even of every good thing of Damascus, forty camels’ burden, and came and stood before him, and said, Thy son Ben–hadad king of Syria hath sent me to thee, saying, Shall I recover of this disease? 10And Elisha said unto him, Go, say unto him, Thou mayest certainly recover: howbeit the Lord hath shewed me that he shall surely die.

11And he settled his countenance stedfastly, until he was ashamed: and the man of God wept. 12And Hazael said, Why weepeth my lord? And he answered, Because I know the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel: their strong holds wilt thou set on fire, and their young men wilt thou slay with the sword, and wilt dash their children, and rip up their women with child. 13And Hazael said, But what, is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing? And Elisha answered, The Lord hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria.

14So he departed from Elisha, and came to his master; who said to him, What said Elisha to thee? And he answered, He told me that thou shouldest surely recover. 15And it came to pass on the morrow, that he took a thick cloth, and dipped it in water, and spread it on his face, so that he died: and Hazael reigned in his stead.

entries.commentary: Elisha warns the Shunammite woman whose son he restored to flee the coming seven year famine, and she sojourns in the land of the Philistines. When she returns to appeal to the king for her house and land, Gehazi is at that moment telling the king how Elisha restored a dead body to life. The timing is of the Most High, so the king restores all that was hers and the fruits of the field from the day she left.

Ben-hadad king of Syria, sick, sends Hazael to inquire of Elisha whether he will recover, for the word of a prophet, also called a seer, was precious in those days. Elisha tells Hazael the king may recover but the Most High has shown that he shall surely die, then weeps because he sees the evil Hazael will do to Israel: burning strongholds, slaying young men, and ripping up women with child. Elisha tells Hazael he will be king over Syria, revealing that leadership can discern spirits at work in a man that the man does not see in himself. Hazael returns and smothers the king with a wet cloth and reigns in his place.

Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat begins to reign over Judah and walks in the way of the kings of Israel because the daughter of Ahab was his wife. He does evil in the sight of the Most High, yet Judah is not destroyed for David his servant's sake, according to the promise.

In Jehoram's days Edom revolts from under the hand of Judah and makes a king over itself, breaking the subjection Edom had been under from the days of David and Solomon. This revolt fulfills the word spoken to Esau, that when he gained the dominion he would break the yoke from off his neck, a pattern reaching to Edom's later rise. Jehoram sleeps with his fathers and is buried in the city of David, and Ahaziah his son reigns in his place. -

Ahaziah son of Jehoram begins to reign over Judah and walks in the way of the house of Ahab, being the son-in-law of that house, a picture of the generational curse passed from father to son. Woe is pronounced on those who decree unrighteous decrees and write grievous laws to turn aside the needy from judgment and take away the right from the poor. And shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me, and keep my commandments. charge: Executing the house of Ahab, then keeping the calves of Jeroboam

The word of the Lord came unto Hosea the son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel.

The Lord tells Hosea to go take a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms, for the land has committed great whoredom, departing from the Lord. He took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim, who conceived and bare him a son. He took a whore because it was symbolic of how the people committed spiritual fornication against the Most High.

The Lord tells him to call his name Jezreel, for in a little while he will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu and cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel. At that day he will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.

She conceives again and bears a daughter, named Loruhamah, meaning no more mercy upon the house of Israel, for he will utterly take them away. But he will have mercy upon the house of Judah and save them by the Lord their God, not by bow, nor sword, nor battle, nor horses, nor horsemen.
When she had weaned Loruhamah she conceived and bare a son, named Loammi, meaning ye are not my people and I will not be your God.

Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered, and in the place where it was said they are not my people, there it shall be said they are the sons of the living God. The blacks, Hispanics, and Native Americans are the ones whose number is as the sand of the sea, not the so-called white man that calls himself a Jew. The so-called white people as a whole are the minority; they do not reproduce at the rate that other nations do, especially the children of Israel. Because they cannot keep up with the numbers, they come up with tactics to stop other people from reproducing. That is one sign right there that they are not the people of God, for God's people are as the sand of the sea, not the minority.

Then the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, both the northern and southern kingdoms, and appoint themselves one head, and come up out of the land, for great shall be the day of Jezreel. Azariah, also called Uzziah, begins to reign over Judah and does that which is right in the sight of the Most High as his father Amaziah had done. The high places were not removed, so the people still sacrificed and burned incense there, an incomplete obedience. The Most High smote him so that he was a leper until his death, and he dwelt in a separate house while Jotham his son judged the people. Azariah's fuller history is written elsewhere, and the teacher directs the reader to [2 Chronicles 26](/bible/2-chronicles/26) for a more detailed account of his life and acts. -

Zachariah son of Jeroboam reigns over Israel only six months and does that which is evil, not departing from the sins of Jeroboam. Shallum conspires against Zachariah, smites him before the people, slays him, and reigns in his place. The end of Zachariah fulfills the word spoken to Jehu, that his sons would sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation. -

Shallum reigns a full month in Samaria before Menahem son of Gadi goes up from Tirzah, smites him, and reigns in his stead. Menahem strikes Tiphsah and its coasts because they would not open to him, and he ripped up the women with child, a mark of his cruelty.

Menahem reigns ten years in Samaria and does evil, not departing from the sins of Jeroboam. Pul the king of Assyria comes against the land, and Menahem gives him a thousand talents of silver to confirm the kingdom in his hand. Menahem raises the tribute by exacting fifty shekels of silver from each mighty man of wealth, so the king of Assyria turns back and does not stay in the land.

Pekahiah son of Menahem reigns two years over Israel and does evil, not departing from the sins of Jeroboam. Pekah, a captain of his, conspires against him and smites him in the king's house at Samaria with fifty Gileadites, then reigns in his room. This is a military coup, where a trusted captain kills the king and seizes the throne.

Pekah son of Remaliah reigns twenty years over Israel, the same Pekah spoken of in the book of Isaiah. In his days Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria comes and takes Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali, carrying them captive to Assyria. Hoshea son of Elah conspires against Pekah, smites and slays him, and reigns in his stead.

Jotham son of Uzziah reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem and does that which is right, according to all his father Uzziah had done. Again the high places were not removed, and the people still sacrificed and burned incense there. Jotham builds the higher gate of the house of the Most High. In those days the Most High begins to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.

name: Athaliah
charge: Destroying the seed royal of Judah; usurping the throne
summary: Ahab's daughter, married into Judah's line, saw her son Ahaziah dead at Jehu's hand and murdered all the seed royal to reign herself. One infant, Joash, was hidden in the house of the Lord for six years. In the seventh, Jehoiada the priest brought him out.
offense: When Ahaziah died, Athaliah rose against the royal seed and seized the kingdom. Jehosheba rescued Joash and hid him with his nurse, preserving a child from the destruction (2 Kings 11:1-3). Athaliah's possession of the throne rested upon violence against the house she should have protected. Her reign also belonged to the corruption of worship. Her sons had broken up God's house and devoted its things to Baalim (2 Chronicles 24:7). The seizure of the kingdom and misuse of holy possessions joined the same disregard for what had been entrusted to the royal house.
judgment: In the seventh year Jehoiada revealed the king's son, arranged his protection, and crowned him with the testimony. Athaliah heard the rejoicing and cried treason when she saw him standing in his place (2 Kings 11:4-14). The cry came from the ruler whose own position had been obtained by destroying the succession. Jehoiada ordered her taken outside rather than killed within the Lord's house. She was slain by the way leading to the king's house, and the people broke down Baal's house (2 Kings 11:15-18). The covenant was renewed, the people rejoiced, and the city was quiet. The hidden child outlasted the reign that had sought to erase him.

The covenant was renewed, the people rejoiced, and the city was quiet. The hidden child outlasted the reign that had sought to erase him.

verses.text: 1And when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal. 2But Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king’s sons which were slain; and they hid him, even him and his nurse, in the bedchamber from Athaliah, so that he was not slain. 3And he was with her hid in the house of the Lord six years. And Athaliah did reign over the land.

entries.commentary: When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw her son was dead, she moved to destroy all the royal seed so she could seize the throne. Jehosheba, sister of Ahaziah, took the infant Joash and stole him away from among the king's sons who were being slain, hiding him in the house of the Most High for six years while Athaliah reigned. The rightful king was preserved and concealed the entire time the usurper sat on the throne.

In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest brought the captains together, took an oath of them in the house of the Most High, and showed them the king's son. He commanded them how to guard the king by watches and companies so that the house would not be broken down. The guard was to compass the king round about, every man with his weapon in his hand, and to stay with him as he went out and came in. -
Every man stood armed around the king, and any who came within the ranges was to be slain.

The captains did according to all that Jehoiada commanded, taking their men to the priest. Jehoiada gave the captains King David's spears and shields that were in the temple, and the guard stood every man with his weapons in hand around the king. Then he brought forth the king's son, put the crown upon him, gave him the testimony, anointed him, and the people clapped their hands and said, God save the king. The weapons they carried then were physical; today the weapon of Israel is the scriptures.

Athaliah heard the noise of the guard and the people and came into the temple, and saw the king standing by a pillar as the manner was. She rent her clothes and cried, Treason, treason, but Jehoiada commanded the captains to have her forth outside the ranges. She was not to be slain in the house of the Most High, so they took her out by the way the horses came into the king's house and slew her there.

Jehoiada made a covenant between the Most High, the king, and the people, that they should be the Lord's people. All the people went to the house of Baal, broke down its altars and images, and slew Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. Joash was brought to the throne, the people rejoiced, the city was quiet, and he was seven years old when he began to reign. This same covenant is what happens today: as a person wakes up, repents, keeps the commandments, and comes out of idolatry, they again become the Lord's people.

The inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah, Jehoram's youngest son, king in his stead, for the band of Arabians had slain all the elder sons. Ahaziah was forty and two years old when he began to reign and reigned one year in Jerusalem, and his mother's name was Athaliah the daughter of Omri. He walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly, and the house of Ahab were his counsellors after his father died, to his destruction. This is a warning against being ruled by the wrong counsel: instead of going to the priests and the judges, he went to his mother, and she counselled him into ruin. A woman with a grudge can rule a kingdom through her son, and that is what Athaliah did.

Ahaziah walked after their counsel and went with Jehoram son of Ahab to war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead, where Jehoram was wounded. He went down to see the wounded Jehoram at Jezreel, and the destruction of Ahaziah was of the Most High, for by going he came into the path of Jehu, whom the Most High had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab. That same Jehu who killed the seventy sons of Ahab found the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brethren and slew them, then sought and caught Ahaziah, who was hid in Samaria. They buried Ahaziah for the sake of Jehoshaphat his forefather who sought the Most High with all his heart; but the house of Ahaziah had no power to keep the kingdom, so the wicked king was cut off by the same hand the Most High anointed to avenge Israel.

When Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the seed royal of the house of Judah, killing the king's sons. But Jehoshabeath the daughter of king Jehoram, wife of Jehoiada the priest and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him from among the king's sons that were slain, hiding him and his nurse in a bedchamber. She hid the child in the house of God six years while Athaliah reigned over the land, showing that Athaliah was ruling in the position of the son she had lost. Athaliah did not carry out this slaughter alone; she had weak men helping her run over everything, which is how she seized and held the throne.

In the seventh year Jehoiada strengthened himself and took the captains of hundreds into covenant with him, and they gathered the Levites and the chief of the fathers out of all the cities of Judah to Jerusalem. The congregation made a covenant with the king in the house of God, and Jehoiada declared that the king's son should reign, as the Most High had said of the sons of David. He set his plan: a third part of the priests and Levites to keep the doors, a third at the king's house, and a third at the gate of the foundation, with all the people in the courts. None but the priests and ministering Levites were to enter the house of the Most High, and the Levites were to compass the king round about, every man with his weapon, and put to death any who forced their way in.

The Levites and all Judah did according to all Jehoiada commanded, each man keeping his company, for Jehoiada did not dismiss the courses of the Levites but kept them at their work with security added for the king. Jehoiada delivered to the captains the spears and shields that had been king David's, kept in the house of God, and set every man with his weapon from one side of the temple to the other, round about the king. They brought out the king's son, put the crown upon him, gave him the testimony, and made him king, and Jehoiada and his sons anointed him and said, God save the king. This was done by the proper custom: a priest anoints the king, as Samuel the priest anointed Saul and then David; so Jehoiada the priest anointed Joash.

When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king, she came into the house of the Most High and saw the king standing at his pillar with the princes, trumpets, and singers rejoicing. She rent her clothes and cried, Treason, treason, but her cry came too late, for the covenant was already made and the true king was crowned. Jehoiada commanded the captains to have her forth from the ranges and to slay any that followed her, but not to slay her in the house of the Most High. They laid hands on her, brought her to the entering of the horse gate by the king's house, and slew her there, ending the reign of the woman who had killed the seed royal.

Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king, that they should be the Most High's people, and the people went to the house of Baal, broke it down, brake its altars and images, and slew Mattan the priest of Baal. Jehoiada appointed the officers of the house of the Most High by the hand of the priests and Levites whom David had distributed, to offer burnt offerings with rejoicing and singing as ordained by David. He set the porters at the gates so that none unclean in anything should enter, then brought the king down and set him upon the throne of the kingdom, and the people rejoiced and the city was quiet. Before a king is set in his position he is under tutors and governors; young Joash was king in rank, yet he was still a learner under Jehoiada, for even kings had to be taught. Athaliah had no place ruling Israel; being the king's mother did not make her the ruler. -

Joash was seven years old when he began to reign and reigned forty years in Jerusalem, and his mother's name was Zibiah of Beersheba. Joash did that which was right in the sight of the Most High all the days of Jehoiada the priest, because that is what he was taught. He had seen the wicked men of Israel try to kill him, so he followed the man who showed him the ropes; Jehoiada taught him how to be a righteous king and keep the commandments. A king had a job to do and could not simply sit back; he had a kingdom to watch over, and he had the priests there to help him do it.

Joash was minded to repair the house of the Most High and gathered the priests and Levites, telling them to go to the cities of Judah and gather money of all Israel to repair the house from year to year, and to hasten the matter. The Levites did not hasten it, so the king called Jehoiada the chief and asked why he had not required of the Levites the collection appointed by Moses for the tabernacle of witness. Money was needed because Israel did not let the workmen labor for nothing; when men did the jobs they were paid, for the workman is worthy of his hire, and we dealt righteously with our people. The sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken up the house of God and bestowed all its dedicated things upon Baalim, which is why so much repair was needed.

At the king's commandment they made a chest and set it at the gate of the house of the Most High, and made a proclamation to bring in the collection Moses laid upon Israel in the wilderness, and the princes and people rejoiced and cast in until they made an end. Day by day the king's scribe and the high priest's officer emptied the chest and gathered money in abundance, and the king and Jehoiada gave it to those who did the work, hiring masons, carpenters, and workers of iron and brass. Money was a defense here because it paid the skilled brothers who got the temple work done; we must deal righteously with our people today, treating a brother's business as a place to help the family and the body. Not everyone was given the same task; masons, carpenters, and metalworkers each had their charge, and every man had to listen to a manager, for business requires order and submission to authority. The workmen perfected the work and set the house of God in its state, then brought the rest of the money to make vessels of gold and silver to minister and offer with, and they offered burnt offerings continually all the days of Jehoiada. -

Jehoiada waxed old and was full of days and died, being a hundred and thirty years old at his death. They buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel both toward the Most High and toward his house. That a priest was buried among the kings shows how much respect and diligence this man had earned; his faithfulness set him alongside the rulers of the land.

After the death of Jehoiada the princes of Judah came and made obeisance to the king, and the king hearkened to them. They left the house of the Most High and served groves and idols, and wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for their trespass. The Most High sent prophets to bring them again unto Him, and they testified against them, but the people would not give ear. As soon as Jehoiada died, Israel went off again, because the king was weak and started listening to those who served other gods; this teaches the lesson that lust drives Israel to idolatry, and that the Most High will always send prophets to warn them.

The spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, who stood above the people and asked why they transgressed the commandments so that they could not prosper, telling them that because they had forsaken the Most High, He had also forsaken them. They conspired against Zechariah and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king, in the court of the house of the Most High. When the prophet came to correct the king, the king had him killed for telling him the truth; this is the same spirit our people show when a laborer brings the medicine and is met with violence. As Zechariah died he said, The Most High look upon it and require it. He prayed for vengeance on his murderer, and this is scripture; it is right to pray for the downfall of enemies who do much wickedness, even while we pray for the recovery and repentance of our own people. -

At the end of the year the host of Syria came up against Joash, destroyed the princes of the people, and sent the spoil to the king of Damascus. The Syrians came with a small company, yet the Most High delivered a very great host of Judah into their hand, because Judah had forsaken the Most High God of their fathers; so judgment was executed on Joash for killing Zechariah. They left Joash in great diseases, and his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada and slew him on his bed, and he was buried in the city of David but not in the sepulchres of the kings. Joash began by doing right under Jehoiada's guidance, repairing the house and clearing out the idols, but none of that was remembered in the end because of the wickedness he turned to after being warned. Amaziah his son reigned in his stead; the fuller record of Joash is written in the story of the book of the kings. -

Elisha warns the Shunammite woman whose son he restored to flee the coming seven year famine, and she sojourns in the land of the Philistines. When she returns to appeal to the king for her house and land, Gehazi is at that moment telling the king how Elisha restored a dead body to life. The timing is of the Most High, so the king restores all that was hers and the fruits of the field from the day she left.

Ben-hadad king of Syria, sick, sends Hazael to inquire of Elisha whether he will recover, for the word of a prophet, also called a seer, was precious in those days. Elisha tells Hazael the king may recover but the Most High has shown that he shall surely die, then weeps because he sees the evil Hazael will do to Israel: burning strongholds, slaying young men, and ripping up women with child. Elisha tells Hazael he will be king over Syria, revealing that leadership can discern spirits at work in a man that the man does not see in himself. Hazael returns and smothers the king with a wet cloth and reigns in his place.

Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat begins to reign over Judah and walks in the way of the kings of Israel because the daughter of Ahab was his wife. He does evil in the sight of the Most High, yet Judah is not destroyed for David his servant's sake, according to the promise.

In Jehoram's days Edom revolts from under the hand of Judah and makes a king over itself, breaking the subjection Edom had been under from the days of David and Solomon. This revolt fulfills the word spoken to Esau, that when he gained the dominion he would break the yoke from off his neck, a pattern reaching to Edom's later rise. Jehoram sleeps with his fathers and is buried in the city of David, and Ahaziah his son reigns in his place. -

Ahaziah son of Jehoram begins to reign over Judah and walks in the way of the house of Ahab, being the son-in-law of that house, a picture of the generational curse passed from father to son. He goes with Jehoram son of Ahab to war against Hazael king of Syria, and the Syrians wound Jehoram at Ramah. Jehoram returns to Jezreel to be healed, and Ahaziah goes down to see him, setting the stage for both kings to meet Jehu's judgment.

name: Jeroboam the son of Joash
charge: Doing evil in the sight of the Lord; not departing from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat
summary: Jeroboam the son of Joash reigned forty-one years over Israel and restored the coast from Hamath to the sea of the plain, as the Lord had spoken by Jonah the prophet. The Lord saw that Israel’s affliction was bitter and saved them by his hand, yet Jeroboam did evil and departed not from Jeroboam’s sins.
offense: Jeroboam the son of Joash began to reign in the fifteenth year of Amaziah and reigned forty-one years in Samaria. He did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord: he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin (2 Kings 14:23–24). The longest reign of any northern king carried no reform with it. He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the Lord spoken by the hand of his servant Jonah the son of Amittai (2 Kings 14:25). The restoration was accomplished through him, yet it was the Lord’s doing, because the Lord saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter: there was not any shut up, nor any left, nor any helper for Israel (2 Kings 14:26).
judgment: The Lord said not that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven but saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash (2 Kings 14:27). The deliverance was not because of Jeroboam’s righteousness but because of the Lord’s mercy toward His afflicted people. Jeroboam slept with his fathers, and Zechariah his son reigned in his stead (2 Kings 14:29). The prosperity of his reign did not secure his house: Zechariah was slain after six months, fulfilling the word that Jehu’s house would sit on the throne unto the fourth generation (2 Kings 15:12). The kingdom was saved through an evil king and then taken from his descendants according to a limit already spoken.

verses.text: 23In the fifteenth year of Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel began to reign in Samaria, and reigned forty and one years. 24And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord: he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin. 25He restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the Lord God of Israel, which he spake by the hand of his servant Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gath–hepher. 26For the Lord saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter: for there was not any shut up, nor any left, nor any helper for Israel. 27And the Lord said not that he would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven: but he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash. 28Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, and all that he did, and his might, how he warred, and how he recovered Damascus, and Hamath, which belonged to Judah, for Israel, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? 29And Jeroboam slept with his fathers, even with the kings of Israel; and Zachariah his son reigned in his stead.

entries.commentary: Amaziah the son of Joash began to reign over Judah at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. He did that which was right in the sight of the Most High, yet not like David his father, meaning he did not serve with a perfect heart. When the kingdom was confirmed, he slew the servants who had killed his father, but did not slay their children, according to the law of Moses that every man is put to death for his own sin. -
Amaziah slew ten thousand of Edom in the valley of salt and took Selah by war, calling its name Joktheel unto this day.

Amaziah sent to Jehoash king of Israel to face one another in battle, and Jehoash answered with the parable of the thistle and the cedar, warning him to stay home lest he fall. Amaziah would not hear, so the two faced one another at Bethshemesh, and Judah was put to the worse before Israel and fled. Jehoash broke down the wall of Jerusalem, took the gold, silver, and vessels from the house of the Most High and the king's house, took hostages, and returned to Samaria.

Jehoash slept with his fathers and Jeroboam his son reigned in his place. Amaziah lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash, and a conspiracy was made against him in Jerusalem so that he fled to Lachish and was slain there. The people took Azariah, sixteen years old, and made him king in the place of his father Amaziah.

Jeroboam the son of Joash, Jeroboam II, began to reign over Israel and reigned forty-one years, doing evil and not departing from the sins of the first Jeroboam. He restored the coast of Israel according to the word spoken by Jonah the son of Amittai, for the Most High saw the bitter affliction of Israel and would not blot out their name. The Most High saved them by the hand of Jeroboam, who recovered Damascus and Hamath, and when he slept with his fathers Zechariah his son reigned in his place. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

name: Hosea the prophet
charge: Obeying the Lord’s command to take a wife of whoredoms as a sign; prophesying Israel’s scattering and restoration
summary: The word of the Lord came to Hosea in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, and of Jeroboam the son of Joash. He was commanded to marry Gomer, a wife of whoredoms, as a living sign of how Israel committed spiritual fornication against the Lord. Three children bore prophetic names—Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah, Lo-ammi—yet the promise followed: the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea.
offense: The Lord told Hosea to go take a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms, for the land had committed great whoredom, departing from the Lord. So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim (Hosea 1:2–3). The prophet’s own household became the picture of the nation’s unfaithfulness. Three children were born, each named by the Lord’s word. Jezreel: the Lord would avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu and cause to cease the kingdom of Israel (Hosea 1:4). Lo-ruhamah: the Lord would no more have mercy upon the house of Israel but utterly take them away (Hosea 1:6). Lo-ammi: ye are not my people and I will not be your God (Hosea 1:9). The names declared scattering, the withdrawal of mercy, and the severing of the covenant. Yet the promise followed: the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered, and in the place where it was said, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said, Ye are the sons of the living God (Hosea 1:10). They would be gathered under one head (Hosea 1:11).
judgment: The Lord commanded Hosea again to love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the Lord toward the children of Israel. He bought her for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley and told her to abide many days (Hosea 3:1–3). For the children of Israel shall abide many days without a king, without a prince, without a sacrifice, without an image, without an ephod, and without teraphim. Afterward shall the children of Israel return and seek the Lord their God, and David their king, and shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the latter days (Hosea 3:4–5). The long dispersion would end in a return.

name: Menahem king of Israel
charge: Ripping up the women with child at Tiphsah, and buying Assyria with money exacted from Israel
summary: Menahem came up from Tirzah, killed Shallum, and took the throne. When Tiphsah would not open to him he smote it and ripped up all the women therein that were with child. He then paid Pul a thousand talents of silver, exacted from the wealthy of Israel, to confirm the kingdom in his hand — and died in his bed.
offense: Menahem struck Tiphsah because it would not open to him and ripped up its pregnant women (2 Kings 15:16). The refusal of entry became an occasion for cruelty against those least able to resist. His rise did not bring a departure from Jeroboam's sins; he continued in them throughout his reign (2 Kings 15:17-18). When Pul of Assyria came, Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver to confirm the kingdom in his hand. He exacted the money from Israel's wealthy men (2 Kings 15:19-20). The people paid for the foreign support by which their ruler sought to secure his own position.
judgment: Assyria withdrew, and Menahem died after a ten-year reign, with Pekahiah succeeding him (2 Kings 15:20-22). No separate personal penalty is recorded against him. The successful payment must not be mistaken for a judgment declaring his cruelty righteous. His son's reign lasted two years before Pekah killed him. Further Assyrian conquest and deportation followed in Pekah's days (2 Kings 15:23-29). The support purchased for Menahem did not establish lasting security for the house or nation. He had obtained time on the throne without addressing the sin that left Israel exposed to further overthrow.
